en: The Commentary on the Mahāyāna by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamata under imperial decree during the Yao Qin dynasty. Volume One.
I pay homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, To the Dharma-treasury realized by that Awakening,
And to the Great Beings who composed the treatises, As well as the assembly of all noble sages.
Desiring to open the gate of the donor’s merit, And to provisionally reveal the stages of the path, [I compose this work].
To benefit all sentient beings, I divide and repay my debt of gratitude to my teacher.
The commentary states:

I now compose this treatise to provide a further explanation of the Mahāyāna, desiring to demonstrate that the essence of my own teacher is profoundly profound and his ultimate realization is subtle and wondrous; yet, for those who have not attained correct realization and have not emerged from erroneous practices, it remains vast and obscure, truly beyond the reach of the eye, having no starting point, and transcending the realm of thought.

Alternatively, it is because he wishes to open the gate of the sudden teaching for sentient beings of both sharp and dull faculties, and to reveal the stages of gradual progress, so that they may enter into the profound principle that is expounded.
Or, it is because the teacher’s nurturing influence was exceedingly deep and weighty; thus, he divided [the work] into small sections as a way of repaying his great debt of gratitude to the teacher.
Alternatively, it may be because he secretly observed that future sentient beings would give rise to hundreds of thousands of disputes to destroy the tenets of their treatises;
or because he personally heard [the Buddha's] intention (*āśaya*).
Due to such causes and conditions as these, it was necessary to compose this treatise.
The fundamental categories have already been explained; next, the classifications of the treatises will be discussed.
How many are there in number?
By how many treatises are they subsumed?
In what are the Mahāyāna treatises subsumed?
The verse says:
The ninety-one thousand sections are, in total, subsumed within ten treatises.
Mahāla, Vaddhi, Ussama, Jatta, Vaṇatissa, Abhaya, Vamma, Hoha, Masana, and Kaṃbamaka-saṅgha.
The treatise states:
In total, the various treatises compiled throughout the entire dispensation number one hundred thousand and nine thousand sections.
These treatises are collectively subsumed under ten categories.

What are the ten? First is the Mākāla treatise; second is the Bāditi treatise; third is the Uśmasa treatise; fourth is the Jātaka treatise; fifth is the Vānatisa treatise; sixth is the Ābuddhi treatise; seventh is the Varmma treatise; eighth is the Hūhaka treatise; ninth is the Maṃsana treatise; tenth is the Kambava treatise. These are called the ten.
The Mahāyāna-śāstra is subsumed within the *Yìrù lùn* (Treatise on the Wish-Fulfilling Gem).
How many treatises did the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa compose? How many words and how many meanings do they contain?
Under what category is the Mahāyāna-śāstra subsumed?
The verse says:
In total there are one hundred sections, consisting of ninety-nine types of texts.
Comprising ten types of meaning, these are contained within this precious volume of treatises.
The commentary states:

Among the one hundred treatises composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, ninety-nine varieties are subsumed under the category of "Floral Text Treatises" (*puṣpavāda-śāstra*), while the remaining ten treatises are subsumed under the category of "Meaning-Treatises" (*arthavāda-śāstra*).
Regarding this treatise, the *Daśadharmaka-śāstra*, what are its titles?
And are the explanations provided therein the same or different?
The verse says:
The *Pien-man* and the *Kuei-chen*, the *Chung-tsang* and the *Miao-miao*,
the *He-i* and the *San-mei*, the *Ch'ing-ching* and the *Pen-yüan-lun*,
the *Hsüan-li* and the *Ch'i-hsin-lun*: these establish the identical single characteristic.

The Treatise says: What are the ten? First, the Discourse on the Universal Pervasion of the Single Mind; second, the Discourse on Merging the Conventional to Return to the Ultimate; third, the Discourse on the Treasury within the Dharma-realm; fourth, the Discourse on the Secret and Subtle; fifth, the Discourse on the Unification of All Lives; sixth, the Discourse on True Suchness Samādhi; seventh, the Discourse on the Purity of the Nature of Mind; eighth, the Discourse on the Immovable Source; ninth, the Discourse on the Profound and Mysterious Principle; tenth, the Discourse on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna. These are called the ten.
Although these ten treatises differ in number, their systematic presentation is identical in kind.
Having explained the distinctions among the treatises, I shall next explain the distinctions among the Piṭakas.
How many collections (piṭaka) are there?
By how many collections are they subsumed?
And by which [collection] is the Mahāyāna-śāstra subsumed?
The verse says:
Either fifty-one *piṭakas*, or simply ten as in the sūtras;
all are subsumed within the three *piṭakas*, while the treatises (*śāstra*) are either general or specific.
The Commentary states:
The fifty-one [factors] are established because they distinguish cause and effect, manifest merit, and guide practitioners.
As it is said in the *Vajra Sūtra*:
The Buddha addressed the Son of the Buddha:
"I shall, for your sake, with unimpeded speech, proclaim and reveal the fifty treasuries of causes and the single treasury of the fruit.
Thus, there may be ten treasuries.
What are the ten? First, there is the establishment of a single treasury that comprehensively subsumes all dharmas, namely, the Dharma-realm Dharma-wheel Treasury (*dharmadhātu-dharmacakra-piṭaka*).
In the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
All the speech and sounds of all sentient beings are encompassed by the sound of the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma.
Second, two collections (piṭaka) are established to comprehensively subsume all dharmas, namely the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* states as follows:
"Although the gateways to the Dharma are boundless, they do not transcend two kinds of treasuries.
Thirdly, the three treasuries are established to comprehensively subsume all phenomena, which includes the addition of the Tathāgatagarbha.
The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states as follows:

"All Buddhas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, shall proclaim only the Dharma-piṭaka of the Śrāvakas, the Dharma-piṭaka of the Bodhisattvas, and the Dharma-piṭaka of the Tathāgatas; there is no other path."
Fourth, the establishment of the four collections (*piṭaka*) to comprehensively subsume all phenomena, namely by adding the *pudgalapiṭaka*.
As it is said in the *Mārgavarga-sūtra*:
"O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you."

The treasury of benevolence, the treasury of righteousness, the treasury of propriety, the treasury of wisdom, and the treasury of faith; as well as the treasury of the śrāvakas, the treasury of the bodhisattvas, and the treasury of the Dharma of Great Enlightenment. Why is this so?

Because all practitioners follow a gradual progression toward increasingly superior stages, fifth, the five treasuries (*pañcapiṭaka*) are established to comprehensively subsume all phenomena; that is, the *Devapiṭaka* is added.
As it is said in the *Sūtra on the Son of Heaven’s Seal*:
The Buddha told Ya-lun:

"The emptiness of the ineffable pure retribution cannot be described; it is for the sake of the great assembly that I extensively proclaim the Treasury of Purity, the Treasury of Humanity, the Treasuries of the Two Vehicles, and the Great Enlightenment Dharma-Treasury of all Buddhas."
Sixth, the establishment of the six treasuries (*ṣaḍ-piṭaka*) which comprehensively subsume all phenomena, namely the addition of the *Naraka-piṭaka*.
In the *Bhaya-sūtra*, it is stated:
"Seated unmoving, I have analytically expounded eighty-four thousand *naraka-piṭakas*," because of the five kinds of treasuries previously mentioned.
Seventh, the establishment of seven treasuries (*piṭaka*) that collectively encompass all phenomena, namely by adding the *Māragautama-piṭaka*.
In the *Bam-po* Sūtra it is said:

"I now speak these words of truth for the great assembly of one hundred million, seventy-three thousand [beings], including the *Bam-po* and others, to distinguish and proclaim fifty-one thousand three hundred and two types of *piṭakas* concerning the realm of spirits and ghosts (*bhūta-yoni*), because of the six types of treasuries previously mentioned."
Eighth, the establishment of eight treasuries (*piṭaka*) that comprehensively encompass all dharmas, namely by adding the *Kambadhānabha* treasury.
In the *Nāgarāja-sūtra*, it is stated:

"The Nāga King Nanda posed eight thousand questions to the Tathāgata; the Buddha then opened ten billion treasuries of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), as previously described regarding the seven kinds of treasuries."
Ninth, the establishment of the nine treasuries (*navakośa*) which comprehensively subsume all phenomena, namely by adding the Treasury of the Receptacle World (*bhājanaloka-kośa*).
In the *Lokadhātu-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the tree deity, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have said.
If you wish to hear it, I shall now explain for you in detail the treasury upon which [the teachings] rely, according to the eight kinds of treasuries previously mentioned.”
Tenth, the establishment of ten *piṭakas* that comprehensively subsume all phenomena, namely by adding the *saṃkīrṇa-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Piṭaka).
In the *Ghoṣānuvartaka-sūtra*, it is stated:
"I now reveal eight kinds of miscellaneous collections (*saṃkīrṇa-piṭaka*), because of the nine kinds of collections previously mentioned."
These are called the ten.
In this way, all these treasuries collectively subsume one billion eight hundred million dharma-treasuries.
Alternatively, the fundamental Tripiṭaka may subsume the ten treasuries.
What are the three? First, the Sūtra Piṭaka; second, the Vinaya Piṭaka; third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka. These are called the three.
The Mahāyāna-śāstra is either subsumed within the various Piṭakas or subsumed solely within the Abhidharma-piṭaka; therefore, the verse says: "either general or specific.
"General" means collectively inclusive, while "specific" means distinctively differentiated.
Because it upholds the dharmas of practice according to their application without loss, it is established as being called a "piṭaka" (storehouse).
Having explained the distinctions among the piṭakas, I shall next explain the distinctions among the sūtras.
How many categories of sūtras are there?
By how many sūtras are they subsumed?
Upon which sūtras does this Mahāyāna śāstra rely now?
The verse says:
In total, numbering one hundred lakṣas, they are subsumed within the twelve divisions of the scriptures:
the Sūtra, the Geya, and the Vyākaraṇa;
Gāthā, udāna, as well as nidāna, avadāna-sūtra, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, and adbhutadharma.
The *Upadeśa-sūtras* are categorized either generally or specifically.
The treatise states:
"In total, there are ten billion collections of various sūtras from throughout the Buddha’s lifetime; all such sūtras are subsumed within the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*)."

What are the twelve? First, Sūtra; second, Geya; third, Vyākaraṇa; fourth, Gāthā; fifth, Udāna; sixth, Nidāna; seventh, Avadāna; eighth, Itivṛttaka; ninth, Jātaka; tenth, Vaipulya; eleventh, Adbhutadharma; twelfth, Upadeśa. These are called the twelve.
The fundamental sūtras upon which the Mahāyāna-śāstra relies are either general or specific.
"General" means universally applicable; "specific" means distinctively differentiated.
Since the text of the Mahāyāna-śāstra is narrow, its phrases few, and extremely minute, why does it take as its basis the ocean of immeasurable and boundless sūtras?
As in the case of the *Vasiṣṭha-gāthā* and as in the case of the *Sātireka-stotra*, there is therefore no fault.
How many other sūtras serving as the basis [for this] are there?
What are their names? How many associates does each have?
The verse says:
In total there are one hundred sūtras; the *Prabhāsa*, the *Mahābodhi*, and so forth—each of the first fifty contains one hundred [verses], while each of the latter fifty contains one thousand.
The treatise states:
The Mahāyāna-śāstra has one hundred distinct sūtras upon which it relies.
What are these one hundred?
First, the *Prabhāsa-mahābodhi-sūtra*; second, the *Gambhīra-yukti-anuvartana-sūtra*; third, the *Vajra-*.

The *Caryā-bhūmi-sūtra* as the ninety-ninth, the *Anupasaṃhita-guṇa-sūtra* as the hundredth,
and the *Mahāsattva-jñāna-megha-sūtra* as the one hundred and first— these are called the "One Hundred."
Thus, there are one hundred such sūtras as retinues; according to their sequence, the first halves each contain one hundred [verses] and the second halves each contain one thousand.
The titles of the sūtras are cited here to correspond with the structural framework of the treatise; these shall be explained and elucidated in accordance with the text below.
The distinctions among the sūtras have already been explained; next, we shall discuss the person who composed this work.
How many different versions of the sūtra are there?
Under which category does the Master Aśvaghoṣa fall now?
The verse says:
In total, there are six "Horse-Neighing" [Sūtras], because the sūtras present different accounts;
yet, because they respond according to the capacities of beings, there is no fault of contradiction.
The treatise says:
Generally, when collecting the various diverse passages from all the sūtras of one lifetime, there are six types in total. What are these six?
First, in the Mahāyāna *Mūla-dharma-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:

When the Unsurpassed Honored One of Great Enlightenment spoke on the conditions for entering *nirvāṇa*, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet with palms joined in reverence, and addressed the World-Honored Buddha in verse:
“O Unsurpassed Honored One, whose great compassion is fulfilled, Who has perfected the myriad practices throughout an ocean of boundless kalpas.”
Out of compassion for the multitude of living beings, the Buddha himself has declared that he enters nirvana;
we and the entire great assembly are left in darkness, our spirits bewildered and lost.
Even the World-Honored One, whose great compassion was fully perfected, abandoned his own children and others to go to another realm;
how much more so for me, whose compassion is not yet perfected—when following the Buddha to another realm, who would slander me?
At that time, having spoken these verses, Aśvaghoṣa beheld the Buddha’s eyes and passed away peacefully.
Second, in the *Nirmāṇaguṇa-sūtra*, it is said as follows:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aśvaghoṣa, saying:

“More than three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, you shall receive my empowering power and, through various skillful means, bring benefit, peace, and happiness to sentient beings of the final age.”
"If I do not exert my power, you will be unable to do so yourself.
Third, it is stated in the Mahāmāyā Sūtra:
"Six hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, ninety-six kinds of heterodox teachers will compete to promote their false views and destroy the Buddha-dharma."
There was a bhikṣu named Aśvaghoṣa who was skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma and subdued all the various non-Buddhists.
Fourth, it is stated in the *Nityatā-samādhi-sūtra*:

"Eight hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be a wise man named Aśvaghoṣa; whether among the assemblies of non-Buddhists or those of the Buddha’s followers, he will refute the various non-Buddhists and establish the Buddha-dharma."
Fifth, the *Maṇiviśuddha-sūtra* states:
"More than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa appeared in the world, protecting the True Dharma and establishing the banner of the Buddha."
Sixth, the *Sūtra of the King of the Supreme Crown* states:

On the seventeenth day after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Karṇa Kauśika who transformed his body into that of a great nāga king. He manifested eighty-six thousand heads and eighty-six thousand tongues, simultaneously posing eighty-six thousand contradictory questions and challenges to the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata then provided threefold responses to resolve all those difficulties.
Thereupon, the Dragon King again posed ten successive questions to the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata provided a hundredfold response, explaining away every difficulty raised by him.
When the questions and answers were thus concluded, the Buddha addressed the Dragon King, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
The Śramaṇa Aśvaghoṣa, for the sake of protecting the city of the Dharma, establishes the Buddha-dharma by means of the characteristic of destruction.
Be patient, be patient! Always cultivate in this way, always act in this way; do not travel in a limited manner, but travel everywhere.

Thereupon, the Dragon King cast off his original form and the characteristics of an animal; before the Unsurpassed Honored One, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and, with an expression of joy, addressed the World-Honored Buddha in verse:
“Excellent, excellent are these words, Which have entered my ears.
Whether they be false or real, or whether they be from yourself— In my heart, there is the utmost doubt.”
I am not the body of an animal, nor am I among the ranks of non-Buddhists;
yet I praise transformation as birth, manifesting such forms through change.
The World-Honored One knows me as clearly as a mirror: that I have entered into this realm.
"Having emerged from other worlds, / You shall travel everywhere as taught.
At that time, after Aśvaghoṣa had spoken this verse, he entered a quiet chamber as if entering meditative absorption.
These are called the six.
Thus, these various sūtras each present their teachings separately; appearing in response to the capacities of beings, they possess no fault of contradiction.
At what stage of realization was the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa?
In which city was he born?
For what reason did Aśvaghoṣa [arise]?
The verse says:
This Buddha of Great Radiance appeared in Western India during the stage of Immovability; he was given his name based on the past.
The commentary states:
As for Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa: if one defines him by his ultimate essence, he is the Buddha Mahāprabha; if one discusses his causal stage, he is a Bodhisattva dwelling in the eighth bhūmi.
He was born in Western India; Loka was his father and Guṇa was his mother, and they were born together to bring benefit to all.

In a past age, there was a great king named Cakrānta who possessed a thousand white birds, all of which had beautiful voices. If these birds uttered their songs, the king’s merit increased; if they did not utter their songs, the king’s merit diminished.
Thus, whenever these birds see a white horse, they immediately utter their cries; when they do not see one, they never sound their voices.
At that time, the Great King searched everywhere for a white horse but could find none all day long, and he spoke these words:

"If these birds were to cry out upon seeing the followers of the non-Buddhist paths, it would mean those paths have utterly destroyed the Buddha's teachings and are now alone held in honor and faith."
"If this bird were to cry out as a disciple of the Buddha, it would utterly destroy the teachings of the outsiders and alone be honored and believed.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, employing his supernormal powers, manifested a thousand white horses and made a thousand white birds cry out, thereby upholding and flourishing the True Dharma so that it would not be severed. For this reason, the World-Honored One is named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Cry).
Having already explained the specific characteristics of the person, I shall next recite the root text and provide its commentary.
The root text says:
I take refuge in those who pervade the ten directions, The most excellent ones, whose activity is all-encompassing wisdom.
"Unimpeded mastery over form, the Great Compassionate Savior of the World.
The commentary states:
Within this single verse, there are two gates.
What are these two? First is the gate that universally encompasses the life-faculties of all sentient beings; second is the gate of turning toward the perfection of Great Enlightenment.

As for the gate of universal encompassment, it universally gathers the life-faculties of all sentient beings within all worlds of the ten directions, just as one's own original life extends throughout the ten directions.

Regarding those who take refuge: because they employ such multitudes of lives to enter into a covenant with the one who is fully endowed with great compassion, they are as originally described—those who take refuge in the Supreme One of Victorious Action, the Omniscient One, whose form is unimpeded and sovereign, the Savior of the World, and the Great Compassionate One.
How many virtues does the Master of Treatises cite to praise the Great Awakened Honored One?
What are their respective characteristics?
The verse says:
In total there are eighty-four thousand, consisting of forty-eight kinds of qualities;
the most excellent [qualities] and so forth each number ten, the unimpeded knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) each number four,
and [the remaining] eighty-four thousand arise from the distinctions among the marks of physical form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*).
"Though his merits are immeasurable, they ultimately do not exceed these numbers.
The treatise says:
Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa has here enumerated in total eighty-four thousand and forty-eight kinds of merit to pay homage to and praise the Unsurpassed Greatly Awakened One.

Although the categories of pure merit within the state of the fulfillment of Buddhahood are immeasurable and boundless, they ultimately do not exceed this numerical scope; therefore, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa offers praise by way of their general characteristics.
What are the eighty-four thousand merits?
They are formed as eighty-four thousand due to the distinctions among the characteristics of form (*rūpa*). What are the forty?
The supreme activities are each tenfold, thus totaling forty.
What are the eight? Wisdom and the unimpeded knowledges each have four types, thus making eight.
What are the ten supremacies?
First is the supremacy of transcendence, because it is far removed from the stages of the two vehicles;
second is the supremacy of renunciation, because it is forever free from the realms of the three worlds.
Third, it is supreme in its antidote, for it suddenly severs the four stages of abiding;
fourth, it is supreme in its revulsion, for it has already passed beyond the village of the five aggregates;
fifth, it is supreme in its detachment from craving, for it is forever parted from the diverging paths of the six realms.
Sixth, his majesty and virtue are supreme, for he has triumphed over the seven armies of evil;
seventh, his host of soldiers is supreme, for they have utterly destroyed the forest of the eight heterodoxies;
eighth, his sword of wisdom is supreme, for it decisively severs the fetters of the nine knots.
Ninth is the supremacy of liberation, because of having severed the ropes of the ten envelopments;
tenth is the supremacy of valor, because of having subdued the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths.
These are called the ten "supremes," which are the ten kinds of foremost qualities within the sūtras.
What are the ten "excellences"?
First is excellence of power, because he is fully endowed with the ten powers.
Second is the excellence of fearlessness, because he is fully endowed with the four fearlessnesses;
third is the excellence of the unshared qualities, because he is fully endowed with the eighteen unshared dharmas;
fourth is the excellence of the factors of enlightenment, because he is fully endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Fifth is the excellence of transformation, because he is fully endowed with hundreds of thousands of kinds of transformations;
sixth is the excellence of vocal sound, because he is fully endowed with eighty-eight kinds of Brahma-voices;
seventh is the excellence of physical majesty, because he is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Eighth is the excellence of auspiciousness, because merit and roots of goodness arise and increase wherever his sphere of activity is established;
ninth is the excellence of rarity, because he alone is uniquely supreme within the three realms;
tenth is the excellence of the dwelling place, because the palace where he resides is adorned with ninety-eight thousand subtle, wondrous, and perfect features.
These are called the ten excellences, the ten kinds of preeminence within the sūtras.
What are the ten types of karma?
First is spontaneous karma, because that which is performed is characterized by mastery.
Second is the activity of equality, because there is no distinction in the benefit provided through teaching and transformation;
third is the activity of correspondence, because it manifests according to the capacities of beings;
fourth is the activity of fulfillment, because it brings to completion the two provisions of merit and wisdom.
Fifth is inexhaustible karma, because it is without limit;
sixth is co-arising karma, because one undergoes birth according to the realms of existence;
seventh is unattached karma, because one is free from worldly entanglements like a lotus flower.
Eighth is the activity of reliance, for it serves as a place of refuge like the great earth;
ninth is the activity of insatiability, for it gathers in sentient beings without end like the great ocean;
tenth is the activity of thorough penetration, for it is without obstruction like space.
These are called the ten karmas, which constitute the ten types of functions within the sūtras.
What are the ten pervasions?

First is the pervasion of the faculties (*indriya-pervasion*): because each and every one of the Buddha’s material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) individually pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Second is the pervasiveness of consciousness, because the Buddha’s various mental cognitions reach everywhere;
third is the pervasiveness of the objective realm, because that which is perceived by perfect wisdom has no boundaries;
fourth is the pervasiveness of lifespan, because it is inconceivable.
Fifth is pervasiveness of retinue, because it cannot be measured;
sixth is pervasiveness of merit, because each individual merit is equal to the realm of empty space;
seventh is pervasiveness of compassion, because it is without discrimination.
Eighth is the pervasiveness of speech, because the Buddha’s vocal sounds reach everywhere;
ninth is the pervasiveness of realization, because there is nothing he does not fathom;
tenth is the incomparable pervasiveness, because there is no one equal to him.
These are called the ten pervasions, which are the ten kinds of universal pervasiveness within the sūtras.
What are the four knowledges?
First is the knowledge of the inexhaustible treasury of radiance, because it can give birth to one billion one hundred million gates of wisdom.
Second is the wisdom of one flavor and one characteristic, because it penetrates all dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges as being without distinction;
third is the wisdom of boundless great compassion, because it manifests a single transformation that pervades all worlds throughout the ten directions;
fourth is the wisdom of unconditioned quiescence, because it is far removed from all conditioned activities and karma.
These are called the four knowledges, the four kinds of perfected knowledge within the sūtras.
What are the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?
First is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), because it thoroughly understands the true mark and true nature of all phenomena.

Second is the unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), because one thoroughly understands the common and distinctive characteristics as well as the characteristics of arising and ceasing of all phenomena;
third is the unimpededness regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), because one teaches the true nature (*dharmatā*) without destroying conventional designations;
fourth is the unimpededness regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), because one brings forth an ocean of sūtras through boundless discourse in an uninterrupted succession.
These are called the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), which are the four kinds of liberative wisdom within the sūtras.
The term "mastery" (*vaśitā*) applies to all of them; therefore, it is not explained separately.
The characteristics of form and the meanings of names are explained extensively in the *Mahādhāraṇī*.
Having already discussed the Jewel of Enlightenment, the Dharma and the Sangha are discussed next.
The root text states:
As well as his physical marks, the ocean of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*),
the treasury of immeasurable merit, and the practice of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*).
The commentary states:
Within this single verse there are further two gates.
What are these two? First, the gate of the essence encompassing all bodies; second, the gate of the Saṃgha that universally penetrates the treasury of the Dharma.

Regarding the gate of encompassing the essence: it encompasses all immeasurable sentient beings in their entirety because they possess bodies that undergo the cycle of birth and death and are impermanent; as stated in the original text, this is because it is the physical form and characteristic of those bodies.

As for the "gate of universal penetration," it is because one universally penetrates all profound treasuries of Dharma with such a multitude of bodies as a practitioner of all things exactly as they are; that is, by practicing exactly as they are according to the fundamental and dharmic nature of the ocean of true thusness and its immeasurable treasury of merit.
The word "etc. (ādi) generally conveys the sense of *praṇāma* (homage).
Based on how many factors of the Dharma and Saṃgha does the Śāstrin offer homage?
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
In total they are subsumed within fourteen, because there are ten types of Saṃgha and four types of Dharma;
alternatively, because they include both the higher and lower [levels], there are many categories of the Saṃgha.
The treatise states:
Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa takes refuge collectively in fourteen bases of virtue, as the ten [aspects of] the Saṃgha and the four [aspects of] the Dharma are each distinct.
What are the ten [aspects of] the Saṃgha?
Because of the distinctions among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). What are the four factors?
They are the distinctions among the teaching (*deśanā*), the principle (*yukti*), the practice (*pratipatti*), and the fruit (*phala*).
"Dharma" refers to the teachings, namely the ocean of all sūtras that accord with the faculties of sentient beings.

"Nature as True Suchness" refers to the dharma of principle; it signifies the equality of the essential nature of all phenomena, because it is free from the falsity of conceptual constructs and transcends the reality of attachment.
The "ocean" refers to the dharmas of fruition; because the myriad virtues within the fruit of wondrous enlightenment are perfectly complete and inexhaustible, it is like a great ocean.

The "inexhaustible treasury of immeasurable merit" refers to the dharmas of practice; because the six perfections, the myriad practices, and their associated pure qualities are inconceivable, they transcend all numerical measure.
The ten kinds of suchness refer to what is called "suchness";
actual practice refers to the ten kinds of correct wisdom.
By realizing the principle of suchness, one establishes the designation of "Saṃgha" based upon true wisdom.
Wisdom and principle, as well as the subject and object, are of one flavor and equal; this is because equality is free from contention.
For what reason is the life-force taken up and designated throughout the ten directions?
It is in order to manifest that the life-faculty it encompasses is vast, perfect, and without limit.
For what reason is the body taken as the sign?

It is because one wishes to manifest that all sentient beings who are deluded by the four marks are entirely encompassed, and one desires to cause them to attain the adamantine, eternally abiding, and immovable body.
Why do the eight types of noble ones not merely dedicate their own bodies and lives, but rather universally dedicate the bodies and lives of all immeasurable sentient beings to the Triple Gem?

This is because they clearly understand that all sentient beings are equal and equal, being nothing other than the single True Suchness (tathatā) without distinction; for the bodies and lives of sentient beings and one’s own body and life are of one flavor and one characteristic, inseparable from one another. Therefore, the verse says "equal," and this term "equal" is profoundly deep.
For what reason does one take up the immeasurable life and bodies of all sentient beings and bring them to the Three Jewels in the form of *vandana* (homage)?

It is because all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are fully delighted; all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time offer praise; and the treasuries of all Dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are perpetually disseminated without interruption.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa has realized the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), and the merits of all lower stages are already fully perfected.
For what reason, then, do all the monks of the lower ranks pay him homage?
It is because those who take refuge are not identical to those who have attained their own respective stages.
If one takes refuge in oneself, one should only pay homage (*vandana*) to the Immovable Ground (*Acalā-bhūmi*), the Perfect Ground (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), and the two grounds above them.
If that is so, why are the grounds prior to these not included?

It is not that there are no persons to take refuge in; they are not mentioned separately because the mention of the higher grounds implicitly indicates the lower ones through this method of "showing by inclusion" (*upary-antarbhāva-pradarśana*).
When a Bodhisattva on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi) takes refuge in the Saṃgha, upon which Saṃgha should he rely?
Since there exists the true Saṃgha within the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhi), there is no fault.
If this is so, why is it not mentioned separately?
Because the following also includes the preceding by way of indirect indication, the verse says: "Either including both above and below, there are thus many classes of the Saṃgha.
Having already explained the Saṃgha of Dharma, we shall next explain the fundamental destinies.
The root text says:
It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments,
to give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna, and so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.
The Commentary states:
Within this single verse there are two gates. What are these two?
First is the gate of severing the bonds of hindrances; second is the gate of continuous liberation.
Within the gate of severance, there are four distinctions. What are these four?

First is the gate of the resolute mind of faith, which is for the purpose of causing all immeasurable sentient beings to sever their minds of doubt and hesitation, to give rise to firm faith, and to become certain regarding the profound, correct path of the Mahāyāna.

Second is the gateway of the mind of renunciation through distancing: it is for the sake of causing all immeasurable sentient beings to distance themselves from the mind of weary renunciation, to increase their aspiration and delight, and to apply themselves with diligence to the profound, correct path of the Mahāyāna.

Third is the gateway of counteracting heterodox arguments, which serves to counteract the ninety-six kinds of great non-Buddhist outsiders along with their ninety-three thousand followers, the four kinds of great Māras along with their thirty-two thousand demonic hosts, and to eliminate one hundred and forty-six million types of worldly treatises, thereby causing beings to enter the profound, correct path of the Mahāyāna.

Fourth is the gateway of dispelling attachment, which serves to cause all infinite ordinary beings, as well as all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, to sever the five kinds of views of a person and realize the five kinds of remedies; to sever the two kinds of attachment to phenomena and realize the two kinds of remedies; and to dedicate themselves toward the profound, correct path of the Mahāyāna.
As in the original [treatise], it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to eliminate doubt, abandon false attachments, and give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna.
Within the section on the "Continuous Gate" (anusaṃdhimukha), there are three distinctions. What are these three?

First is the gate of the uninterrupted great awakening, which serves to integrate the causes of the ten thousand practices and adorn the fruit of great awakening, because the unsurpassed Dharma King is never interrupted.

Second is the gate of the uninterrupted treasury of Dharma, which causes the emergence of sublime and wondrous Brahma-sounds by proclaiming the ocean of all sūtras, so that the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma are never interrupted.

Third is the gate of not severing the Saṃgha: it is for the purpose of cultivating the Great Path both prior to and upon the stages, establishing the palace of the *tathatā-dharmadhātu*, and dwelling in the two types of Saṃgha—the *saṃgha* of those on the path of correct practice and those who have already attained realization—so that they are never severed; this is because, as in the original [sūtra], the lineage of the Buddha is never severed.
What is the scope of the verse regarding sentient beings?
For the sake of counteracting the severance of what, are the Three Jewels established as being unsevered?
The verse says:
Comprehensively subsuming the three groups of persons, because they have not yet attained perfection,
and in contrast to the four kinds of abandonment, three types of non-abandonment are established.
The treatise says:
Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa takes all three aggregates as his objective sphere. Why is this?
Because he has not yet realized the perfect fruition.
However, there are three types within the gateway of the three groups (*tri-nikāya*). What are these three?

First, those prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are called the group of the definitely wrong (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), because they are unable to believe in the retribution of karma and its fruits.

The three levels of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood are called the "group of those fixed in the right" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), because they are definitively established in a stage from which there is no regression.
The ten kinds of faith are called the "group of those not yet fixed" (*aniyata-rāśi*), because they may either advance or regress and have not yet reached a definitive state.

Second, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and the preceding ten stages of the mind of faith are called the "group of those fixed in error" (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), because they all lack roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*).
The fruit of unsurpassed great enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is called the "group of those fixed in correctness" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), because it is already fully perfected.
The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages are called the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), because none have yet reached ultimate realization.
The stage prior to the ten faiths is called the determinate group of the heterodox (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), because there is no aspiration to seek [the truth].
The ten stages of the Sages are called the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), because they have already attained true realization.
The ten stages of faith and the three stages of the worthies are called the group of those not yet fixed (*aniyata-rāśi*), because they have not yet attained correct realization.
These are called the three.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa relied upon that first gate; wishing to provide an antidote to the four kinds of nihilism, he established the principle of the non-interruption of the Triple Gem.
What are the four?
First is abandonment through doubt, because a mind of hesitation lacks decisiveness and thereby severs the lineage of the Three Jewels;
second is abandonment through weary rejection, because a mind possessed by craving finds no joy in the Dharma and thereby severs the lineage of the Three Jewels.
Third is the severance through false views, because the mind of deluded conceptualization is unable to see correctly, thereby severing the seeds of the Triple Gem;
fourth is the severance through fixed attachment, because the mind of grasping at reality is unable to abandon clinging, thereby severing the seeds of the Triple Gem.
These are called the four abandonments.
Having already explained the primary orientation, the general structure is now opened up.
The original text says:
There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it should be explained.
The treatise says:
Within this passage, there are two gates.
What are the two? First, the door of entry; second, the door of that which is entered.
The door of entry refers to the skillful entry into the principles being elucidated.
"Those who enter through the gates" refers to the fact that they skillfully take those dharmas as their basis.
"There are dharmas" is a general designation for the sixteen dharmas that serve as the gates of entry.
"Able to give rise to the faculty of faith" is a general designation for the characteristics of the functional activity of these gate-dharmas.
The Mahāyāna is a general designation for the sixteen dharmas that constitute the essence of entry, as well as the non-dual essence of the Mahāyāna itself.

With faith, one attains certainty; with diligence, the faculties grow and the practices are cultivated. Since there is no way to enter into principle without these two, they are called the "faith-faculty."

Furthermore, "faith" refers to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), while "roots" refer to the stages from the initial stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*) up to the Cloud of Dharma stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). Why is this so?
Because the initial faith lacks roots and thus advances or retreats according to conditions, just like the *bandhujīvaka* flower.
Subsequently, faith becomes increasingly superior, firm, and unshakable, like the *kiṃśuka* tree.
How many meanings does the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) have,
and what are their respective characteristics?
The verse says:
Each has ten meanings, such as clarity, purity, downward-turning, and so forth.
The commentary says:
Faith has ten meanings. What are these ten?
First is the meaning of clarity and purity, because it can cause the nature of the mind to be pure and lucid.
Second is the meaning of determination, because it enables the nature of the mind to become pure and steadfast;
third is the meaning of joy, because it enables the severing of all sorrows and afflictions;
fourth is the meaning of tirelessness, because it enables the severing of the mind of indolence.
Fifth is the meaning of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), because one gives rise to a mind of concord toward the superior practices of others;
sixth is the meaning of respect (*satkāra*), because one does not treat those with virtue with contempt;
seventh is the meaning of compliance (*anuloma*), because one does not oppose or contradict what is seen or heard.
Eighth is the meaning of praise, because one follows those superior practices and extols them from the depths of one's heart;
ninth is the meaning of non-destruction, because one remains in single-minded concentration without losing it through delusion;
tenth is the meaning of affection and joy, because it enables the accomplishment of a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
These are called the ten.
There are ten meanings of the faculties (*indriya*). What are these ten?
First is the meaning of downward turning, because it can eliminate arrogance;
second is the meaning of concealment, because it can express the most profound principle;
third is the meaning of production, because it causes various merits to grow.
Fourth is the meaning of firmness, because all things are fully sustained without deficiency or loss;
fifth is the meaning of continuity, because they increase further and further without interruption;
sixth is the meaning of transcendence, because one gradually moves away from [defilements] as each stage becomes increasingly superior.
Seventh is the sense of accumulation, because one cultivates and gathers the various factors of enlightenment;
eighth is the sense of flourishing, because it is adorned with the virtues of all practices and is thus exceedingly lovely and delightful;
ninth is the sense of fulfillment, because within the state of perfect awakening, the causal practices are brought to completion.
Tenth is the meaning of supreme excellence, because the fruit of wondrous enlightenment is most excellent, vast, and unsurpassable.
These are the ten. The various distinctions between that which can enter and that which is entered shall be explained in detail within the section on the establishment of the doctrine.
The general structure has already been explained; next, the formal establishment is clarified.
The root text states:
"It is said that there are five divisions."

What are these five? First, the section on causes and conditions; second, the section on establishing the doctrine; third, the section on explanation; fourth, the section on practicing faith; and fifth, the section on the benefits of encouraging practice.
The treatise says:
Why is the sequence as it is?
Because such is the nature of the appearance of the Dharma teachings.
What is the meaning of this?

It is intended to demonstrate that the sublime medicine of the supreme flavor manifests only through the appearance of the diseases and obstacles it opposes; likewise, the transformative teaching is necessarily initiated only by the capacity of the faculties of those to be trained whom it subdues. This is because there can be no medicine prior to the disease, nor any teaching prior to the capacity of the faculty.
The initial section on the establishment of causes and conditions is intended to demonstrate that although the wish-fulfilling jewel is but one, it serves as the fundamental source of all jewels;

likewise, although the Mahāyāna Dharma is but one, it constitutes the essential nature of all Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, for it is that which is utilized by the majestic great dragons and understood by those of sharp faculties and wisdom.

The second section establishes the "Section on the Proposition" (*pratijñā-vibhāga*). This is intended to demonstrate that although the treasury of mani jewels contains immeasurable tens of thousands of treasures and opens a thousandfold gates, it is understood by the various dragons;

likewise, although the fundamental dharma of the Mahāyāna is perfect with boundless thousands of meanings, it is explained separately and taught in detail so that those of dull faculties may clearly discern it.

The third section establishes the interpretation, which aims to demonstrate that although one may perceive the wondrous artifice of the "Rain of Jewels" through the eyes and ears, and understand its inexhaustible perfect virtues within the mind of contemplation, it is nevertheless manifested through the majesty of the tongue; thus, without competing for entry, it opens the way toward non-distant and unobstructed generosity (*dāna*).

Although one may obtain a treasury of wish-fulfilling jewels, there is no way to ascend to the palace on its tiered dais; likewise, though one may orally recite the venerable words of the teachings' doctrines and mentally contemplate the profound principles of their extensive and concise versions, it is only by diligently applying oneself to superior progress that one gains firm faith in the Unarisen (*akṣaya*) Vajra. Without this, one cannot attain the treasure-trove of the *dharmadhātu* nor realize the profound principle.

The fourth section establishes the "Chapter on Cultivating Faith in Practice. Although the methods for entering [the path] have been shown through both extensive and concise teachings, sentient beings who are timid and weak find the extensive Dharma-gates unbearable for practice, while those with dull faculties cannot understand the concise Dharma-gates and thus give rise to a mind of weary detachment.

For such classes of beings as these, if they encounter conditions for exhortation and entreaty, they will gradually advance in their practice, perfecting the causes of the hundred practices until they reach the fruit of the ten thousand virtues.

If they do not encounter conditions for exhortation and encouragement, they will regress further and further, eventually succumbing to afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and falling into the state of lack of nature (*abhāva*).

Because the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa perceived this benefit, he manifested these benefits and exhorted others to practice; therefore, the "Section on the Benefits of Exhortation to Practice" was established last.
For what reason are exactly five sections established, neither more nor less?
The verse says:
Because it subsumes those great general grounds through fifty dharma-gates, there is neither increase nor decrease; thus, only five sections are established.
The treatise states:

Within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-mahā-vaipulya-sūtra* consisting of one hundred thousand *udānas*, composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, fifty topical sections (*mukha*) were established in total to analyze and explain the principles of all teachings.

In this present treatise, each of the fivefold dharma-sections (*pañcāṅga-dharmamukha*) subsumes ten of those sections; therefore, neither increasing nor decreasing, only five sections are established.
That which is called the ten gates, beginning with the establishment of the perfection of those to be converted, is subsumed under the Section on Causes and Conditions (*nidāna-vibhāga*).
The ten gates, beginning with the one hundred and sixty Mahāyāna [dharmas], are subsumed under the Section on the Establishment of the Meaning (*siddhārtha-vibhāga*).
The ten gates, beginning with the establishment of conformity to definitive discernment (*niścaya-anukūla-vyavasthāpana*), are subsumed under the section on "Exegesis" (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*).
The ten gates, beginning with the cultivation of certainty and entry (*bhāvanā-niścaya-praveśa*), are subsumed under the section on "Practice" (*pratipatti-bhāga*).
The ten sections—Exhortation, Rebuke, Guidance, and so forth—are subsumed under the Section on Exhortation to Practice.
Having already explained the Section on Establishing the Framework, next is explained the Section on the Exposition through the Presentation of Chapters.
The text states:
First is the Section on the Exposition of Causes and Conditions. Question:
For what causes and conditions was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
there are eight such causes and conditions.
What are the eight?
First is the general characteristic of the causal conditions: namely, to cause sentient beings to leave all suffering and attain ultimate bliss, rather than seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Second, it is because he wishes to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata so that all sentient beings may attain correct understanding without error.
Third, it is because he wishes to enable those sentient beings who have perfected their roots of goodness to become capable of maintaining non-retrogressive faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Fourth, it is to cause sentient beings with meager roots of goodness to cultivate faith.

Fifth, it is to demonstrate the skillful means for eliminating the obstacles of evil karma, to well-guard their minds, and to lead them away from delusion and pride so they may escape the net of heterodoxy.
Sixth, it is to demonstrate the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote to the mental faults of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
Seventh, it is to demonstrate the skillful means of single-minded mindfulness for being born before the Buddha, so that one’s faith will certainly never regress.
Eighth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the benefits and encouraging practice.
For such reasons as these, this treatise is composed.
The treatise says:

Among these eight causes and conditions, the first serves as the primary cause and condition for the Section on Establishing the Thesis; the next two serve as the primary cause and condition for the Section on Explanation; the next four serve as the primary cause and condition for the Section on Cultivating Faith; and the final one serves as the primary cause and condition for the Section on Encouraging Practice and its Benefits.
Within the first set of causal conditions, there are four gates; within each of the subsequent seven sets of causal conditions, there are three gates respectively.

What are the four? First, the gate of the emergence of the transformative teachings; second, the gate of the scope of the sentient beings to be transformed; third, the gate of the skillful means of the activities of emergence; and fourth, the gate of the removal of disputes and slanders.
What are the three? They are the aforementioned three gates.
I shall now set forth their characteristics and explain them individually in their proper order.

Regarding the general characteristics of causes and conditions (*nidāna-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): this refers generally to the gateway through which the transformative teachings arise; that is to say, they serve as the direct causes and conditions for the eight fundamental general entities, and are thus called "causes and conditions. Furthermore, they collectively serve as the direct causes and conditions for the twenty-four distinct specific characteristics, and are thus called "the characteristics of causes and conditions."
The thirty-two kinds of general and specific characteristics of phenomena will be explained in detail within the section on the Establishment of the Meaning (*Liyi-fen*).

The phrase "for the sake of sentient beings" generally indicates the scope of the beings to be converted; that is, it encompasses one billion eight hundred and sixty thousand kinds of beings in the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), thirty kinds of beings in the group of those not yet fixed (*aniyata-rāśi*), and one hundred and twenty kinds of beings in the group of those fixed in the right [path] (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).

"Leaving all suffering behind to attain ultimate bliss" is a general presentation of the skillful means for manifesting enlightened activity; that is, taking the three aggregates as one's objective domain.

"Proclaiming and revealing the essentials of the sublime Dharma" is intended to cause all immeasurable sentient beings to distance themselves from the suffering of birth, death, and impermanence, and to obtain the fundamental bliss of the universal characteristic.

The phrase "not for the sake of seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor" generally summarizes the refutation of the gateway of contentious debate and slander. It refers to the doubts raised by foolish sentient beings:

"Since the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa dwells in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) and has not yet reached the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), his taking the Bodhisattvas of the higher stages as the objects of his transformation is merely a display of his own superiority; it is empty talk for the sake of fame and profit, devoid of any real meaning."
How could a Bodhisattva of a lower stage be capable of teaching and transforming a Bodhisattva of a higher stage?
Therefore, in order to dispel such lack of faith and doubt, Aśvaghoṣa provides his own explanation, saying:

"I attained perfect enlightenment many kalpas ago, yet I assist in the work of transformation and benefit all sentient beings. To fulfill my original vow, I have provisionally manifested the stage of a blue-lotus practitioner; it is not that I speak thus out of a desire for fame or profit."
The first causal condition has already been explained.

Regarding the second causal condition, which speaks of "explaining the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata," this refers generally to the gateway through which the transformative teachings emerge; that is, because these causal conditions are able to manifest the correct meaning and serve as the primary causal conditions for counteracting false attachments, they are termed "the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata."

Why is this so? Because among all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, there is not a single Buddha who did not achieve perfect enlightenment by means of the fundamental one mind, the two gates, and the seven kinds of counteractive measures.

"Causing all sentient beings [to attain]" is a general enumeration of the scope of those to be converted; it refers to the inclusion of ten billion, eighty-six thousand types of sentient beings within the category of the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).

Regarding the phrase "because correct understanding is non-erroneous," this generally summarizes the skillful means of manifesting activity. That is to say, taking as their object those sentient beings of the fixed category of the heterodox who are deranged, they proclaim, expound, and reveal the true meaning—the profound Dharma that serves as an antidote to false attachments. This is done in order to correct the errors of those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to destroy the rebellious views as many as motes of dust, and to sever the barrier of lack of faith in those icchantikas, thereby causing them to enter the Great Path of the ten stages of faith.
The second causal condition has already been explained.

The third causal condition serves as the primary causal condition for the analytical discernment of the characteristics of setting out upon the path; this is called the gateway for the emergence of the transformative teaching, namely, the three types of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

"Bringing sentient beings to fulfillment through roots of goodness" is a general enumeration of the scope of the beings to be transformed; that is, it refers to the inclusion of all sentient beings belonging to the superior grade of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the three grades of the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*), the three grades of the ten stages of practice (*caryā*), the three grades of the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and the three grades of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the phrase "because they are capable of not regressing in their faith in the Mahāyāna dharma," this generally presents the skillful means of manifesting activity. That is to say, taking the two accumulations of sentient beings as their objective domain, they proclaim and reveal the three types of bodhicitta, so that those beings may transcend their own level and attain superior progress.
The third causal condition has already been explained.

The fourth causal condition serves as the direct causal condition for the four kinds of faith and the four kinds of practice within the "Section on Cultivating Faith. This is called the gateway through which the transformative teaching arises.

"Sentient beings with meager roots of goodness" refers to the general categorization of the scope of those to be converted; that is, it includes sentient beings of middling capacity within the first five minds of the stage of the ten faiths.
Because they have already attained the first five, it is not the case that they are entirely devoid of roots of goodness; however, these are termed "subtle" and "few.
Because they have not yet attained the latter five, they cannot be complete and thus are not said to be "accomplished."

Regarding "by cultivating faith," this is a general enumeration of the skillful means for initiating activity; that is to say, it is for the purpose of enabling the accomplishment of the latter five types of faith.
The fourth causal condition has thus been explained.
The fifth causal condition serves as the conclusion of the section on "Cultivating Faith" for entering the gate.

Furthermore, if a person, although practicing faith, succeeds in escaping all obstacles and causing their roots of goodness to increase, this constitutes the primary causal condition; this is termed the "Gate of the Emergence of the Transformative Teaching."

In this context, because it encompasses sentient beings at the initial stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) who are of inferior capacity, it is called the "gate of the limits of the sentient beings to be converted.

Regarding the phrase "eliminating evil karmic obstructions," etc., this generally enumerates the gate of skillful means for manifesting activity; that is, by demonstrating expedients such as prostration and repentance, one eliminates the ocean-like sea of various karmic obstructions.
The fifth causal condition has already been explained.

Regarding the sixth causal condition, the statement "cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*" generally enumerates the gateway through which the transformative teaching arises; that is to say, it serves as the direct causal condition for the gateway of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the section on the cultivation of faith.

"Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles" refers to the gate of enumerating the scope of the sentient beings to be transformed; that is, it includes sentient beings at the lower level of the two minds within the stage of the ten faiths, as well as all those of the two vehicles who are categorized within the group of the definitely wrong.

Regarding the "remedy for mental faults," this generally presents the skillful means of engaging in activity; that is, the two wheels are universally employed as remedies for the faults of the views and attachments of both ordinary beings and followers of the Two Vehicles.
The sixth causal condition has already been explained.
The seventh causal condition serves as the conclusion of the section on "Cultivating Faith.

Furthermore, for sentient beings who first study this Dharma until they ultimately attain birth in the stage of the Rightly Established (samyaktva-niyāma), it acts as the primary causal condition; this is called the gateway for the emergence of the teaching that transforms others.

Among these, sentient beings who have attained the first four minds prior to the stage of the Ten Faiths, yet are unable to further advance—namely, those inferior beings who dwell in this world because their accomplishment of faith is characterized by extreme fear—are called the "gate of the limits of the sentient beings to be converted."

"Because they will certainly not regress from their faith" refers to the general presentation of the skillful means for manifesting activity; that is, establishing them in the group of those destined for rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by the power of superior conditions.
The seventh causal condition has already been explained.

The eighth causal condition serves as the primary causal condition for the section on the benefits of exhortation to practice; this is called the gateway for the emergence of the transformative teachings.

In this context, because it encompasses ten billion and eighty-six thousand types of sentient beings belonging to the category of those fixed in error, this is called the "gate of the limits of the sentient beings to be converted."

Regarding "for the purpose of demonstrating benefits and encouraging practice," this is a general presentation of the skillful means for manifesting activity; that is to say, it is intended to cause the proclamation of merits so as to increase aspiration, and to demonstrate faults so as to bring about awakening and renunciation.
The eighth causal condition has already been explained.

All the teachings of the Dharma are fully contained within the section on the Establishment of the Meaning, and all the capacities of those to be converted are fully contained within the first section on the Causal Conditions.
Why are the three divisions opened to provide separate explanations, while the seven causal conditions are established to be expounded diffusely?
It is because one wishes to demonstrate the differences between the sharp and dull faculties, as well as the extensive and concise, the general and the specific.
For what reason do those of the Two Vehicles repeatedly take up the four stations?

It is because one wishes to demonstrate that the followers of the Two Vehicles are inferior and narrow-minded, and that for them to resolve upon the Bodhicitta and head toward the Unsurpassed Way is exceedingly difficult and arduous, as they must surpass all other classes of sentient beings.
For what reason do the remaining beings of fixed wrongness take rebirth only in three places?
It is because one wishes to demonstrate that the physical forms of these remaining beings are inferior to those of the Two Vehicles, thereby highlighting their faults.
Why does the text specifically distinguish three categories for those of indeterminate nature?

It is because it seeks to demonstrate that for sentient beings of indeterminate nature who possess feeble faculties and dull darkness, the arousal of a resolute mind directed toward the unsurpassed path is exceedingly difficult and arduous, surpassing even that of sentient beings who are already fixed in the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Why are those of right determination not distinguished into three grades but subsumed collectively?
It is because one wishes to demonstrate that sentient beings of right determination, when compared with those of no fixed determination, reveal the gravity of the latter's faults.
By what causes and conditions are exactly eight types established, neither more nor less?
Why is their sequence as it is?
The verse says:
The Great Universal Ground is comprehensively subsumed;
Because of eighty causal conditions, One practices and transforms the increasingly superior dharmas, Following this sequential order.
The treatise says:

In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Great Compendium Treatise) consisting of one hundred thousand *udānas* by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, eighty causal conditions (*nidāna*) are established in total as the basis for the treatise.

In this present treatise, eight kinds of causal conditions are each subsumed within those ten kinds of causal conditions from that [earlier] work; therefore, neither increasing nor decreasing [the number], only eight kinds are established.
For this reason, it is said "such as these," where the word "etc. (等) collectively subsumes those eighty [stages].

Because the sequence of causes and conditions for the practice of the Dharma is the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one attains the ten stages of faith by removing the obstacle of lack of faith in the icchantikas; one attains the ten abiding minds (*daśa-vihāra-citta*) by removing the obstacle of attachment to a self; one attains the ten practice minds (*daśa-pratipatti-citta*) by removing the obstacle of fear of suffering; one attains the ten transference minds (*daśa-pariṇāmana-citta*) by removing the obstacle of abandonment; and one realizes the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*) by severing the ten kinds of obstacles, including the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The eight causal conditions have already been explained; next, the four kinds of faculties will be explained.
The root text says: Question:

Question: Since this Dharma is already contained within the *sūtras*, why is it necessary to explain it again? Answer: Although this Dharma exists within the *sūtras*, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal and the conditions for their reception and understanding differ—specifically, when the Tathāgata was in the world, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties, the speaker’s physical and mental karma was superior, and a single utterance of his perfect voice was understood differently by various species—it was unnecessary to have a treatise (*śāstra*). However, now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, sentient beings’ faculties are dull, the speaker’s physical and mental karma is inferior, and the sound of the teaching is not as pervasive; thus, there are those who cannot understand through the mere words of the *sūtras*. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* is composed to provide a detailed explanation of the meaning of the *sūtras*. Furthermore, the *sūtras* are vast and extensive, and if one were to explain them all in detail, it would be difficult to master them. Consequently, by summarizing the essential points, we compose this treatise to facilitate easy comprehension. Moreover, the *sūtras* are concise and profound, and without a commentary, they are difficult to understand. Thus, we rely on the *sūtras* to establish our principles and rely on this treatise to clarify the meaning of the *sūtras*. Finally, the *sūtras* are scattered across many locations, making it difficult to find the specific passage one seeks. By collecting these scattered teachings into a single volume, one can easily access them. For these reasons, although the Dharma exists within the *sūtras*, it is necessary to explain it again. This is like a king who possesses a treasury of jewels but lacks a catalog; if he wishes to retrieve a specific gem, he must first consult the catalog to know its location. Only then can he obtain it. If he did not have the catalog, even if he searched throughout the entire treasury, he would not know where the jewel was and would fail to find it. It is the same with the Dharma: although the *sūtras* contain the Dharma, without a treatise to explain it, one cannot easily comprehend it. If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there are sentient beings who are able to attain understanding through extensive hearing by means of their own power; or those who, likewise by their own power, attain much understanding from little hearing; or those who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding by relying on extensive treatises; or those who, finding the abundance of words in extensive treatises to be cumbersome, delight in *dhāraṇī*—which condenses many meanings into few words—and are able to attain understanding thereby—for such reasons, this treatise should be expounded, as it is intended to comprehensively summarize the boundless meanings of the vast and profound Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The Commentary states:
Within this text there are two sections. What are these two?
The first is the gate of questioning regarding no difference in what is taught; the second is the gate of resolving doubts by citing temporal stages. If one asks:

"Since these teachings are already fully contained within the *sūtras*, why is it necessary to explain them again?"—this constitutes the gate of questioning. It means that within the hundred *sūtras* such as the *Mahāprabhāsa-avabodha*, all immeasurable treasuries of the Dharma are revealed; according to the capacities and faculties of sentient beings, they are gathered and benefited without any deficiency.
Why would a person of middling capacity trouble themselves to compose this treatise? To re-transmit those teachings again would possess no power to further clarify them.
Now, in composing this treatise to restate those teachings, do you perhaps not seek such things as praise and renown?
To ultimately hold in deep respect [the teaching] without exhausting its underlying principles is called the "Gate of Questioning Without Discrepancy in What is Taught. The response states:

Although this Dharma exists within the Sūtras, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal and their conditions for receiving and understanding are distinct, there is a general presentation of the "Gate of Resolving Doubts. That is to say, according to Aśvaghoṣa’s own explanation: the teachings and principles of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are naturally and eternally abiding, of a single flavor and equality; they do not shift, nor do they arise or cease.
Therefore, although titles and banners differ and the written records vary, the teachings themselves are of but one flavor and are entirely equal; they are neither divided nor distinguished.

However, because the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ—some being sharp and others dull—and because their mental activities vary in their breadth and brevity, the capacities of those to be transformed being diverse, the teacher cannot remain uniform. Thus, the names of the teachings received are each distinct, and the causes and conditions for understanding the words and meanings are each distinct.

That is to say, there are some sentient beings who attain understanding by relying on the *sūtra* (gāthā) and *vyākaraṇa* (śloka-vyākaraṇa) of the Buddha, while there are other sentient beings who attain understanding only by relying on the *vyākaraṇa* (śloka-vyākaraṇa) of the Bodhisattvas; therefore, for the sake of these people, this treatise must be composed.

Furthermore, while the Tathāgata was in the world, those he transformed were purified; his capacity to transform was perfected through eighty-four thousand kinds of forms, four kinds of universal knowledge of the mind, ten kinds of activities, ten kinds of excellences, sixty-eight pure Brahma-spheres, and eighty-eight sublime tones. These were expounded simultaneously without sequence, infinite and boundless, consisting of various distinct categories.

There are sentient beings who attain liberation upon seeing the Buddha’s wondrous form; there are sentient beings who attain liberation by contemplating the Buddha’s mental states; there are sentient beings who attain liberation by observing the Tathāgata’s ten karmas and ten excellences; and there are sentient beings who attain liberation by hearing the Buddha’s pure, perfect, and sublime voice. For those who thus clearly understand and thoroughly penetrate with equanimity, no further discourse is required.

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the objects to be transformed (the converts) become disordered and the means of transformation (the teachers) are deficient, then the sūtras and śāstras will differ according to the faculties and dispositions of beings, varying between extensive and concise treatments for different capacities.
"Faculties" refers to the four types of faculties; "dispositions" refers to the dispositions of the three vehicles.

What are the four? First, the faculty of extensive self-power; second, the faculty of concise self-power; third, the faculty of extensive lack of power relying on others; and fourth, the faculty of concise lack of power relying on others.
Among these four types of root-natures (*indriya-gotra*), the first two constitute the *sūtra* assembly, while the latter two constitute the *upadeśa* assembly.
Why is it that those to be converted are complete within the gate of causes and conditions (*nidāna-mukha*), yet few within the gate of root-natures?

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the pure *saṃnāha-āśaya* (resolute intention) is without limit, and for the purpose of demonstrating that there are limits to the categories of sentient beings who receive the teaching and practice it accordingly.
For what causes and conditions do the two layers of extensive and concise teachings arise?
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Because it is bound by his original vow, he has brought forth this Dharma-gate;
for it is clearly and explicitly taught in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The Commentary says:
Because they are bound by the power of causes and conditions, two layers of profound Dharma gates arise. Why is this so?
Because it is clearly explained in the sūtras; specifically, it is stated thus in the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:

"I recall that in the past, across an ocean of immeasurable kalpas, for five hundred lifetimes as a rishi of forbearance, I dwelt in mountain forests, single-mindedly practicing the pure dharmas of the fourfold noble assembly—namely, fewness of desires and contentment."
At that time, a great serpent descended from the mountain peak and came to where I was; upon hearing me recite, it cast itself down, prostrating in worship and repentance.
Having finished casting his body down, he pressed his head against the ground and, composing himself with great effort, spoke this verse:
"In a past life, I was a Rishi of Forbearance; Dwelling on this mountain, I practiced the Way during the six periods of the day."
Yet because of the power of a single moment of anger, you have now obtained this snake body and constantly undergo great suffering.
If, after the end of your life, you obtain a human rebirth, I shall become your disciple and follow you in spiritual practice.
"What you have recited is what I have always recited; therefore, I now feel great shame and remorse.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately passed away. Later, having obtained a human body, he became my disciple.
At that time, they made mutual vows of commitment, saying:
"If I should realize the Unsurpassed Way, I shall proclaim ninety million (ninety *lakṣa*) extensive *sūtras* and benefit the vast multitude of sentient beings through my altruistic intention."
"I shall proclaim the ten lakṣas of the *Saṃkṣipta-sūtra*, with the altruistic intention to benefit and sustain sentient beings through dhāraṇī. Then my disciple made this vow:
"After the Teacher’s parinirvāṇa, I shall compose ninety sections of the *Vistara-upadeśa* (Extensive Exposition), with the altruistic intention to benefit the great masses of sentient beings."

I have composed ten sections of a brief exposition on the *Upāsaka-vidhi* (Lay Disciple Precepts), with the altruistic intention to sustain all sentient beings through their retention [of these teachings].
For this reason, I now proclaim the ocean of all sūtras.
"For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, my disciples will manifest the composition of treatises and teachings.
Having thus explained the section on causes and conditions, next follows the section on establishing the thesis.
Regarding the names of the dharma-gates within the "Section on Establishing the Meaning," how many are there in number,
and what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
There are thirty-three kinds: the sixteen dharmas of entry, the sixteen gates of entry, and the distinction of non-duality.
The treatise says:
In the section on the Establishment of the Thesis (*siddhāntabhāga*), there are thirty-three types of distinctions among the dharma-gates.
