The section on the Gate of Initiating Questions and Answers to Resolve Doubts has already been explained; next, the Gate of Provisional Designation Opening onto the Aspect of True Suchness (Tathatā) will be explained.
Within this, there are two gates. What are these two?
The first is the gate of the suchness of emptiness as it truly is; the second is the gate of the suchness of non-emptiness as it truly is.
Regarding "emptiness as it truly is": within the essence of suchness, all defiled dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, are entirely empty, void, and non-existent.
Regarding "non-empty as it truly is": within the essence of suchness, all pure dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, are fully present without any deficiency.
Thus, these two gates each possess [the other], and they are never separated from one another.
Thereupon, one should recite the verses on the profound principle,
as those verses state:
"Far removed from the three provisional characteristics, Perfectly complete in the three real virtues."
For these reasons, the True Suchness of Essence is established;
it is far removed from the characteristics of the four extremes and is perfected by the virtues of the four dharmas.
For these reasons, the True Suchness of Characteristics is established.
All modes of conduct involving faults, Have the three and four characteristics as their basis;
All categories of meritorious qualities, Have the three and four virtues as their basis.
For this reason, They neither increase nor decrease.
Ceasing at the chapter on "Quantities," he establishes it in this manner.

Now, in reciting this verse-text, one should maintain the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*); because it is a realm free from discursive thought and corresponds only to direct realization, this is the realization of abiding in stillness, not the realization of progression toward a goal.
Having explained the gate of the suchness of mind, next is explained the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind.
The original text states:
"Regarding the arising and ceasing of mind: because it relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind that arises and ceases."
That which is called the non-arising and non-ceasing in conjunction with arising and ceasing—neither identical nor different—is named the ālayavijñāna.
This consciousness has two aspects: it can encompass all dharmas and it can give rise to all dharmas.
What are these two? First, the meaning of awakening; second, the meaning of non-awakening.
The treatise says:
Within this, there are two gates.
What are the two? First is the gate of the general characteristics of the basis; second is the gate of the specific characteristics of that which depends upon it.
Within this, there are two layers of abiding that should be contemplated through reflection: namely, that the gate of arising and ceasing takes the one mind as its basis.
This is because the gate of arising and ceasing subsumes both the meaning of awakening and the meaning of non-awakening, taking the ālayavijñāna as their basis.
First, the initial gate is explained.
Regarding the phrase "the arising and ceasing of the mind," this is stated because it was established above.
Regarding the phrase "based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*," this refers to the single mind as the basis; since that very single mind is also called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This means that the "mind" (citta) of the higher [truth] descends to establish various names;
those who possess a mind subject to arising and ceasing are able to rely upon the gate of the Dharma, namely, the gate of arising and ceasing.
Now, I shall clearly demonstrate the gateway of the Tathāgatagarbha in accordance with the sūtras.
How many are there in number regarding the Tathāgata’s treasury?
And by what is this Tathāgatagarbha currently subsumed?
The verse says:
The Tathāgatagarbha has ten aspects, because they are explained differently in various sūtras;
herein, the Tathāgatagarbha is subsumed under both its activities and its characteristics.
The treatise says:
There are ten kinds of *tathāgatagarbha*, because they are explained individually within the sūtras. What are these ten?
The first is the Great Totality Dhāraṇī Tathāgatagarbha, because it completely encompasses all tathāgatagarbhas.
In the *Sūtra on the Inexhaustible Treasury of All Buddhas*, it is stated as follows:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:

“There is a Tathāgatagarbha named the Great Jewel, Inexhaustible, Supreme, and Perfect Dhāraṇī; it encompasses all treasuries, penetrating everything without exception and corresponding to everything without fail—perfectly perfect and perfectly equal.”
Of all the Tathāgatagarbhas that exist, there is none that does not have this as its root.
Why is this? This Tathāgatagarbha is the king of the Tathāgatagarbha, the master of the Tathāgatagarbha, the deity of the Tathāgatagarbha, and the ground of the Tathāgatagarbha.
"For this reason, it is called the Great Jewel, Inexhaustible, Supreme, and Perfect Dhāraṇī Tathāgatagarbha.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

This refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) upon which the treasury of dhāraṇīs relies; it is distinct from the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgatagarbha found in other sūtras, which are the phenomena that rely [upon it].
In what sense is it called the "Tathāgatagarbha"?
This refers to its being sustained.
Second, the Tathāgatagarbha is far removed from transmigration and far removed from bondage, because it is pure and full.
As stated in the *Bhūtakoṭi-sūtra*:
O Son of the Buddha!

The Tathāgatagarbha is nothing other than pure awakening and nothing other than suchness; it is free from the causes of saṃsāra and free from the bonds of discursive cognition. It is individually and utterly pure; therefore, it is called the "Tathāgata-garbha."
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

It reveals that the single mind of the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) has no cause for delusion and no cause for awakening; it has no fruit of delusion and no fruit of awakening. It is a single reality and a single suchness, for there exists only the pure and wondrous essence of the Tathāgata.
In what sense is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*?
It is because it is unmixed.
Third, regarding the *tathāgatagarbha* as both activity and characteristic: it causes the *dharmakāya*—which possesses the power of transmigration—to remain concealed.
In the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra it is said:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it experiences suffering and pleasure, arising and ceasing together with its causes, just like an actor."
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals that within the single mind of the gate of arising and ceasing, there appear the phenomena of birth-and-death and nirvana through the power of delusion and the power of awakening.
For example, it is like a non-illusory person who, regarding illusory phenomena, bestows their functional power upon them as appropriate.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? It is because it causes [the Buddha-nature] to be concealed.
Fourth is True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Tathāgata-garbha, which exists solely as suchness.
As stated in the *Tattvārthā Sūtra*:

"The Tathāgata-garbha, according to the principle of suchness, is neither established nor denied; it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is not that which is realized by the wisdom of the true essence (*samyaktva-jñāna*), nor is it an objective sphere perceived by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)."
Why is this? Because there is only principle (nyāya), and no such things as "this" or "that.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

This refers to the manifestation of the principle of the nature-as-such (*tathatā*) within the gate of suchness; it is the principle itself as the principle, for it is not the wisdom itself as the principle.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*?
This refers to the absence of anything else.
Fifth is the *tathatā* (suchness) of arising and ceasing, the *tathāgatagarbha*, which, though neither arising nor ceasing, is defiled by the stains of arising and ceasing.
Thus it is stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
Mahāmati! Foolish ordinary beings, failing to perceive and failing to understand, cling to the notion that all phenomena do not abide for even a moment; falling into false views, they speak thus:
"Even the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not abide for even a moment."
Because it destroys that *tathatā* and *tathāgatagarbha*.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the *vajra-tathāgatagarbha*, the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, is not momentary and does not abide.
Mahāmati! If the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata were not to abide for even a single moment, then all noble ones (ārya) would fail to become noble ones.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

This refers to revealing the principle of the True Suchness (tathatā) within the gate of arising and ceasing, which is a dharma that is free from the marks of impermanence and is neither born nor extinguished.
For what reason is it called the Tathāgatagarbha?
That is to say, because it is defiled.
Sixth is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, because all forms of emptiness conceal the *Tathāgata*.
As it is said in the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*:
"Bhagavān! The empty Tathāgatagarbha is so called because it is separated from, liberated from, and distinct from the storehouse of all afflictions.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?"
What is meant by "revealing all defiled phenomena within the gate of arising and ceasing"?
It is because they conceal the immeasurable qualities of the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya*) and its own characteristic.
For what reason are all defiled phenomena collectively termed "empty"?

All defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are like magical illusions; their substance and characteristics lack reality, and their functions are not true. Therefore, they are called "empty. Yet, they are able to conceal and obscure the true essence of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and its real virtues; for this reason, it is called the "Tathāgata-garbha" (*tathāgatagarbha*), as its name is established based on its capacity to conceal the defilements.
Seventh is the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, because all that is non-empty is defiled by emptiness.
As it is said in the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra:
"World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgatagarbha is not empty because it transcends the sands of the Ganges [in number] and consists of the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas that are inseparable, non-detached, and non-different [from it].
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

It reveals that within the gate of arising and ceasing, the self-characteristic of original enlightenment is endowed with all merits beyond the sands of the Ganges and is defiled by all defiled phenomena beyond the sands of the Ganges.
For what reason are all pure phenomena collectively termed "not empty"?

It is because within the very essence of all pure phenomena, there is a truly existent, superior, and wondrous activity that is far removed from the false and transcends artifice; therefore, they are called "not empty."

When obscured by defilements, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*; when manifest, it is called the *dharmakāya*. Because it is termed the *tathāgatagarbha* during the period of concealment—its name being established based on the purity that is contained within—it is so designated.
Eighth is its ability to encompass the *tathāgatagarbha*, because within the *avidyāgarbha*, the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛtiprabhāsvaracitta*) can encompass all meritorious qualities.
The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta Sūtra* states as follows:

"The essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* associated with the primordial limit and its pure phenomena—these phenomena are suchness, non-false, inseparable from, and not detached from the inconceivable dharma of wisdom; for since the beginningless primordial limit, this essence of the pure associated dharma has existed."
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

It reveals that the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*) of all sentient beings has, from time immemorial, been fully endowed with the three wisdoms and perfected in the four virtues, without any deficiency whatsoever.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*?
Because, due to the inverted mind’s lack of knowledge and realization, its name is established based on the purity of both the subject and the object.

Ninth is the *tathāgatagarbha* as that which is contained: it is the storehouse of all defiled phenomena and ignorance, for once one has emerged from these, the Perfectly Awakened One is what is contained within.
In the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:

"The Tathāgatagarbha is by nature dissociated from the afflictions and impure dharmas that have been present since beginningless time; yet, these afflictions and impure dharmas, which are dissociated, detached, and non-associated with it from the very beginning, can only be severed by the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s bodhi."
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals that the Buddha of perfected initial awakening (*ādikṣayajñāna*) has severed all obstacles and is endowed with all-encompassing wisdom.
Here, the clarity of wisdom is the external, while the darkness of obstacles is the internal; for all defiled phenomena are subsumed and sustained by wisdom.
In what sense is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? It is because it "holds" [the Tathāgata].
Tenth is the "concealed *tathāgatagarbha*," because the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata is covered and hidden by afflictions.
In the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta Sūtra*, it is stated as follows:

"The Tathāgatagarbha is equal and constant throughout the future limit and possesses all phenomena; it is the root of all dharmas, encompassing all dharmas and endowed with all dharmas, for it is neither separate from nor detached from worldly phenomena."
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

It reveals that the single essence of the mind is equal to the dharma-realm, pervades the three periods of time, and is fully endowed with all defiled and pure phenomena, for there is nothing it does not penetrate and nothing to which it does not reach.

Furthermore, within the gateway of manifesting according to conditions, the intrinsically pure mind is concealed and submerged within defiled phenomena because the Dharmakāya Tathāgata has not yet appeared.
These are called the ten.
Within these ten, we now address the Tathāgatagarbha in terms of its activity and characteristics.
Having already explained the gateway of the Tathāgatagarbha, we shall next explain the gateway of the Ālayavijñāna.

That which is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*—defined as the non-arising and non-ceasing conjoined with arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different—is established by omitting its partial names to establish its complete name; for although its meaning is fully present, the expression is not yet exhaustive.
Regarding what is taught here concerning non-arising and non-ceasing, as well as arising and ceasing: what dharmas do these refer to, and what are their respective boundaries?
The verse says:
Comprehensively subsuming all unconditioned phenomena is called "non-arising and non-ceasing";
comprehensively subsuming all conditioned phenomena is therefore called "arising and ceasing.
The Treatise says:
Because it comprehensively subsumes all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), it is therefore called "neither arising nor ceasing.
This "neither arising nor ceasing" is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all unconditioned phenomena.
Because it encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it is called "arising and ceasing" (*utpāda-nirodha*).
The term "arising and ceasing" is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena.
Thus, how many types of each are there for these two categories: the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
What are these names?
The verse says:
Although the unconditioned is immeasurable, it is briefly explained as being of four kinds.
That is to say: True Suchness, Original Enlightenment, Initial Enlightenment, and Space.
Although conditioned phenomena are immeasurable, briefly stated there are five kinds:
namely, Fundamental Ignorance, and the category of the Four Characteristics.
The treatise says:
There are four kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). What are these four?

First, the unconditioned of suchness; second, the unconditioned of original enlightenment; third, the unconditioned of initial enlightenment; and fourth, the unconditioned of empty space—these are called the four.
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are of five kinds.

What are these five? First, conditioned phenomena of fundamental ignorance; second, conditioned phenomena of the characteristic of arising; third, conditioned phenomena of the characteristic of abiding; fourth, conditioned phenomena of the characteristic of change; and fifth, conditioned phenomena of the characteristic of cessation. These are called the five.
Furthermore, what constitutes the essence of the four unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*),
and what are their functions?
The verse says:
Each basis has two kinds, namely the general and the specific;
as it is with the essence, so it is with the function—this should be observed according to the explanation.
The Treatise says:
The unconditioned *tathatā* has two bases. What are these two?
First is the universal basis, which takes as its essence the fundamental dharma of the one mind that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Second is the specific basis (*viśeṣāśraya*), because it takes the principle of quiescence within the gate of arising and ceasing as its essence.
Fundamental awakening (*mūlajñāna*), being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), has two bases. What are these two?
First is the universal basis, which takes as its essence the fundamental dharma of the one mind that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
second is the particular basis, which takes as its essence the natural, original wisdom within the gate of arising and ceasing.
Initial awakening as unconditioned has two bases. What are these two?
First is the universal basis, which takes the fundamental dharma of the one mind—being neither conditioned nor unconditioned—as its essence.
Second is the distinct basis (*viśeṣāśraya*), because within the gate of arising and ceasing, it takes the wisdom that arises in accordance with others as its essence.
Unconditioned space has two bases. What are these two?
First is the universal basis, which takes as its essence the fundamental dharma of the single mind that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
second is the particular basis, which takes as its essence the non-existent phenomena within the gate of arising and ceasing.
These are called the two bases.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of functions of suchness, which is unconditioned. What are these two?
First is the universal function, because it causes all dharmas to arise;
second is the specific function, because it ensures that the nature of equality is not lost.
Thus, the unconditioned original enlightenment possesses these two kinds of functions.
What are these two? First is the universal function, because it does not maintain its own nature;
second is the specific function, because it does not undergo transformation.
The unconditioned initial awakening has two kinds of functions. What are these two?
The first is the universal function, because it follows along with delusion.
Second is its specific function, which serves as an antidote to one's own faults.
The unconditioned space has two kinds of functions. What are these two?
First is the universal function, which causes desire and existence to come into being;
second is the specific function, which ensures that the nature of emptiness and non-existence is not lost.
These are called the two functions.
What is explained here is general in that it refers to the meaning of others, and specific in that it refers to one's own meaning.
Based on these two statements, one should conduct a thorough investigation.
The various distinct characteristics will be clearly explained in their respective textual passages.
What constitutes the essence of the five types of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*),
and what are their functions?
The verse says:
Each basis has two kinds, namely the general and the specific;
as it is with their essence and function, so it is here—this should be observed according to the explanation.
The Treatise says:
Fundamental ignorance as a conditioned phenomenon has two kinds of bases. What are these two?
The first is the universal base, which takes the fundamental dharma of the one mind as its essence, being neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Second is the specific basis (*viśeṣāśraya*), because within the gate of arising and ceasing, it takes the powerful abiding ground (*mahābalasthiti-bhūmi*) as its essence.
Regarding the conditioned state of the characteristic of arising, there are two kinds of bases. What are these two?
First is the universal basis, because its essence consists of the fundamental dharma of the one mind, which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
second is the specific basis, because its essence consists of the defiled dharmas minutely differentiated within the gate of arising and ceasing.
The conditioned state characterized by abiding has two kinds of bases. What are these two?
First is the universal base, which takes as its essence the fundamental dharma of the single mind that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Second is the distinct basis (*pṛthag-āśraya*), because it takes the coarse categories of defiled phenomena within the gate of arising and ceasing as its substance.
Regarding the conditioned phenomenon of "distinct characteristics" (*visadṛśa-lakṣaṇa-saṃskṛta*), there are two kinds of bases. What are these two?
First is the universal basis, because its essence consists of the fundamental dharma of the one mind, which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
second is the specific basis, because its essence consists of the coarse categories of defiled dharmas within the gate of arising and ceasing.
The characteristic of cessation in conditioned phenomena has two kinds of bases. What are these two?
First is the universal base, which takes as its essence the fundamental dharma of a single mind that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
The second is the specific basis (*viśeṣāśraya*), because it takes the coarse categories of defiled phenomena within the gate of arising and ceasing as its substance.
These are called the two bases.
Furthermore, fundamental ignorance has two kinds of functions.
What are these two?
First is the universal function, which is able to give rise to all defiled phenomena;
second is the specific function, which acts as an obstacle wherever it reaches.
The characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa) as a conditioned phenomenon has two functions. What are these two?
First is its universal function, which provides its power to those above, below, and in between.
Second is their specific function: they act as obstacles wherever they occur.
As it is said regarding the characteristic of arising (*jāti*), so it is with abiding (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*).
The characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*) has two functions regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
What are the two? First is the universal function, because it bestows its power upon others as well as upon itself;
second is the specific function, because it is capable of performing obstructive actions.
These are called the two functions.
The various distinct characteristics will be explained in detail in their respective textual passages.
For what reason is it said that all phenomena, both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), have the single mind as their universal essence?
Because it is stated thus in the sūtras.
Which sūtra? It refers to the *Mārgajñatā-sūtra*.
How is it explained?
In that sutra, it is stated as follows:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The ālayavijñāna possesses all dharmas and is endowed with all dharmas.
Of these various dharmas, which exceed the sands of the Ganges and exceed the sands of the Ganges, what serves as their fundamental basis?”
“In what place do they arise?
The Buddha said:
“In this way, for all phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—their places of arising are supreme and inconceivable.”
"Why is this? Because within that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, these conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena are able to arise.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by the ‘state that is neither conditioned nor unconditioned’?
The Buddha said:

"That which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned is what is called the fundamental dharma of the single mind. Because it is not conditioned, it can produce the conditioned; because it is not unconditioned, it can produce the unconditioned. Therefore, I say that this place of birth is preeminent and inconceivable."
Furthermore, good son!
For example, an illegitimate son has two supports: first, the great king; second, his parents.
All conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are likewise; each has two supports, namely, the support of penetration and the support of constituent parts.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as all grasses and trees have two supports—the first being the great earth and the second being the seed—so too it is with all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;
each has two supports, namely, the support of penetration and the support of constituent parts.
...and so on, as explained at length.
"In conjunction with" means that it reveals the distinction between the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the object perfumed (*vāsya*).
How does it reveal this?
This refers to the manifestation that all phenomena—both defiled and pure—possess either power or lack thereof, and thus have varying degrees of superiority or inferiority.
Now, these shall be clearly explained through two gates. What are these two?
First is the gate of downward transformation, and second is the gate of upward transformation; within the gate of birth-and-death, nothing occurs outside these two.
How do these two gates differ?
The verse says:
When all defiled dharmas possess power and all pure dharmas lack power,
turning away from the source and descending stage by stage, it is called the gate of downward progression.
All pure dharmas possess power, while all defiled dharmas lack power;
turning toward the source in an upward progression is called the "gate of upward turning.
The treatise says:
Because defiled and pure phenomena possess mutual degrees of superiority and inferiority, the two modes of transformation are established.
Now, first, the initial downward mode of transformation shall be explained.
By what phenomena is fundamental ignorance perfumed?
At what time does the process of perfuming occur?
The verse says:
There are five kinds of that which is perfumed, namely, the mind of the single dharma-realm.
And the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are neither beginning, middle, nor end;
yet they are grasped as having a beginning, middle, and end, as clearly explained in the Sūtras.
The Treatise says:
Fundamental ignorance takes five kinds of dharmas as its objects of perfuming (vāsya), namely: the one dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) and the four unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas.
What is the nature of its perfuming of the one dharma-realm?
The verse says:
The single dharma-realm mind possesses two kinds of mastery,
namely, the conditioned and the unconditioned.
This fundamental ignorance, relying upon the first sovereignty, is able to perform the act of perfuming.
The commentary states:
the single dharma-realm mind possesses two kinds of sovereignty.
What are these two? First is mastery over the conditioned, because it serves as the support for conditioned phenomena;
second is mastery over the unconditioned, because it serves as the support for unconditioned phenomena.
Fundamental ignorance performs the function of perfuming based on the first stage of sovereignty, not the subsequent stages of sovereignty.
The *Madhyamaka-tattva-sūtra* states this as follows:
"Fundamental ignorance perfumes the extent of its own basis, not that of another's basis."
What are the characteristics of the perfuming of the *tathatā* (suchness)?
The verse says:
The unconditioned dharma of *tathatā* Has two kinds of functions.
What are called the universal and the particular are as explained in the previous *Viniścaya*.
This fundamental ignorance, relying upon its initial activity, is able to perform the function of perfuming;
the other unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are likewise.
The Commentary states:
True Suchness (*tathatā*) as an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entity has two kinds of functions, namely general and specific, as previously explained.
Fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), relying on the first function, is able to perform the act of perfuming (*vāsanā*); it does not rely on the latter function.

As it has been said regarding *tathatā* (suchness), the same applies to the other three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); for all of them rely on the initial activity and not the subsequent activity.
At the time when the work of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is performed, the measure is neither the beginning, nor the middle, nor the end, because it encompasses the beginning, the middle, and the end.
In the *Mūlaprajñā-sūtra*, it is stated:
"When powerful ignorance performs the act of perfuming, it simultaneously grasps [the object] in its initial, middle, and final stages, rather than grasping them separately."
Regarding the "perfuming agent" (*bhāvakam*) and the "perfumable" (*bhāvyam*) mentioned herein, for what reason are they termed "perfuming"?
It is because they can induce those dharmas to conjoin with their own substance, proceeding and evolving together without being separated; therefore, they are called the "perfuming agent."
Furthermore, because those dharmas do not create obstacles—neither following nor conforming to them, nor opposing or contradicting them—they are called "perfumable" (*bhāvya*).
This refers to the five conditioned dharmas which can perfume the four kinds of unconditioned dharmas and the single dharma-realm of mind.

The five dharmas that are perfumed arrive accordingly and, together with the five perfumers, meet, harmonize, and function as a single entity; therefore, it is said that the unarisen and undying are in conjunction with the arisen and ceasing.
Just as the fundamental dharma of the single mind of great ignorance serves as the universal basis, it relies upon the initial sovereignty to perform the activity of perfuming;
one should understand that the four marks of conditioned existence function in this same way.

Just as great ignorance, by relying on the four unconditioned phenomena, performs the function of thorough penetration and can act as a perfuming agent, one should understand that the four characteristics of the conditioned are likewise so.
Such meanings will become clear in their principles when they reach their own definitive analysis.

"Neither identical nor different" means that it reveals the distinctions between the similarities and differences of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). How is this revealed?

It is by demonstrating that the unconditioned sovereignty of the single *dharmadhātu*-mind and the functional activities of the four types of unconditioned phenomena differ in principle from the conditioned sovereignty of the single *dharmadhātu*-mind and the penetrative functions of the four types of unconditioned phenomena; therefore, they are called "not identical."

In order to demonstrate that the *dharmadhātu-citta*—which is capable of being perfumed by defiled phenomena—is sovereign over conditioned phenomena and possesses the function of penetrating the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena, it is called "non-different" because it is not distinct in principle from the five kinds of conditioned phenomena that perform the act of perfuming.
Furthermore, because the perfumed pure dharmas and the perfuming defiled dharmas are each distinct, they are said to be "not one.
Because both the perfumer and the perfumed function within a single mind and have no other [entity], they are said to be "not different."
That which is called *ālayavijñāna* is the complete and perfect term.
Having already explained the downward-turning gate (*adhaḥpravṛttimukha*), I shall next explain the upward-turning gate (*ūrdhvapravṛttimukha*).
To establish this upward-turning gate, one must further set forth the words of the scriptural text.
As it is said in the Laṅkāvatāra-rāja-sūtra:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!..."
"I recall that in the past, during the time of going forth, I came to rely on others; during the time of entering [the path], others came to rely on me.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
This means it reveals two types of transformation (*parāvṛtti*). How does it reveal them?
That which says, "I have come to rely upon others" during the process of emergence, is the downward transformation (*adhaḥ-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding the phrase "at the time of entry, others come to rely upon me," this refers to the upward transformation (*ūrdhva-vṛtti*).
What is the meaning of this?

"Me" refers to the Tathāgata-garbha, the Buddha of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Original Enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). "Come" has the sense of being perfumed (*vāsana*). "Relying on others" means turning one's back on one’s own Original Enlightenment and relying on the "other" of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because this explanation is formulated based on the wording of this sutra, it is said that the union of the unarisen and undying with the arisen and dying constitutes the downward-turning gate (adharānulomika-mukha).
If one wishes to establish the upward-turning gate (ūrdhvānulomika-mukha), one may say that the arisen and dying are in union with the unarisen and undying.
For this reason, these terms are preserved in the *Mādhyamika-hṛdaya-vṛtti*.

The fundamental intention (*āśaya*) of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa has been clearly and distinctly revealed through the preceding sequence; he merely cited one while implicitly indicating the other by way of analogy. Therefore, there is no fault of omission or deficiency.
The principle of the upward-turning gate (*ūrdhva-vivarta-mukha*) is self-evident within the section on remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
Having explained the upward-turning gate, I shall next explain the gate of comprehensive inclusion and systematic establishment (*saṃgraha-vyavasthāna-mukha*).
How many are the various distinctions of consciousness?
How many types of consciousness are taught in each of the sūtras?
The verse says:
Within the holy teachings throughout one lifetime by the Muni, the Greatly Awakened Honored One,
There are ten types of compendiums, each explaining the sūtras differently.
Beginning with one type and ending with ten types,
they are clearly and explicitly taught in such sūtras as the *Prakṛti-saṃgraha*.
The Treatise states:

Generally speaking, among the various divergent explanations found within the sūtras taught by the various sages throughout the one lifetime [of the Buddha], there are ten types in total; that is, from one kind of consciousness up to ten kinds of consciousness.
What are the ten types of differentiated sūtras?
First is the establishment of a single consciousness that subsumes all consciousnesses;
herein there are four [points].

What are the four? First, establishing that the single mind-consciousness universally subsumes all consciousnesses; that is to say, because the single mind-consciousness pervades two kinds of mastery, there is nothing in which it is not securely established.
In the *Ekacittadharmasūtra*, it is stated as follows:
At that time, Mañjuśrī, receiving the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how many kinds of consciousness do you teach?”
"What are its essential nature and characteristics?
I pray that you will analyze and explain them for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! For the sake of this great assembly, you should inquire about this matter.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.”
Thereupon Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"I establish only one kind of consciousness; the remaining consciousnesses are not established. Why is this so?"

A single consciousness consists of many individual cognitions; this consciousness possesses various powers capable of producing all manner of names and designations, yet it remains ultimately nothing but a single consciousness, devoid of any other phenomena.
Therefore, I say that one kind of consciousness is established, while the remaining consciousnesses are not so established.

Second, the ālayavijñāna is established as the comprehensive synthesis of all consciousnesses; this is because the ālayavijñāna possesses both the sense of obstruction and the sense of non-obstruction, such that there is nothing it does not encompass.
In the *Ārya-vijñāna-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is meant by the thorough understanding of consciousness as a universal characteristic?
For what reason is it called a ‘universal characteristic’?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"What is called the 'thoroughly penetrating consciousness of general characteristics' is precisely the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This consciousness possesses both obstructed objects and non-obstructed objects; it contains all phenomena and is fully equipped with all phenomena."
For example, the great ocean serves as the general designation for its waves and other phenomena; by this principle, it is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Third, the *manas* consciousness is established as the comprehensive synthesis of all consciousnesses, meaning that because the *manas* consciousness possesses eleven types of meanings, there is nothing it does not encompass.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states in its exposition of the sūtras as follows:
"Although various forms of consciousness are immeasurable, it is only the manas that transforms, and no other dharma does so. Why is this?"
This manas-consciousness is fully endowed with eleven meanings, for there is nothing it does not perform.

Fourth, a single consciousness is established to subsume all consciousnesses; that is to say, because the mental consciousness possesses seven kinds of transformative mastery, it can accordingly carry out its various functions.
In the *Saptapuruṣa-nirmita-sūtra*, it is said as follows:
"For example, there is a single illusionist who, by the power of his illusory arts, conjures seven persons.
A fool sees them and thinks there are seven persons, whereas a wise person sees that there is only one person and no other seven."
The magician of the mental consciousness is also like this: it is but a single consciousness that can perform seven functions.
Ordinary people see them and say there are seven things, whereas the awakened one sees only the mental consciousness, because there are no other seven things apart from it.
This is called the establishment of the four types of sūtras concerning the single-layered consciousness (*eka-tantra-vijñāna*).
Second is the establishment of two types of consciousness that collectively subsume all consciousnesses. What are these two?
The first is the ālayavijñāna and the second is the manovijñāna.
The term "ālayavijñāna" is used to collectively refer to the three consciousnesses of karma, transformation, and manifestation.
The term "manovijñāna" is used to collectively refer to the seven types of evolving consciousnesses.
In the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra it is said: "O Mahāmati!
To speak extensively, there are eight kinds of consciousness; to speak briefly, there are two kinds."
What are these two? First is the consciousness that discerns [objects], and second is the consciousness that discriminates phenomena.
This is explained at length, and so forth.
Third, three types of consciousness are established to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses. What are these three?
First, the ālayavijñāna; second, the manas-vijñāna; and third, the manovijñāna.
The *ālayavijñāna* is so called because it subsumes the three types of fundamental consciousness;
the *manas* is so called because it is the direct mental faculty (*manendriya*);
and the *manovijñāna* is so called because it subsumes the six types of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
In the *Maitreyavyākaraṇa-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"Furthermore, O Venerable Head!
To speak extensively, there are ten kinds of consciousness; to speak in summary, there are three kinds of consciousness."
What are the three?

First, the consciousness of the nature of subtle marks; second, the consciousness of the nature of the sense-faculties' marks; and third, the consciousness of the nature of separated marks, as explained at length.
Fourth, four types of consciousness are established to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses. What are these four?
They are the aforementioned three, with the addition of the single mind-consciousness (*eka-citta-vijñāna*).
In the *Nirnimitta-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"Although the dharmas of consciousness are immeasurable, they do not transcend four kinds of consciousness. What are these four?"

First is the fundamental single consciousness which is the basis; second is the *ālayavijñāna* which is the supporting consciousness that is maintained; third is the *manas* consciousness which maintains; and fourth is the pervasive discriminating consciousness; thus it is explained at length.
Fifth, five types of consciousness are established to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses. What are these five?
They consist of the previous four, with the addition of the consciousness that functions in accordance with and pervades all [objects].
In the *Mahāpramāṇa-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:

"Furthermore, there is a consciousness that is not subsumed under those various [specific] consciousnesses, yet pervades them all; this is because it is the so-called 'conformable, universally operating consciousness' (*anuvartaka-vijñāna*)."
Sixth, the six types of consciousness are established to comprehensively subsume all forms of consciousness. What are these six?
They are the five distinct consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, and the sixth, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In the *Catuḥsatya-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
The Buddha addressed the King of Trees:

"For the sake of sentient beings with inferior faculties, I have uttered this proclamation with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), saying that there are only the six consciousnesses and no other consciousnesses."

However, the actual underlying intention was to cause [them] to know that all consciousnesses are contained within the six types of consciousness; thus, he made such a proclamation in the midst of the great assembly.
Seventh, he established seven types of consciousness to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses.
What are the seven?
They are the aforementioned six, with the addition of the *manas* consciousness.
Thus it is stated in the *Dharmamukha-sūtra*:
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are seven kinds of consciousness-elements. What are the seven?
These refer to the six groups of consciousness together with the manas-consciousness.
These seven consciousnesses may evolve simultaneously or evolve sequentially.

Furthermore, because the seventh consciousness possesses a preeminent power, it sometimes performs the function of maintaining the ālayavijñāna, and at other times it acts as the basis for discrimination.
Eighth, eight kinds of consciousness are established to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses. What are these eight?
They consist of the preceding seven, with the addition of the ālayavijñāna.
In the *Mārgajñatā-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"The sovereign mind has eight [aspects]. What are these eight?"
First is the eye-consciousness mind-king, up to the eighth, the ripening-retribution consciousness mind-king, for all various types of consciousness do not exceed this number.
Ninth is the establishment of nine kinds of consciousness to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses.
What are the nine?
They are the aforementioned eight with the addition of the amala-vijñāna.
Thus it is said in the Vajrasamādhi Sūtra:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anabhiniveśa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what means of transformation do you transform all the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings and cause them to enter Oṃ-mā-ra?"
The Buddha said:
"All Buddhas and Tathāgatas constantly transform the various consciousnesses by means of a single awakening so that they enter the *amala*.
Tenth: establishing ten types of consciousness to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses.
What are the ten? They consist of the preceding nine with the addition of the single-minded consciousness of all things.
Thus it is stated in the *Dharmamukha Sūtra*:
Although the measure of the mind is immeasurable, it does not exceed the ten consciousnesses, as explained at length.
These are called the ten types of differently expounded sūtras.
How, then, are these ten types subsumed within the Precious Register?
How is it established?
The verse says:
Although this has been clarified in the root treatise, I shall now provide a further detailed explanation.
The prose of the sūtras is now linked to the general statements of this treatise.
The treatise says:

Although it has been clearly explained within the root treatise, we now provide a further detailed exposition for those of dull faculties, linking the scriptural passages of the sūtras to the words of this treatise.

That which is called the "consciousness of the single mind" (ekacitta-vijñāna), as generally established in the *Ekacittadharmaparyāya-sūtra*, is subsumed within the "single dharma-realm" (*ekadharma-dhātu*) according to the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*; its meaning is as previously explained.
The *ālayavijñāna* established in the *Ālayavijñāna-sūtra* is subsumed within the *ālaya* in the Mahāyāna treatises. Why is this so?
In this treatise it is stated as follows:
that which is neither identical to nor different from the conjunction of the unarisen and undying with the arisen and dying is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This consciousness has two meanings, which are capable of encompassing all phenomena and giving rise to all phenomena.
What are these two? First is the meaning of awakening; second is the meaning of non-awakening. Thus it is said.
This clarifies that the Great Manas-consciousness, which is established in general within the Sūtras, is subsumed under the "General Manas" in the Mahāyāna treatises. Why is this so?
For it is stated thus in the root treatise:
Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing: it refers to sentient beings revolving in dependence upon mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
What is the meaning of this?

It is because, based on the *ālaya-vijñāna*, there is the manifestation of ignorance and non-awakening; it is able to see, manifest, and grasp objects, giving rise to a continuous stream of conceptualization; therefore, it is called "mind" (*manas*).
This mind further has five names. What are these five?
First, it is called the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), meaning that through the power of ignorance, the mind moves without awareness.
The second is called the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), so named because it relies on the moving mind and is able to perceive objective signs.
The third is called the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*); that is to say, it is able to manifest all objective realms, just as a clear mirror manifests forms and images.

The manifesting consciousness is likewise: as the five sense objects arrive in opposition to it, they are immediately manifested without any sequence of before or after, for it arises spontaneously at all times and is always present before one.
The fourth is called the cognitive consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*), because it discriminates between defiled and pure phenomena.
The fifth is called the continuous consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*), because it is uninterrupted through its association with mindfulness.
This is because it is explained at length [in the scriptures].

That which is established as a single, unified consciousness (*eka-vijñāna*) throughout the *Saptavāstu-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Seven Transformations) is subsumed under the "single-part consciousness" (*eka-amśa-vijñāna*) in the Mahāyāna treatises.
Although the explicit description is lacking, because it possesses an underlying intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), the root treatise states as follows:

"Furthermore, that which is called 'mental consciousness' (*manovijñāna*) is precisely this continuous consciousness; because its grasping and attachment have become increasingly deep among ordinary beings, it conceives of a self and what belongs to a self through various false attachments, and by following after objects and apprehending them, it discriminates the six sense-objects—this is termed 'mental consciousness'."
This is because it has been explained at length, and so forth.
In this manner, the various sūtras should be appropriately correlated with their respective passages as they correspond.
Having already explained the door of comprehensive inclusion and establishment, next is explained the door of analyzing the characters of the *ālayavijñāna*.
How many are the different names and designations for the ālayavijñāna?
What are the characteristics according to the various explanations in the sūtras?
To which specific points do these terms and their meanings correspond?
The verse says:
There are ten Āryas, because they are mentioned differently in the sūtras:
Mahākātyāyana, Kātyāyanīputra, Kātyāyanīputra, and Kātyāyanīputra.
Pāṇḍaromāra, Kṛṣṇomāra, Karalakṣma, Vātadikṣma, Śakhanakṣma, Vākṣaṇīra.
Pure-white Kāśāla, black-and-white Kāśāla—
these ten kinds of consciousness are clearly and explicitly explained within the Mahāyāna treatises;
therefore, they should each be assigned accordingly.
The Treatise says:
The ālayavijñāna, in total, comprises ten types. Why is this so?
Because it is explained individually within the sūtras. What are these ten?
The first is called the Great Sovereign Ālayavijñāna; that is to say, it is the universal characteristic of the Great Consciousness, the meaning of which is as previously stated.
The second is called fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), which is the *ālayavijñāna*; this is because fundamental ignorance is established separately as the *ālaya*.
As it is stated in the *Daśa-vikalpa-saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*:
"King Kṣatriya-dhṛti, consciousness is itself a false dharma; it is unable to realize the essence of the single *dharmadhātu*."
All defiled phenomena take the ālayavijñāna as their root; they are produced and increase without interruption.
If the sovereign king-consciousness did not exist, the retinue of the dark category would have no basis whatsoever and could not grow or develop.
Under which category of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this ālayavijñāna be subsumed?
In this treatise it is stated as follows:

"As for the meaning of 'non-awakening' (*abodha*), it refers to not knowing, as they truly are, that the dharmas of *tathatā* are one; thus, through non-awakening, the mind arises and possesses mentation," and so forth, as explained at length.
The third is called the pure original enlightenment *ālaya-vijñāna*. This is because the natural, original wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is established separately as the *ālaya*.
As it is stated in the *Prakṛti-pratibhāsa-ālaya-sūtra*:

"The self-substance of the pure Buddha-ālaya-vijñāna is fully endowed with untainted, perfect merits; it is eternally pure and eternally determinate. It has no characteristic of being perfumed and no characteristic of transformation; its essence of wisdom is immovable and fully possesses the category of purity (*śukla-pakṣa*). Therefore, it is named the solitary, pure consciousness."
Under which category of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this *ālayavijñāna* be subsumed?
In this treatise, it is stated as follows:
"Furthermore, regarding the essential characteristics of awakening, there are four kinds of great meanings that are equal to space, like a pure mirror," and so forth, as explained at length.

The fourth is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* of the fundamentally awakened nature of both defilement and purity; that is to say, because the *dhāraṇī*-wisdom of not abiding in its own nature is established separately as the *ālaya*.
In the *Mūlapratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
At that time, the youth Prabhāketu addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Venerable One!..."

For what reason, within this unprecedented assembly that is difficult to enter, do you speak thus, stating that the wisdom of the *dhāraṇī* of dependent origination according to others is called the consciousness of the King of Laṅkā?
"What is meant by the 'King of Laṅkā'?
By what means is it used as a metaphor to demonstrate the wisdom of the *dhāraṇī* of dependent origination?
Thereupon, the Venerable One addressed the youth Prabhāvyūha:
"This King of Laṅkā constantly dwells upon Mount Malaya in the great ocean, leading a retinue of one hundred and six thousand spirits as his attendants.
All such attendants travel through various buddha-fields riding upon transformed palaces; it is only by relying upon this King of Laṅkā that they are able to journey forth."
The assembly of various spirits and ghosts spoke thus:
"We, the host of deities, possess neither majestic power nor vital strength; we have no capability for any undertaking."
"As is fitting, Great King!
We shall grant you the power and capability within our assembly.
Thereupon, the King of Laṅkā immediately granted him that supreme power at that very moment, so that they might proceed together without ever being parted.
This means that although the King of Laṅkā is not a divided body, he is able to pervade the midst of all the divine hosts, causing each one to perceive him as being the size of their own entire body.
At all times and in all places, he turns together with them without ever departing.

The wisdom that does not abide in its own nature is likewise: it can receive the perfuming of all immeasurable and boundless afflictions, defiled dharmas, and the hosts of spirits, revolving together with them without ever being separated.
"For this reason, it is difficult for me to enter the assembly and speak thus: that which follows and turns according to awakened wisdom is called the *laṅkāpura-rāja-vijñāna*.
Under what category should this *ālayavijñāna* be definitively determined?"
In this treatise, it is stated as follows:
"The intrinsically pure mind, moved by the wind of ignorance, is conjoined with ignorance; both are without form and are inseparable," and so forth, as explained at length.

The fifth is called the "characteristic of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*), which refers to the *ālayavijñāna* as the "consciousness of karma. This is because the fundamental characteristic of karma (*mūlakarmalakṣaṇa*) and the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*) are established separately as the *ālayavijñāna*.
In the *Prakṛtijñāna-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:

"The ālayavijñāna has no agent of cognition and no object of cognition; it cannot be analyzed and cannot be differentiated. It is called 'kaṇḍa' (root) solely because of its meaning of subtle movement and hidden flow."
Under which category of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this ālayavijñāna be subsumed?
In this treatise, it is stated as follows:
"Furthermore, based on non-awakening (*a-vibodha*), three kinds of characteristics arise; these are associated with and inseparable from that non-awakening."
What are the three?

First is the phase of the karma of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*). Because it relies on non-awakening (*abodha*), the movement of the mind is termed "karma"; if there were awakening, there would be no movement.
Where there is movement, there is suffering, for the fruit does not depart from its cause.

The sixth is called the "transformative characteristic" (pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa) of the transforming consciousnesses and the ālayavijñāna; that is to say, it is so called because the characteristics of the perceived objects and the transforming consciousnesses are established separately as the ālayavijñāna.
In the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*, it is stated:
"Because the ālayavijñāna has a seeing aspect that transforms and a non-seeing aspect that arises.
To what category of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this ālayavijñāna be assigned?
In this treatise it is stated as follows:
"The second is the characteristic of seeing; for it is through dependence on movement that there is seeing, whereas without movement there is no seeing.

The seventh is called the characteristic of manifestation; the manifest consciousness and the *ālaya-vijñāna* are established separately, namely, the characteristic of the objective realm and the manifest consciousness are each posited as the *ālaya*."
In the *Tattvārtha-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"It manifests and evolves in various distinct ways; it evolves through the complete performance of various distinct characteristics. For this reason, it is called the ālayavijñāna."

Furthermore, this ālayavijñāna is truly a dharma that is the maturation (vipāka) and is ethically neutral (avyākṛta), because its characteristic is pure and white, or because it is called "accomplishment" (siddhi).
Under which category of definitive analysis (viniścaya) is this ālayavijñāna subsumed?
In this treatise it is stated as follows:

"The third is the characteristic of the objective realm; because it depends upon the seeing subject, the objective realm falsely manifests, for apart from the seeing subject, there is no objective realm."

The eighth is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* of the principle of the true suchness of nature (*dharmatā-tathatā*); this is because the pure *tathatā* realized by correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is established separately as the *ālaya*.
In the *Sarvadharmasamatā-samavasaraṇa-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"There is consciousness that is consciousness, yet not subsumed under the category of consciousness; this refers to suchness, the ālayavijñāna."
Under which category should this *ālayavijñāna* be definitively classified?
It is subsumed under the true suchness (*tathatā*) that is the objective realm of pure *prajñā*.

Ninth is what is called the *ālayavijñāna* of pure initial awakening (*viśuddha-ādi-bodhi*), because the originally present, pure, and pristine initial awakening *prajñā* is established separately as the *ālaya*.
In the *Phala-pariniṣpatti-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
The Buddha addressed the King of Bodhi Trees, saying:

"The *ālaya-vijñāna* of original awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) shall never be separated from the pure fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), and the pure fundamental awakening shall never be separated from the pure consciousness of original awakening."
"Because it exists following that [object], and because that [object] exists following it, whether they are of the same kind or not of the same kind.
To what category of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this *ālaya-vijñāna* be assigned?
In this treatise it is stated as follows:
"The meaning of original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) is spoken in contrast to initial enlightenment (ādi-awakening), because initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment.

Tenth is called the defiled-and-pure initial enlightenment *ālaya-vijñāna*; that is to say, the *prajñā* of initial enlightenment, which accords with conditions, is established separately as the *ālaya*.
In the *Phala-pariniṣpatti-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"Furthermore, O King of Trees!

Just as the pure consciousness of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-vijñāna*) and the primordially pure original awakening (*prakṛti-prakṛty-ādi-bodhi*) are explained as the impure and pure initial awakening and the *ālaya-vijñāna*, so too is the original awakening of dependent origination that does not abide in its own nature."
Under which category of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this *ālayavijñāna* be subsumed?
In this treatise, it is stated as follows:

"The meaning of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*) exists because of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); and because of non-enlightenment (*a-bodhi*), initial enlightenment is said to exist."

Furthermore, because one awakens to the original source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening; because one does not awaken to the original source of the mind, it is not ultimate awakening, as explained at length.
Such meanings will be fully expounded in their own respective determinations when they are reached.
The ten types of *manas* and the six types of consciousness will be explained in sequence in the subsequent text; therefore, they are treated briefly here.

Having already explained the gate of analyzing the characters (*akṣara*) and the gate of distinguishing the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *ālayavijñāna*, next is explained the gate of the comprehensive consciousness encompassing the perfection of birth.
This consciousness has two meanings: it can encompass all phenomena and it can give rise to all phenomena.

What are these two? First is the meaning of awakening; second is the meaning of non-awakening. These collectively reveal the extraordinary and perfect characteristics of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
What is the meaning of this?
It refers to being fully endowed with two kinds of perfection. What are these two?
First is the perfection of merit; second is the perfection of faults. Regarding the perfection of merit:

it is because the meaning, words, and phrases of "awakening" (bodhi) can encompass all immeasurable, boundless, and more numerous than the sands of the Ganges qualities that are inseparable and uninterrupted, and because they can give rise to all immeasurable, boundless, and more numerous than the sands of the Ganges qualities that are inseparable and uninterrupted.

Regarding the perfection of the elimination of faults: it is because one does not perceive that meanings, words, and phrases can encompass all immeasurable and boundless faults—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—that one is able to eliminate or transcend them; and it is because they can give rise to all immeasurable and boundless states of being free from or having transcended faults—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges.

These various characteristics of the distinctions in the habitual perfusions (*vāsanā*) that encompass sentient beings will be clearly demonstrated in the section on the "Discrimination of Particular Characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-viniścaya*).
*Śikṣānanda’s Commentary on the Mahāyāna*, Fascicle Two;
*Śikṣānanda’s Commentary on the Mahāyāna*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamata under imperial decree during the Yao Qin dynasty.

Having already explained the section on the comprehensive consciousness that encompasses the perfection of birth, next is explained the section on the analytical exposition according to general characteristics.
The text states:
"That which is called the meaning of 'awakening' refers to the essence of the mind being free from the marks of thought.

Being free from the marks of thought means it is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception; it is the single mark of the Dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharmakāya."
Based on this dharmakāya, it is designated as "original enlightenment" (benjue). Why is this?
The meaning of original enlightenment is spoken of in contrast to "initial enlightenment" (shijue), because initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment.
Regarding the meaning of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*): because of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), there is non-awakening; because of non-awakening, one speaks of initial awakening.

Furthermore, because one awakens to the original source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*); because one does not awaken to the original source of the mind, it is not ultimate awakening.
The Commentary states:
Within this passage, there are two gates. What are these two?

First is the brief exposition of the gate of the establishment of original enlightenment (mūla-awakening); second is the brief exposition of the gate of the establishment of initial enlightenment (ādi-awakening).
Within the gate of original enlightenment, there are two gates. What are these two?
First is the gate of the intrinsically pure original enlightenment; second is the gate of the originally enlightened nature that is both defiled and pure.
Within the gate of initial enlightenment, there are further two gates. What are these two?
First is the gate of the pure initial awakening; second is the gate of the defiled-and-pure initial awakening.
What is meant by "pure original awakening"?
It is because the primordially existing *dharmakāya* has, from time immemorial, been fully endowed with virtues exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges, and is eternally luminous and pure.
What is meant by the "fundamental awakening of defilement and purity"?
It is because the intrinsically pure mind, being permeated by ignorance, undergoes the cycle of birth and death without interruption.
What is meant by the "initial awakening of purity"?
The untainted nature of wisdom transcends all immeasurable ignorance because it is not permeated by any ignorance.
What is meant by "the initial awakening of defilement and purity"?
Because initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) is permeated by ignorance (avidyā), it cannot be separated from it.
Thus, all such forms of awakening are attendants of wisdom (jñāna).
What principle should they realize to constitute their essential nature?
This refers to the principle of the true nature (*tathatā*) and the principle of space (*ākāśa*).
How many kinds does each of these two principles have?
Each has two, respectively.
What are called the two kinds of suchness?
First is the suchness of purity; second is the suchness of defilement and purity.
The principle of space is likewise so.
What is called "pure suchness"?
It is the suchness realized by the two kinds of pure awakening, because it is free from habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
What is called "defiled-and-pure suchness"?
The two kinds of true suchness realized by defiled and pure awakening do not exist apart from perfuming;
the principle of space is likewise so.
For what reason is it forcibly designated as "original awakening" (mūla-awakening)?
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between the letters and their referents?
The verse says:
The fundamental awakenings each possess ten; though their essence is identical to the letters and their referents, [they differ in manifestation].
"Because each is distinct, they are termed the meanings of the 'root,' the 'mirror,' and so forth.
The Treatise says:
"Fundamental awakening consists of ten for each."
What are the ten fundamental bases?

First is the fundamental basis of the substance of the root-syllable: the primordially existing *dharmakāya* is able to skillfully sustain all merits, just as a tree root can skillfully sustain all branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits so that they are not lost or destroyed.
Second is the fundamental basis of the substance of the original-syllable: the primordially existing *dharmakāya*, from time immemorial, exists by its own nature and does not begin to arise.
Third is the basis of the matter of the syllable *yuan* (far): the primordially existent *dharmakāya* is profoundly and eternally distant because it is without boundaries;
fourth is the basis of the matter of the syllable *zi* (self): the primordially existent *dharmakāya* is self-constituted by itself, as it is not constituted by another;
fifth is the basis of the matter of the syllable *ti* (substance): the primordially existent *dharmakāya* serves as the support for all its various qualities.
Sixth is the basis of the matter of the character *xing* (nature): because the meaning of the primordially existent *dharmakāya* being immutable is eternally established;
seventh is the basis of the matter of the character *zhu* (abiding): because the primordially existent *dharmakāya* abides in non-abiding, as it has no coming or going;

eighth is the basis of the matter of the character *chang* (constancy): because the primordially existent *dharmakāya* is the definitive reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), as it does not undergo transmigration.
Ninth is the basis of the matter of the syllable *kaṭha*: the primordially existent Dharmakāya is far removed from the characteristics of wind, for it is firm and immovable like a vajra.
Tenth is the basis of the matter of the syllable *ta*: the primordially existent Dharmakāya is vast and perfectly complete, pervading all without exception as its universal essence.
These are called the ten.
What are the ten awakenings?
First is the awakening to the matter of the syllable *kaṃ*, because the wisdom of *saj-jñāna* is pure, bright, and free from the accumulation of dust.
Second is the realization of the affairs of opening letters, because the *sāmbhogika-prajñā* penetrates and clearly manifests them without obstruction;
third is the realization of the affairs of the single letter, because the *sāmbhogika-prajñā* is uniquely honored, solitary, and beyond measure;
fourth is the realization of the affairs of transcending letters, because the *sāmbhogika-prajñā* is by nature liberated, having emerged from all various kinds of bonds.
Fifth is the awakening to the reality of the full letter (*pūrṇākṣara*): because the *sāmbhogika-prajñā* is fully endowed with immeasurable and manifold merits, lacking nothing;
sixth is the awakening to the reality of the illuminating letter (*avabhāsākṣara*): because the *sāmbhogika-prajñā* emits great radiance that universally illumines all immeasurable objects;
seventh is the awakening to the reality of the examining letter (*parīkṣākṣara*): because the *sāmbhogika-prajñā* is eternally constant, distinct, and free from confusion.
Eighth is the awakening to the manifestation of the meaning of syllables, because within the pure essence of *sāmbhogika-prajñā*, the retinue of all pure qualities manifests before one;
ninth is the awakening to the knowledge of the meaning of syllables, because *sāmbhogika-prajñā* penetrates all phenomena without exception;

tenth is the awakening to the realization of the meaning of syllables, because all merits of *sāmbhogika-prajñā* consist solely of awakened illumination, such that there is not a single phenomenon that is not awakened.
These are called the ten.

These ten kinds of meanings of the term "original enlightenment" (mūla-bodhi) are explained through various nuances based solely upon one single nature, the Dharma-body; they are distinguished only according to their respective meanings, while in their essential substance, they are without difference.
Among the two types of original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) mentioned here, which one is it?
It refers to the pure original enlightenment, not the defiled-and-pure original enlightenment.
What are the characteristics of the semantic distinctions between these two terms, "defiled-and-pure" and "pure" original enlightenment?
The verse says:
Within the fundamental awakening of defilement and purity, there are perhaps ten meanings for each;
among the ten matters previously explained, each possesses its own distinct nature.
The Commentary says:
Within this fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening), there may be ten meanings for each. Why is this so?
Because within each of the ten preceding meanings there is the sense of not maintaining its own nature (*asvabhāva*),
the correspondence between the characters and their referents should be understood according to what precedes.
Are these two types of awakening the same or different?
Because they are neither identical nor different, by virtue of this principle they may be either identical or different;
yet they are neither identical nor different. Therefore, they are simply both "all" and "not all."
For what reason is it forcibly termed "initial awakening" (*ādikṣaya*)?
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between its words and its referents?
The verse says:
Since beginningless time, there has never been a moment of delusion or confusion;
today, for the first time, awakening occurs, and thus it is called "initial awakening" (*ādikṣānti*).
The treatise says:

Since beginningless time, the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti-prajñā*) has never been subject to delusion; yet, because it is only now that one first awakens to this state of non-delusion, it is called "initial enlightenment" (*ādikṣānti*).

Regarding such initial enlightenment: if there were delusion first and awakening later, it would not be initial enlightenment. However, because the principle of the state of non-delusion is eternally present and always at the very beginning, it is named "initial enlightenment."
Regarding such initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), among the two types of initial awakening, which one is it?
It is the pure initial awakening, not the defiled-and-pure initial awakening.
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between the terms and matters of the defiled-and-pure initial awakening?
The verse says:
The wisdom of the pure initial awakening, because it does not abide in its own nature, is able to receive the permeation of defilement; therefore, it is called the "defiled-and-pure awakening."
The Commentary states:
Although the pure initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is devoid of delusion, it does not abide in its own nature; therefore, it can receive defiled perfuming and flow according to conditions.
For this reason, it is termed "defiled-and-pure initial awakening."
For what reason is it forcibly designated as "True Suchness" (tathatā)?
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between the word and its referent?
The verse says:
The essence of the principle of the true suchness of nature is equal and equal, one;
it possesses neither the characteristic of unity nor multiplicity, and is therefore called "true suchness" (*tathatā*).
The treatise says:
The principle of the true suchness of nature is equal and perfectly equal, possessing only a single characteristic; yet it is neither a single characteristic nor manifold characteristics.

Because it lacks a single characteristic, it is remote from identical conditions; because it lacks manifold characteristics, it is remote from diverse conditions. For this reason, it is called "true suchness" (tathatā).
Suchness (tathatā) is that which is personally realized within by two kinds of pure wisdom.
Furthermore, there are ten meanings for each instance of suchness. What are these ten?
The first is the reality of the matter of the radical syllables, up to the tenth, the reality of the matter of the collective syllables.
These ten realities correspond to ten fundamental meanings; they coexist and are inseparable, and are therefore merely designated by these names.
What are the ten suchnesses?
First is the suchness of the matter of the letter *ka* (mirror), up to the tenth, the suchness of the matter of the letter *ja* (awakening).
These ten suchnesses are associated with and coexistent with the ten meanings of awakening; they are inseparable from one another, and are therefore merely designated by these names.
Why is this so? The ten kinds of ultimate truth are the fundamental dharmakāya, possessing the skillful means of virtue.
The ten kinds of accord with reality are the *sajjñāna* (all-knowing) wisdom, possessing the skillful means of awakening.
For this reason, the words are repeated and shown in this way.
Of the two kinds of *tathatā* (suchness) mentioned here, which one is it?
It refers to the *tathatā* of purity, not the *tathatā* of both defilement and purity.
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between the letters and phenomena of defiled and pure *tathatā*?
The verse says:
The principle of pure *tathatā*, Because it does not maintain its own nature,
Yet it is capable of receiving defiled perfuming; this is called the "defiled-and-pure True Suchness.
The Commentary says:
The pure True Suchness has been equal and impartial from beginningless time; its self-nature is pure, neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, and having no place of abiding.
However, because the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) does not abide in its own nature, it moves and shifts according to conditions; therefore, it is termed "defiled and pure *tathatā*.
Such *tathatā* is that which is personally and internally realized by the two types of defiled and pure wisdom, with which it is associated, co-existent, and inseparable.
These and other such meanings should be understood by analogy with what has been explained previously.
For what reason is it forcibly designated as "space"?
What are the characteristics of the distinction between the word and its referent?
The verse says:
Space has ten meanings; although its essence is one, the referents of these meanings are each distinct, namely the meanings of non-obstruction and so forth.
The treatise says:
The principle of the nature of space has ten meanings. What are these ten?
First is the meaning of non-obstruction, because there is no obstruction among all material phenomena;
second is the meaning of pervasiveness, because there is nowhere it does not reach;
third is the meaning of equality, because there is no discrimination.
Fourth is the meaning of vastness, because it has no boundaries;
fifth is the meaning of signlessness, because it is severed from all forms and appearances;
sixth is the meaning of purity, because it is free from the accumulation of defilements.
Seventh is the meaning of immovability, because there is neither arising nor perishing;
eighth is the meaning of the emptiness of existence, because it extinguishes all that is finite;
ninth is the meaning of the emptiness of emptiness, because it is free from attachment to emptiness.
Tenth is the meaning of non-attainment, because there is no grasping.
These are called the ten.
Thus, while these ten matters differ in their functional meanings, they are simply without distinction when based upon their essential substance.
