This principle of space is that which is personally realized internally by two kinds of pure wisdom; it is associated with them, co-existent with them, and never separated from them.
Between these two spaces, which one is the true space?
This refers to the pure empty space, not the defiled-and-pure empty space.
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between the words and referents of "defiled-and-pure empty space"?
The verse says:
The principle of pure space, because it does not abide in its own nature, is able to receive the permeation of defilement; this is called "defiled-pure space.
The Treatise says:
The pure empty space is endowed with ten virtues; it possesses neither the characteristic of defilement nor the characteristic of purity.

Because the nature of empty space does not cling to its own nature, it can receive the perfuming of defilement and flow according to conditions; therefore, it is called "defiled and pure empty space."

The various gateways, such as the establishment of the perfuming agent and the perfumed object, as well as refutation and so forth, will have their principles fully revealed in the section on extensive explanation.
Having already explained the gateway of words and phenomena, next is the gateway of sequential interpretation.
The phrase "that which is called the meaning of awakening" is the general statement; from this point downward, all are specific statements.
The general [statement] universally expresses all forms of awakening, whereas the specific [statements] explain each one according to its distinct differences.

Within these distinct phrases, first the pure original enlightenment (*viśuddha-mūla-awakening*) and the pure initial enlightenment (*viśuddha-ādi-awakening*) are explained; next, the defiled-and-pure original enlightenment and the defiled-and-pure initial enlightenment are explained.
The characteristics of these [categories] can be seen according to their respective order.
That which is called the essence of mind free from the marks of thought is precisely the pure fundamental awakening (*amala-vijñāna*).
"Mind" refers to the intrinsically pure mind of self-nature; "essence" refers to the essence of the originally existing Dharma-body. Such an essence of mind is termed fundamental awakening.
That which is free from the characteristics of thought (*citta-nimitta*) demonstrates the meaning of purity.
Because it is far removed from the thought of great ignorance (*avidyā*), it is called "free from thought.
Because it is far removed from the four kinds of marks of impermanence (*anityatā-lakṣaṇa*), it is called "free from marks."

The retinue of afflictions, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, takes these five conditioned phenomena as its root; therefore, by negating the root, it is shown that the retinue is entirely empty.
"Free from the characteristics of thought" refers to the proclamation of the pure original enlightenment (*viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*).
"The word 'person' (*pudgala*)" refers to the fact that it is a person.

"Equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception" means that such an enlightened one has perfectly realized the principle of emptiness, which is fully endowed with ten kinds of virtuous meanings.

Regarding the single characteristic of the dharma-realm: one who awakens in this manner is in harmonious union with the true suchness of the dharma-realm that has been realized, because it is of a single flavor, a single characteristic, and without differentiation.
That which is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body is the excellent realization of two kinds of sublime principles.
The "purely awakened one" (viśuddha-bodhi) is precisely the self-nature and essential body of the Dharma-body Tathāgata.

Regarding the statement that this dharmakāya is designated as "original enlightenment" (mūla-awakening): it is because one takes refuge in the intrinsic virtues of the primordially existent dharmakāya, thereby establishing the designation of "pure original enlightenment."
Having already explained the pure fundamental awakening (*viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*), the pure initial awakening (*viśuddha-ādi-bodhi*) is now explained.
As for the phrase "Why is this so?", it is a word of inquiry; that is, wishing to establish the pure initial awakening, he makes such a request.
Question: What are the characteristics?
It refers to sentient beings who raise this objection:
"The originally existent Dharmakāya has, from the very beginning, been fully endowed with immeasurable qualities of nature; it is eternally luminous and pure, and eternally sovereign."

Regarding the statement that it is called "original enlightenment" (mūla-awakening) based on this meaning: at what time and by what causes and conditions is this original enlightenment endowed with all immeasurable merits such that it is named "original enlightenment"?
If one were to say:

"This primordial awakening (mūla-awakening) possesses great power of wisdom, is able to thoroughly sever all faults and afflictions, and is fully endowed with all perfected virtues," then this primordial awakening would be a state where delusion precedes and awakening follows; it would not be the luminosity of primordial awakening.
It is simply that these merits are obscured prior to their cessation and manifest after their cessation; they are not luminous by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*).
How, then, could the meaning of being "originally present" be established based on the obscuration and manifestation of delusion and awakening?

If one were to say that what was eternally severed is no longer severed, and what was eternally complete is no longer complete, it would follow that there must be an original severance and an original virtue.
This argument is also untenable, because it entails the fault of [imputing] non-existent virtues.
This means that all hindrances have been severed from the very beginning and no longer require severance;
all virtues have been complete from the very beginning and no longer require completion. Such awakening is *shijue* (initial awakening), not that *benjue* (original awakening).
Therefore, it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"That which is awakened is initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*); that which is not awakened is ignorance (*avidyā*).
To be free from these two is called original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*)."
For what reason is this said?
It is because taking refuge in the intrinsic virtues of the originally existent *dharmakāya* is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūlapratyavekṣa*).
Why is it that the meaning of original enlightenment is explained in contrast to "initial enlightenment" (*ādikṣa*)?

To directly resolve that doubt, Master Aśvaghoṣa speaks from his own realization: the pure original enlightenment (viśuddha-mūla-āśraya) is, from the very beginning, neither born nor extinguished; it is neither established as existent nor denied as non-existent, and it is neither a fault nor a virtue. It transcends the path of language and ceases all mental activity, yet it is expressed through words.

That which is fully endowed with immeasurable qualities of nature exceeding the sands of the Ganges and is termed "original enlightenment" (mūla-awakening) should be understood as follows: from beginningless time, there has existed a pure "initial awakening" (ādi-awakening) that gives rise to great power of wisdom and great power of concentration. At all times and in all places, it constantly and eternally counteracts the ocean of immeasurable, boundless faults exceeding the sands of the Ganges, and is fully endowed with immeasurable, boundless pure qualities exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
Because this refers to the pure initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*), it is designated by the term "pure original awakening" (*prakṛti-bodhi*).

The reason for this is that initial awakening is identical to original awakening; since natural initial awakening is the same as that original awakening, one can point to original awakening by means of initial awakening.
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between the perfuming of these two types of awakening?
The verse says:
The pure, fundamental, and primordial awakening, From time beginningless, has existed.
Far removed from all defilements, it is as profoundly clear and luminous as empty space.
Therefore, within this gateway, there is no dharma that can act as a perfuming agent, nor is there any dharma to be perfumed and purified; there is only the virtue of one's own house.
The treatise says:
These two types of awakening lack the distinction between the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed object (*vāsya*), for they possess only one's own true merits.
Within this gate, one should not establish the categories of the perfuming agent and the perfumed object.
If this is so, what is the meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) within this gateway?

That which is called "having perfuming" means that defiled phenomena and pure phenomena do not arise in dependence upon one another; this is precisely what is meant by "perfuming as complete transformation."
What is this perfuming?
It is because it is white and pure.
In the *Tri-kāya-mūla-astitva-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:

This is because there is fundamental awakening and initial awakening, only the perfuming of virtue and not the perfuming of afflicted virtues, and only the transformation of fulfillment and not the transformation of partiality.
Having already explained the pure initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), next I shall explain the two types of awakening that are free from intrinsic nature.

Regarding the meaning of initial awakening: because there is non-awakening (*a-bodhi*) based upon original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), and because initial awakening is said to exist based upon non-awakening, this universally demonstrates the two kinds of original and initial [awakenings] that are free from intrinsic nature.
That which is called "non-enlightenment" existing in dependence upon fundamental enlightenment (mūla-awakening) refers to fundamental enlightenment as free from intrinsic nature;
that which is called "initial enlightenment" being spoken of in dependence upon non-enlightenment refers to initial enlightenment as free from intrinsic nature.
What is the meaning of this?

Because fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) does not cling to its own nature, it readily receives the permeation of defilements; that these various defiled dharmas are able to abide and persist therein is precisely the meaning of fundamental awakening being devoid of inherent nature.

Because initial enlightenment (ādikṣaya-bodhi) does not abide in its own nature, it arises only now in dependence upon various defiled dharmas and is deceived by them; this is precisely the meaning of initial enlightenment being free from intrinsic nature.
Since initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) is able to sever all hindrances and realize all meritorious qualities, why is it said that the wisdom of initial awakening is defiled and deluded?
It is because one establishes various faults where there are no faults, thereby severing hindrances;
and one establishes various merits where there are no merits, thereby realizing the principle.
If that is so, at what time does initial awakening (ādi-bodha) become free from delusion?

It is only at the time of the path of ultimate liberation (atyanta-vimukti-mārga) that it attains final freedom from delusion, because at that time one reaches the state of non-conceptualization (amanasikāra).
The two matters concerning the fulfillment of the [perfections] will be demonstrated below.

Having already explained the section on the brief presentation of the establishment of the two types of awakening, next is the section on the detailed analysis and determination of the two types of awakening.
The text states:
What is the meaning of this?
It is like an ordinary person who, upon becoming aware that a preceding thought has given rise to evil, is able to restrain the subsequent thought so that it does not arise.
Although it is called "awakening," it is in fact non-awakening.

This is because those such as the practitioners of the Two Vehicles and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds perceive a difference in thought, yet thought itself possesses no characteristic of difference.
Because one abandons the coarse marks of conceptual attachment, it is called "similar awakening" (*sādṛśa-bodha*).

For instance, Bodhisattvas on the level of the Dharma-body awaken to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), perceiving that mindfulness has no abiding mark; because they have departed from the coarse marks of conceptual thought, this is called "partial awakening" (*prādeśika-bodha*).

When the stages of the Bodhisattva are exhausted and skillful means are perfected, there is a single thought-moment of correspondence; one awakens to the fact that when the mind first arises, it has no initial characteristic, because of being far removed from even subtle thoughts.
To realize the nature of the mind and for that mind to be eternally abiding is called ultimate awakening. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are already heading toward the stage of Buddhahood."
Furthermore, as for the arising of the mind, there is no initial characteristic that can be known.
To speak of knowing an initial characteristic is precisely what is meant by non-thought (amanasikāra).

For this reason, all sentient beings are not called awakened, because from the very beginning their thoughts have continued in succession, never having been separated from thought; thus, it is called "beginningless ignorance" (anādikālikāvidyā).
If one attains non-conceptualization (amanasikāra), one then knows the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the marks of the mind.
Because of the equality of non-conceptualization and so forth, there is in reality no distinction between initial awakening (ādi-bodhi).
Because the four phases exist simultaneously, none possess independent establishment, being fundamentally equal and identical to a single awakening.
The Treatise states:
This is the detailed exposition of the section on the definitive discernment of initial awakening (*ādikṣaṇabodhi*).
In this text there are two sections.
What are the two? First, the section on establishing the four characteristics; second, the section on establishing the subsequent realization.
Within the gateway of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), there are four types. What are these four?

First, the four characteristics of the affliction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*); second, the four characteristics of the affliction of subtlety; third, the four characteristics of impermanent merit; and fourth, the four characteristics of eternally abiding merit.
The four coarse characteristics are so called because they pertain to a long duration;
the four subtle characteristics are so called because they pertain to a short duration.
The characteristic of impermanence is the characteristic of a fault that arises in opposition to the initial emergence of virtue.
Regarding the characteristic of permanence: because it possesses the quality of permanence that is contrary to the characteristics of faults.
Within the gateway of realization, there are two gateways. What are these two?
The first is the gate of complete awakening; the second is the gate of partial awakening.
The gate of complete awakening clarifies the single awakening.
The gate of partial awakening fully displays both awakening and non-awakening.
What are called the four characteristics of the long duration?
They are so named because they are finally and completely abandoned only upon reaching the stage of ultimate liberation, starting from the stage of the ten faiths.
What are called the four characteristics of the short duration?
Since phenomena arising from causes and conditions do not endure for more than a single moment, what are called the four characteristics of initial origination? They are:
arising-arising, cessation-cessation, change-change, and duration-duration; and arising-production and duration-production. Therefore, they are called the four characteristics of initial origination.
Because they overturn afflictions and calamities, they are called "virtues.
Because they have only now begun to arise, they are called "impermanent.
What, then, are the four characteristics of permanence?
Since the virtues that have now begun to arise are fundamentally inherent,
how can they be called "one kind of awakening"?
This is because there is no duality between awakening and non-awakening.
What is meant by "awakening" and "non-awakening"?
It refers to whether awakening is permeated by defilement or not.
According to this sequence, the characteristics can be observed as they are explained.
Within these four characteristics, there are two types of sequential order. What are the two?
First, the sequential order of before and after; second, the sequential order of simultaneous existence.
Regarding "before and after": this refers to the absence of temporal distinctions between before and after within that state.
Regarding "simultaneous existence": this refers to the presence of before, after, and simultaneity within that state when time exists.
That which is "without time" is so designated in reference to the cessation of time.
Regarding the phrase "at times," this refers to periods of disorder.
What are the characteristics of their simultaneous existence and sequential order?
The verse says:
The characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation—these four types of characteristics exist simultaneously as both prior and subsequent; they are not attained through gradual transition.
Because they are simultaneous, they coexist; because they are prior and subsequent, they follow in sequence.
Because they exist together, they constitute a single characteristic; because they are distinct, they constitute four characteristics. The treatise says:

The four characteristics that exist simultaneously and follow one another are: first, the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); second, the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*); third, the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*); and fourth, the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding these four characteristics, they may occur simultaneously or sequentially.
For what reason are they said to be simultaneous?
Because they are acquired together.
For what reason are they called "prior" and "subsequent"?
Because of the distinction between the coarse and the subtle.
As for the phrase "not attained through gradual transformation," this is specifically intended to demonstrate the meaning of simultaneity.
For what reason is it called "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*)?
Because it occurs at one and the same time.
For what reason is it called "successive" (*anupūrva*)?
Because of their sequence,
these four characteristics are one in terms of their coexistence, yet four in terms of their grossness and subtlety.
At this point, at what time do they occur simultaneously?

When fundamental ignorance perfumes the true mind, at that time it gives rise to the four marks in their entirety. It is characterized by an ignorance and lack of awareness regarding the true nature of all phenomena, which pervasively establishes itself; thus, the immeasurable afflictions, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, are able to obscure the inherently pure mind, such that there is no day of returning to its source. For this reason, these are called the "four marks existing simultaneously."
Why are they called "arising" and so forth, up to "cessation"?
What are the characteristics of the distinctions between these terms and their meanings?
The verse says:
When the great ground of abiding ignorance perfumes the original enlightenment, three kinds of subtle marks arise; therefore, it is called the "mark of arising.
The Commentary says:
When fundamental ignorance perfumes the original enlightenment, three kinds of characteristics arise; therefore, they are called the "characteristics of arising. What are these three?
First, the characteristic of independent activity; second, the characteristic of independent conformity; and third, the characteristic of combined movement.
Regarding the characteristic of the independent karma, it does not take the essence of ignorance, but rather takes the activity of ignorance.
Regarding the characteristic of the independent following, it does not take the essence of original enlightenment, but rather takes the function of original enlightenment.
Regarding the characteristic of movement as a combination of both: it is because one grasps the characteristic of movement through their conjunction.
These three are collectively designated as the "characteristic of arising" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*);
the designation "arising" is established because it refers to the very first moment of birth.
Regarding the characteristics and meanings of the "abiding" (*sthiti*) aspect, what are its characteristics?
The verse says:
The abiding aspect has four kinds: The aspect of transformation and the aspect of manifestation,
The characteristic of wisdom and the characteristic of continuity—these are called the four kinds.
The Treatise says:
There are four characteristics of abiding.

What are the four? First, the characteristic of transformation; second, the characteristic of manifestation; third, the characteristic of cognition; and fourth, the characteristic of continuity. These are called the four.
Regarding these four characteristics, for what reason is the one called "abiding" (sthiti)?

Herein, the meaning of abiding is distinguished according to its application: that is to say, if one speaks of its characteristic of abiding based on the aspect of transformation, it is called the characteristic of abiding because it is able to sustain and maintain the perfuming of consciousness.

If one speaks of its characteristic of abiding (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) based on its manifest aspect, it is called the characteristic of abiding because it can maintain and sustain the perfuming of material forms (rūpa-lakṣaṇa).

If one speaks of its characteristic of abiding based on its cognitive aspect (jñāna-lakṣaṇa), it is called the characteristic of abiding because it can maintain and sustain the six kinds of gradual, successive defilements associated with discriminative cognition.

If one explains the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) based on the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati*), it is called the characteristic of abiding because it is able to maintain and sustain the continuity of the defiled discriminative consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*).
This refers to its subtle aspect rather than its coarse aspect.
What are the characteristics of the meaning of the term "distinctive characteristic" (*vilakṣaṇa*)?
The verse says:
The distinctive characteristic is of two kinds: Grasping at signs and conceptualizing names.
These two kinds of characteristics are precisely the category of the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*).
The treatise says:
There are two types of distinct characteristics.
What are these two? First is the characteristic of grasping, and second is the characteristic of calculating names; these two characteristics pertain directly to the category of human attachment.
For what reason are these two characteristics called "distinctive characteristics"?

If one speaks of its distinct characteristic (*vilakṣaṇa*) based on grasping, it is able to take as objects all infinite distinct characteristics; according to those various characteristics, the coarse conceptualizing consciousness is able to grasp at difference and thus itself becomes different. Therefore, it is called the "distinct characteristic."

If one speaks of their distinct characteristics based on names, names are established according to those characteristics; because one gives rise to attachment based on these names, they are called "distinct characteristics.
As for the meaning of the term "characteristic of cessation," what are its characteristics?
The verse says:
There are two kinds of the characteristic of cessation: the arising of karma and its retribution.
It destroys prior divergent states of mind and causes one to experience suffering; this is called cessation.
The treatise says:
There are two aspects of cessation. What are these two?
First is the characteristic of initiating karma; second is the characteristic of suffering bound by karma.
These two characteristics destroy the preceding state of diversity and cause one to undergo the wheel of suffering; therefore, they are called the characteristic of cessation.
Furthermore, when undergoing the wheel of suffering, one is able to extinguish all immeasurable categories of wholesome qualities; therefore, it is called the characteristic of extinction.
Furthermore, when karma is initiated, the Buddha-nature and its roots of goodness are gradually diminished and extinguished; therefore, it is called the characteristic of extinction.
Having explained simultaneous existence, next the sequential [existence] will be explained.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
The characteristics of cessation, duration, change, and arising—
these four types of characteristics vary in number according to whether one's power of wisdom is inferior or superior.
The treatise says:

Regarding the sequence of the preceding and succeeding [phases]: first is the characteristic of cessation, second is the characteristic of change, third is the characteristic of abiding, and fourth is the characteristic of arising; these four characteristics vary in their increase and decrease according to the measure of wisdom.

What is the meaning of this? Those at the stage of faith lack one [of the four marks] and possess three; those at the stage of the three types of worthies lack two and possess two; within the ten stages, in the ninth stage they lack three and possess one; in the tenth stage they lack one coarse portion and possess one subtle portion; and in the stage of the Tathāgata, the four marks are entirely absent, being ultimately pure. Therefore, it is said that their increase and decrease differ.
The section on the establishment of the framework has already been explained; next, the section on the sequential interpretation will be explained.
Based on those four characteristics, there are five stages that clarify the distinctions of awakening. What are these five?

First is the stage of the ten faiths; second is the stage of the three worthies; third is the stage of the nine grounds; fourth is the stage of the fulfillment of causes; and fifth is the stage of the fulfillment of fruits.
Within each of the first four stages, there are four matters.

What are these four? First, the practitioner who is progressing; second, the causal characteristics of practice; third, the characteristics of the cause and fruit of practice; and fourth, the characteristic of being permeated by and separated from both [cause and fruit]. Within the fifth stage, there are only three matters.
What are the three?

First, that which is able to bring to fulfillment; second, the aspect of the remedial practice; and third, the aspect of ultimate fulfillment. One should understand the corresponding contemplation according to this sequence.

Regarding the statement that "the first stage is like that of an ordinary person," this refers to the practitioner who is still in the process of progressing; their station is within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Because they have not yet attained the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), they are termed an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Having emerged from false concentration is called being "awakened.

To be aware that a preceding thought gave rise to evil is a manifestation of the causal characteristics of practice; that is to say, prior to attaining entry into the ten stages of faith, one was unaware and unconscious of the two kinds of cessation-characteristics as being great calamities, thereby committing all manner of various evil karmas and universally undergoing immeasurable fruits of suffering, constantly cycling through the five destinies and four modes of birth without a moment's rest.

Now, by virtue of having received the sublime conditions of spiritual friends and the holy teachings on purity, one is able to enter the stage of the ten faiths; therein, one realizes that all evil karma is an ultimate transgression and understands that all bitter fruits of suffering are truly devoid of joy.
To say that one "becomes aware" when a prior thought arises as evil is to demonstrate the meaning of the characteristic of awakening to cessation.

Thus, being able to stop a subsequent thought so that it does not arise demonstrates the characteristic of the causal aspect of practice; this means that within this stage, the remedial path has only just begun and its power is extremely weak, which is why it is called "old," whereas from the moment the mind is generated onward, the remedial path is initiated and becomes increasingly sovereign.

Furthermore, whereas previously one was unaware and constantly gave rise to unwholesome karma, now, because of this awareness, there arises a sense of shame and remorse such that one no longer commits unwholesome deeds; thus, the defilement of the characteristic of cessation is stilled and does not arise.

Regarding the statement, "Although it is called awakening, it is in fact non-awakening," this demonstrates the characteristics of both permeation (*vāsanā*) and detachment. That is to say, one awakens to the knowledge that phenomena characterized by cessation are in reality defects; since those factors of the category of cessation do not perform the act of ceasing, it is called "permeation-detachment."

In that "Chapter on the Characteristic of Cessation," it is stated that from time immemorial the essential nature has been pure and is in truth a merit; yet, because this is neither known nor realized, it is said to be "perfumed together" (*vāsanā-sahita*).
The meaning of these words and phrases flows far back and should extend even to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is shown that awakening and non-awakening are mutually interpenetrating because they are of one flavor.

Regarding the second stage, the mention of those such as the wisdom of contemplation of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds refers to practitioners who are heading toward [enlightenment], whose stage is within the Three Degrees of Worthiness (trīṇi śaikṣāṇi).

In this stage, because one has realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and attained mastery over the untainted (*anāsrava*), being free from doubt and fear, the two vehicles are merely explained in general as being identical to those of the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, this demonstrates that all followers of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) practice the path of the bodhisattva, thereby attaining entry into the ocean of the stage of sovereign great enlightenment.

Regarding "awakening to the difference in thought," this indicates the characteristics of the causal phase of practice; it means that two kinds of differences mutually provide support, enabling one to grasp the marks of objects, give rise to attachment and the seeking of names, and differentiate verbal expressions.
Therefore, there is no satiety; the proliferation of "I" and "mine" becomes ever more intense, and as攀緣 (pāraṇa) and discursive thought increase, they continue throughout the day without ceasing.

Now, by initiating the *prajñā* of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and establishing skillful means (*upāya*), the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) manifests before one. One realizes that the originally awakened pure mind has been asleep through ignorance (*avidyā*) and has given rise to all obstacles within the realm of differentiated marks. Gradually, moment by moment, one enters into correspondence with the wisdom of detachment; from those dream-like thoughts, one attains awakening. For this reason, it is said: "one awakens to the difference in thoughts."

The phrase "mindfulness without distinct characteristics" reveals the characteristics of the cause and fruit of practice; this is because within the correct mindfulness of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*), the two kinds of distinct characteristics do not exist.

Regarding "by abandoning the coarse marks of conceptual attachment," this indicates the condition of non-differentiation; that is to say, the mental consciousness possesses two types of discrimination, by which it is able to discriminate all phenomena.
What are the two? First, coarse discrimination; second, subtle discrimination.
The coarse arises as greed, hatred, and so forth, because it is able to skillfully discriminate between favorable and unfavorable objects.
The subtle refers to the conceptualization of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*), because it flows continuously.
What is now to be abandoned is that coarse conceptualization, not the subtle conceptualization.
This is because the subtle conceptualization is completely abandoned at the stage of the Joyous (*pramuditā*).

The phrase "therefore it is called similar cognition" serves both to conclude the preceding section and to provide a rough demonstration of the mutual exclusion between perfuming (*vāsanā*) and separation (*viyoga*).
Within this context, there are two kinds of similarity.
What are the two? First, similarity with those of a different class; second, similarity with those of the same class.
Similarity with those of a different class refers to similarity with the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding "similar and analogous," this refers to the similarity with Bodhisattvas.
The emptiness of the two vehicles is made analogous to the emptiness of the three stages of worthies (śaikṣa);

the emptiness of the expedient means of the Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthies is made analogous to the Pure Mind Ground (śuddhacitta-bhūmi). For this reason, they are collectively termed "analogous awakening."
Regarding the third category, those described as "Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas" and so forth, these are practitioners who are progressing toward realization and reside in the ninth stage (*bhūmi*).

For a Bodhisattva at the ninth stage, the *tathatā* dharmadhātu constitutes their own body, and the wisdom of *prajñā* constitutes their own mind. Having already emerged from defilements and having severed all fetters and obstructions, they are pure, lucid, unimpeded, and sovereign; therefore, they are called Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas.

"Awakening through the foundations of mindfulness" indicates the characteristics of the causes for cultivation; that is to say, the four modes of abiding can, at all times, give rise to the conceptualization of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*), while the fundamental awakening (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*) is able to cause [that grasping] to fall asleep.
The mind of original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti) has been dreaming within the state of abiding in signs; unable to awaken, it remains in a state of madness and confusion.

Now, the sun of initial enlightenment (ādikarmika-prajñā) has risen, illuminating the darkness of the deluded state of abiding in signs. Initial enlightenment is the nature of non-discriminative correct wisdom, whereas the deluded state of abiding in signs is the nature of discrimination. Because existence and non-existence, as well as awakening and confusion, are utterly contradictory, they cannot coexist.
When this principle is clearly manifest before one, it is therefore said that one awakens to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
That mindfulness has no abiding characteristic (*an-avasthita-lakṣaṇa*) demonstrates the characteristic of the cause and effect of practice.

The phrase "by being free from the characteristics of coarse conceptualization" indicates the condition of non-abiding; this is because the four types of abiding characteristics appear extremely coarse when compared to those arising characteristics.
Fearing that the limits of arising and abiding might become mutually confused, it is said that one should cease such conceptualization and practice contemplation.

These four kinds of deluded characteristics of abiding are, in their respective order, abandoned one by one within the Ground of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the Ground Beyond the Three Realms of Existence (*tridhātu-samatikrāntā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Tranquil Purity (*śāntaviśuddhā-bhūmi*), and the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

The phrase "therefore it is called partial awakening" serves to conclude the preceding section; it also roughly demonstrates that while one has abandoned both types of characteristics through cultivation, the subtle thought of the characteristic of arising has not yet been transcended.
Regarding the fourth position, which speaks of those who have "exhausted the Bodhisattva-bhūmi," these are those who are progressing toward it.
Within this phrase, there are naturally two types of persons. What are these two?
The first is the perfection of the cause, and the second is the perfection of the fruit.
The perfection of the cause refers to the exhaustion of all stages of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*).
The perfection of the fruit refers to the ultimate fulfillment of the fruit of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
The former person’s antidote counteracts the combined moving aspect, while the latter person’s antidote counteracts the independent activity aspect and great ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because the independent secondary aspect is not a dharma subject to cessation, there is no path of antidote for it.
From this point onward, two kinds of perfection are revealed.

"Fulfilling the means through a single moment of correspondence" reveals the perfection of the cause; that is to say, within this stage, there are two types of vajropama-samādhi (diamond-like concentration).
What are the two? First is the vajra of skillful means (*upāya*), and second is the vajra of the essential body (*svabhāva*).
For one whose conduct is stainless, these two kinds of vajras are metaphorically taken as the essence of samādhi; therefore, by mentioning the path, that person is designated.
The statement that "when the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic" is a manifestation of the perfection of the fruit.

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom appears clearly before one, penetrating all things without exception and exhausting all depths without limit; it is of one essence with the Dharma-realm and has no equal. Consequently, the fundamental ignorance of the individual karma-characteristic cannot exist independently.
Equal to empty space, it is of one mark and yet markless, for there is no initial thought.
Because one is far removed from even subtle thoughts, one perceives the nature of the mind; this mind is then eternally abiding.
The term "ultimate awakening" (atyanta-bodhi) reveals the characteristic of the perfection of *ādi-bodhi* (*prajñā*), because one has attained the awakening to non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Therefore, when the Sūtra states, "If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought (*amanasikāra*), they are heading toward the stage of Buddhahood," this is a citation of scripture to praise what has been taught here.
What meaning does this scriptural passage serve as proof for?
It serves as proof for the fruit of Buddhahood.
How does it serve as proof?
This means that within the state of Buddhahood, one realizes and achieves the distancing from two kinds of mindfulness. What are these two?
First, the mindfulness of great ignorance; second, the mindfulness of subtle karmic characteristics.

In this way, these two types of thought—the state of extreme liberation and its opposite—cannot function simultaneously as they are mutually exclusive; therefore, it is said that the fruit of Buddhahood is without thought.
If there is no deluded thought, what kind of thought could there possibly be?
It is because of right mindfulness. What is called right mindfulness?
It is because it is associated with ten virtues.
What are the ten? First is the merit of renunciation, because it distances one from all places of difficulty;
second is the merit of identical essence, because all defiled phenomena return to the self.
Third is the merit of eternal abiding, because it is free from the fault of having a beginning;
fourth is the merit of a single flavor, because it perfects initial enlightenment as the eternally present original enlightenment;
fifth is the merit of being free from both, because it is detached from all phenomena of defilement and purity.
Sixth is the merit of returning and transforming, because it brings about birth throughout all realms of existence;
seventh is the merit of non-abiding, because there is no place of abiding in any location;
eighth is the merit of cultivation, because one cultivates the ten thousand practices for the sake of all sentient beings.
Ninth is the perfection of merit, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to the path of enlightenment;
tenth is the merit of space, because the various merits previously described have, from the very beginning, been empty of intrinsic nature and non-existent.
These are called the ten.
These ten virtues, together with the initial moment of ultimate liberation, proceed and arise simultaneously, without sequence, turning all at once; this is called right mindfulness.
The scriptural passages cited do not go beyond this meaning; one should examine them carefully.

Furthermore, regarding the arising of the mind, there is no initial characteristic (ādi-lakṣaṇa) that can be known; yet, to speak of "knowing the initial characteristic" refers precisely to the state of non-thought (amanasikāra). This is intended to eliminate doubt and give rise to resolute conviction (adhimukti).
It refers to those sentient beings who harbor such doubts:
"When the path of ultimate liberation meets with original enlightenment (primal awareness), does one know that something has arisen subtly at the very beginning?
Or does one know that nothing has arisen?"
If one knows that there is [a first thought], then the path of ultimate liberation must not be without mindfulness.
Why is this? Because one knows that there is a first thought; since there is a first thought, [the path] cannot be without mindfulness.
If one knows that [the path] does not exist, then the path of ultimate liberation could not possibly exist.
Why is this? Since there is no initial thought, in dependence upon the absence of what thought could the existence of the path of liberation be established?
Because of such doubts, I now provide this clarification:

the characteristics of the objects of knowledge have been empty of intrinsic nature from the very beginning, and the wisdom that knows them has likewise never had a time of arising from the very beginning.
Since there is neither the characteristic of that which is perceived nor the wisdom that perceives it, how could one say that there exists a subtle initial characteristic that can be known by wisdom?
To speak of knowing an initial characteristic is itself a demonstration of the principle of non-thought.

Why is this so? Although the principle of the dharma-nature has neither the initial characteristic of that which is known nor the initial awakening wisdom that knows it, one is nonetheless able to penetrate the absence of characteristics in what is known and the absence of wisdom in the knower; yet this awakening to nothingness is by no means a void non-existence.
Therefore, for the time being, we shall don this principle and speak thus, knowing only the initial characteristic.

For this reason, all sentient beings are not called "awakened," because from the very beginning their thoughts have been in continuous succession, never having been separated from mentation; thus, what is called "beginningless ignorance" establishes the aforementioned meaning of "non-mentation."

This means that from the stage of the *vajra* downward, all sentient beings have not yet emerged from the mental state of great ignorance (*avidyā*), which is characterized by the individual karmic marks of their own power.
This demonstrates that all sentient beings are called "sentient beings" because they possess mentation, whereas all Buddhas are called "Buddhas" because they have attained non-mentation.
From this point onward, it is shown that the realm of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) is all-pervasive and perfect.

This means that the Great Awakened One has reached the other shore, because he universally knows that the single mind of all immeasurable sentient beings flows and revolves through the four phases (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*).
As the original text states: "If one attains non-thought (amanasikāra), one immediately knows the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the marks of the mind.
For what reason is it known in this way?
Because when one attains one's own non-thought, all sentient beings attain it equally; as the original text says: "Because of the equality of non-thought."
For what reason, when a single practitioner attains the state of non-thought, do all sentient beings likewise attain non-thought?
It is because every single sentient being possesses their own original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
What is the meaning of this?

It means that when the initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) of a single practitioner becomes perfected and identical to the original awakening (*mūlapratibodha*), it is universally identical within the original awakening-minds of all immeasurable sentient beings, rather than being limited to one's own original awakening.
Why is this so? Because the self-nature of original enlightenment pervades the realm of sentient beings, reaching everywhere without exception.

When a pure awakened one attains the state of non-thought, do all sentient beings likewise attain non-thought? When a pure awakened one cuts off ignorance, can all sentient beings likewise cut it off?
If that were so, what would be the fault?

If, at the moment the *ādikṣāntika* (initial awakening) severs ignorance, all sentient beings were simultaneously to sever it as well, why did you previously state that from the stage of the *vajra* [samādhi] downward, because all sentient beings have not yet escaped the great ignorance of the conceptualization of individual karma (*kevala-karma-lakṣaṇa-mahāmoha*), they are not called "awakened"?

If all sentient beings have not yet attained liberation from beginningless ignorance, yet were to attain non-conceptualization (amanasikāra) simultaneously with the Buddhas, then the meaning of "equality through non-conceptualization" would be merely a verbal expression devoid of actual reality; how then could it be said that all sentient beings possess both original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) and initial awakening (ādi-awakening)?
There are two gates for resolving this difficulty.
What are the two? First, resolution according to one's own school; second, resolution by way of comparison with others.

Regarding the definitive conclusion of our own school: this is the primary thesis of this treatise. It is intended to demonstrate that all sentient beings share a single, undifferentiated continuum; therefore, when one practitioner exhaustively severs beginningless ignorance, all sentient beings likewise sever it completely, and when one practitioner fulfills the stage of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), all sentient beings likewise attain fulfillment.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Sūtra on the Primordial Existence of the Three Bodies*:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
"I have attained perfect enlightenment by means of two aspects."
What are these two? First, the equality of abandonment; second, the equality of attainment.

Regarding the equality of abandonment: when my path of ultimate liberation first arises, all the immeasurable, beginningless ignorance possessed by all sentient beings is completely and suddenly severed at once.

Regarding the phrase "attaining equality" (*samatā-lābha*): when I first attained enlightenment and fulfilled *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*, all sentient beings were likewise fully perfected; this is called "equality.
As for the definitive judgment based on distinction:
taking the state of perfection as the standard and comparing it to the realm of sentient beings, there is not a single dharma that is not pure.

When all sentient beings look toward the Unsurpassed Honored One, they enter the treasury of ignorance where there is no conscious perception; yet all are entirely pure and without obstruction, and the principle of non-thought and so forth is thereby established.
Entering the treasury of ignorance (*avidyā-kośa*), there is nothing to be perceived; thus, the aforementioned text contains no contradiction.
This single instance should serve as a starting point for extensive investigation.

From this point onward, the various initial awakenings (*ādi-bodhi*) are integrated so as to become identical with the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). That is to say, regarding the initial awakening that fulfills the fifty-one stages, in reality there are no distinctions of progressive superiority or gradual succession, nor is there any ultimate limit of perfection.

Why is this so? Because all aspects of initial awakening abide simultaneously with the four phases; none possess independent existence. From the very beginning, they are of a single flavor and equal in nature, perfectly complete, in accord with the non-dual realization of the single characteristic.

In accordance with the fundamental nature, there is in fact no distinction between original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), because the four marks exist simultaneously, none of which possess independent self-existence, as they are from the beginning equal and identical to a single awakening.
The *Mahādhāraṇī-sūtra* states as follows:

"The *prajñā* of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) within the category of the realization of the characteristic of cessation exists simultaneously with the state of the characteristic of cessation; when there is no time of cessation, initial awakening likewise ceases to exist."

The *ārambha-lakṣaṇa* (initiation) stage of *ādikṣānti-prajñā* (initial awakening wisdom) exists simultaneously with the state of the initiation characteristic, and when that state of no-initiation exists, the initial awakening accordingly ceases to exist.

The *sthiti-lakṣaṇa* (abiding) stage of *ādikṣānti-prajñā* exists simultaneously with the state of the abiding characteristic, and when that state of no-abiding exists, the initial awakening accordingly ceases to exist.

The *prajñā* of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) that realizes the aspect of arising exists simultaneously with the state of arising; when there is no arising, initial awakening likewise ceases to exist. Why is this so?
All initial awakening cannot arise by itself; it must depend upon defiled phenomena before it can arise. All defiled phenomena cannot be extinguished by themselves;

they must depend upon the power of wisdom before they can be utterly extinguished. To speak extensively, this extends even to the fact that from the very beginning, the intrinsic nature of all defiled phenomena has been empty and non-existent.

Furthermore, initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) originally does not involve the conceptualization of existence within a state of non-existence; because it evolves simultaneously [with fundamental awakening], it is not termed "correct" (*samyak*).

Having explained the section on the detailed exposition of the determination of initial awakening, next is the section on the detailed exposition of the determination of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
The text says:
Furthermore, fundamental enlightenment, following along with defilement, gives rise to two kinds of characteristics that are not separate from that fundamental enlightenment. What are these two?
The first is the characteristic of the purity of wisdom; the second is the characteristic of inconceivable activity.

Regarding the characteristic of the purity of wisdom: it means that by relying on the permeation of the power of the Dharma and through the fulfillment of skillful means in accordance with reality, one destroys the characteristics of the synthetic consciousness (*saṃhatavijñāna*) and extinguishes the characteristics of the continuous mind (*prabandhacitta*), thereby manifesting the wisdom of the Dharmakāya in its pure essence.
What is the meaning of this?

All characteristics of mind-consciousness are ignorance; yet the characteristic of ignorance does not depart from the nature of awakening. It is neither destructible nor indestructible, like the waters of the great ocean stirred into waves by the wind.

The characteristics of water and wind are inseparable; yet water is not of the nature of motion. If the wind ceases, the characteristic of motion is extinguished, but the moist nature remains undestroyed.

Thus, the intrinsically pure mind of sentient beings is stirred by the wind of ignorance; the mind and ignorance are both formless and inseparable from one another, yet the mind is not of a nature that moves. If ignorance ceases, the continuity [of delusion] is extinguished, for the nature of wisdom is indestructible.

Regarding the characteristic of inconceivable activity: by relying on the purity of wisdom, one is able to produce all kinds of supreme and wondrous realms. That is to say, the characteristics of immeasurable merit are eternally uninterrupted; they manifest in various ways, spontaneously corresponding to the faculties of sentient beings, because they bring about their benefit.
The Commentary states:
This is the section on the detailed exposition of the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) as it accords with defilement.
Within this text, there are two gates.
What are these two? First is the gateway of the purity of the originally existing nature-wisdom; second is the gateway of unimpeded mastery over karmic functions.
Within the first gateway, there are further two gateways.
What are these two? First is the gate of not guarding one's own nature but following conditions; second is the gate of counteracting all karmic obstacles.
Within the second gate, there are further two gates.
What are these two?
First is the gate of accordance with capacities and faculties; second is the gate of the immovable original nature, which is eternally quiescent.
These four gates should be assigned accordingly as they are explained.
"Intrinsic awakening following defilement" is a term of exclusion, intended to distinguish it from the wisdom of pure intrinsic awakening.
What meaning does this phrase seek to demonstrate?
It is intended to demonstrate the sense of being susceptible to perfuming.

Because fundamental enlightenment directly undergoes the permeation of ignorance, does not maintain its own nature, and functions unimpededly in accordance with conditions at all times, it is therefore called "fundamental enlightenment following defilement."
These very words and phrases are merely designated according to the defilements they follow.
From this point onward, the text directly reveals the essence and characteristics of the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) which follows them;
it gives rise to two kinds of differentiated aspects that are never separated from that fundamental awakening.

What are these two? First, the mark of the purity of wisdom; second, the mark of inconceivable activity. These two kinds of sublime marks function and evolve together with the fundamental awakening and intrinsic wisdom that follow defilement, for they are never separated from one another.
What are the characteristics of the pure aspect of the wisdom of such fundamental enlightenment?
The verse says:
It destroys and eliminates all obstacles, And manifests the Dharma-nature body.
Because true wisdom is pure, it is called the "characteristic of the purity of wisdom.
The Commentary says:
Severing all evils and cultivating all virtues, being fully endowed with merit and perfect in wisdom, and thereby adorning the Dharma-body—this is called the characteristic of the purity of wisdom.
What power is required to sever all obstacles?
It requires the power of fulfillment.
How many such powers of fulfillment are there?
Because there are two kinds. What are these two?
First, the power of the method of fulfilling the perfuming of the Dharma; second, the power of the method of fulfilling practice in accordance with reality.
These two kinds of power of skillful means have been spontaneously and eternally present since beginningless time, not arising for the first time.

Among these two, by means of the fulfillment of the power of skillful means through the perfuming of the power of the Dharma, one destroys fundamental ignorance and the karma-characteristic of independent power.

By virtue of fulfilling the power of skillful means through practice in accordance with reality as it is, one extinguishes the characteristics of karma associated with both [subject and object], the characteristic of the perceiving faculty, the characteristic of the manifesting aspect, the characteristic of discriminative cognition, and the characteristic of continuity.
Because the solitary karmic characteristic of fundamental ignorance has been destroyed, the body of intrinsic nature manifests clearly before one.
Because the continuity of the characteristics of combined and concurrent conditions has ceased, the true wisdom of prajñā is pure, pristine, and luminous.

Regarding the characteristic of the purity of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as it is in the original [text]: this means that by virtue of the power of the Dharma and its permeation (*vāsanā*), one practices according to reality and brings the skillful means (*upāya*) to fulfillment;

thus, the characteristics of the synthetic consciousness (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*) are shattered and the characteristics of the continuous mind (*prabandha-citta*) are extinguished, so that the wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) manifests in its pure essence.
For what reason are the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of faith (*adhimukti*) not briefly displayed?
Because their sequence has already been clearly explained previously.

For what reason, in this present section, does it begin with the remediation of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and conclude with the remediation of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodhalakṣaṇa*)?
This is intended to distinguish it from the sequential awakening of *ādikṣāntika-prajñā*.
Why is it that initial awakening (*ādikṣāntika*) turns away from the ordinary toward the sacred, progressing upward and further upward in a sequential transformation;
whereas fundamental awakening (*mūlaprakṛti*), following its defilements, turns away from the sacred toward the ordinary, descending lower and further downward in a sequential transformation?
Because it is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
do these two revolutions occur simultaneously,
or do they occur sequentially?
Since they are determined to exist at one time, there is no sequence of before and after.
In which sūtra are such meanings clearly and explicitly taught? They are taught in the *Sūtra on Realization* (*Upadeśa-sūtra*).
How is it stated in that sutra? That is to say, in the *Sūtra on the Realization of the Teaching*, it is stated as follows:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī posed ten thousand questions to the Tathāgata; thereupon, the Tathāgata provided one hundred thousand answers to resolve those doubts and difficulties, opening up the Bodhisattva’s inquiries."
Having answered those questions in their proper sequence, he then addressed the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī,
saying: "For what reason, O Noble One,
do you not ask about one matter, but instead ask about other matters?"
“It would be fitting, Son of the Buddha, for you to inquire further so as to bring forth an exposition; ask the Tathāgata for the sake of the benefit of yourself and others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason did you proclaim these words among the great assembly:
"Listen attentively, O sons of the Buddha! From the state of an ordinary being bound by all fetters, I have traversed all the stages and perfected the ocean-like causes of practice."
Adorning the fruit of great enlightenment,
having traversed all stages, and bringing all myriad practices to completion,
one attains the foremost stage of faith and enters the ocean of the treasury of ignorance.
"Thus these two great matters occur simultaneously, not sequentially.
"I and this entire ocean-like assembly of all beings are all harboring doubts, with no time for liberation."
"It is well, World-Honored One!
Please employ various skillful means to reveal this appropriately for the sake of the sons of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Dhāraṇī, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall briefly explain its essentials for you. Good son!
These two great matters reveal two kinds of prajñā-awakening wisdom."
What are these two? The first is the wisdom of initial awakening (ādikṣaṇabodhi-prajñā), and the second is the wisdom of original awakening (mūlabodhi-prajñā). Good son!

Initial awakening wisdom (*ādikṣānti-prajñā*) refers to the gradual emergence from the stage of those bound by all fetters, continuing until the ultimate path is developed through the perfection of causal practices at the diamond-like stage (*vajropama*). At that point, fundamental ignorance and its underlying ground (*mūlāvidyā-ālaya-bhūmi*) are suddenly severed; the sun of awakening shines perfectly, pervading everywhere without exception. Therefore, it is called initial awakening wisdom.

"Good son! Original awakening-prajñā (prakṛti-awakening wisdom) gradually distances itself from its pure nature until, reaching the initial stage of faith and the ultimate wisdom, it enters the ocean of ignorance by severing the aspect of cessation and moves and turns according to conditions; therefore, it is called original awakening-prajñā."

Thereupon, when Dhāraṇī and the great assembly heard these words, they realized that all dharmas are of a single characteristic and a single essence; yet they are neither of a single characteristic nor of a single essence. They are empty and ineffable, and even this emptiness and ineffability are themselves empty.
Furthermore, because the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is also the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), is also eternally abiding (*nitya*), is also definitive (*niyata*),
and is also substantially existent (*dravyasat*), the following section provides a detailed, separate explanation to elucidate the causes and conditions.
"What is the meaning of this? constitutes the general question.
"Because all characteristics of consciousness are ignorance" constitutes the general answer.

That which is called the various consciousnesses of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which give rise to various objects of cognition (*ālambana-pramāṇa*) and deliberate upon all immeasurable realms, or that which clings to the characteristics of all realms and does not relinquish them—all these are portions of the essence of ignorance. This establishes the two meanings of "destruction" explained above.
From this point onward, the distinctions between what is to be abandoned and what is not to be abandoned are demonstrated.
In this regard, is ignorance definitively subject to abandonment,
or is it not subject to abandonment?
What is the basis for this doubt?
If that which can be severed were [the true nature], then the mind of original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) would also be subject to severance. Why is this so?

Ignorance and the fundamental awakening-nature wisdom of defiled phenomena proceed together and evolve together, never being separated from one another; this is like a sleeping person and a waking person, who proceed and evolve together without being parted.
Nor can it be said that when the sleeping person is cut, the awakened person is not wounded, because their continuity is one.
Nor can it be said that at the time the awakened person is attained, the sleeping person becomes empty and non-existent, because their continuity is identical.
If one says they are different, the fault is too great.
If it cannot be severed, then the intrinsically pure mind would be perpetually shrouded by ignorance, and one would cycle through the five destinies without any time of liberation.
Therefore, if one says that it cannot be severed, that fault is likewise excessive.
Thus, this ignorance can both be severed and not be severed.
What is the meaning of this?
Because fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) and ignorance (avidyā) possess two meanings.
What are these two? First, the meaning of being of the same substance and the same characteristic; second, the meaning of being of different substances and different characteristics.
Regarding the sense of identity: it is because all phenomena are, in their entirety, the ultimate principle (*tattva*).
Regarding the sense of difference: it is because the virtues and faults of all phenomena are each distinct and differentiated.
If based on the first gate, they cannot be severed;
if based on the latter gate, they can also be severed.
As it is said in the *Sarvadharmācārya-sūtra*:
Greed is nirvāṇa; hatred and delusion are likewise so.
Within these three matters, there lies the immeasurable path of the Buddha.
To see and not to see are of one single mark; the same applies to attachment and non-attachment.
Herein there is neither Buddha nor Dharma; to know this is called worldly wisdom.
In the *Mūlaprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is said as follows:
"Because the power of fundamental ignorance is the greatest,"
It can obstruct all-encompassing wisdom, Causing one to fail to abide in self-mastery.
To sever it, one must use the sword of prajñā; To adorn it, one must use the jewels of merit.
The ocean of ignorance gradually dries up, And the mountain of the dharmakāya slowly reveals itself.
Just as the characteristic of fundamental ignorance does not depart from the nature of awakening, because it is neither destructible nor indestructible.
From this point onward, a metaphorical explanation is shown.
The great ocean is a metaphor for the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This consciousness has two meanings: it is vast and perfect like the great ocean.
Water is a metaphor for the mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya-parāvṛtti*); the intrinsically pure mind is clearly manifest and lucid, just like clear water.
The wind is a metaphor for fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*);
because fundamental non-enlightenment is able to activate the evolving consciousnesses of thought and cognition, it is like that wind.

The surging waves are a metaphor for the various consciousnesses of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because these various consciousnesses shift, move, and flow in a cycle of coming and going, they are impermanent, like the waves of the sea.

The fact that the characteristics of water and wind are inseparable serves as a metaphor for how the true and the deluded mutually support one another, functioning and evolving together. This means that the mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) does not arise of its own accord;
it can only arise by relying on the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). Likewise, fundamental ignorance does not evolve of its own accord; it can only evolve by depending on the power of the true mind.
Just as water does not produce its own waves, it must rely on the power of the wind to form them;
yet the wind does not manifest its own moving characteristics, for it must depend upon that water to manifest the appearance of movement and transformation.

That water is not of a moving nature serves as a metaphor for the originally enlightened mind being free from conditioned characteristics. This means that the true mind of original enlightenment has, from the very beginning, been remote from discursive thoughts and liberated from fetters; its essence is pure and its functions are sovereign. Yet, because it does not cling to its own nature, it manifests various appearances in accordance with the conditions of ignorance.
Just as water is not of a moving nature yet does not maintain its own nature because it produces various waves according to the conditions of the wind—

if the wind ceases and the appearance of movement is extinguished— this is a metaphor for the cessation of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), whereby all conceptualizing consciousnesses (*prapañca-vijñāna*) are extinguished without remainder.

Fundamental enlightenment (mūla-vidyā) first counteracts the obstacle of fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā), and subsequently counteracts the various consciousnesses that involve deliberation, cognition, and objective grasping.

Regarding the phrase "the moist nature is indestructible," this is a metaphor for the wisdom of fundamental enlightenment being free from the dharma of annihilation; it means that when ignorance ceases and all consciousnesses are exhausted, the true mind of fundamental enlightenment undergoes no destruction or extinction.
Just as when that wind ceases, all waves subside, yet the clear, pure water itself is never destroyed;
from this point onward, the application of the analogy is shown, which should be correlated with the text in its respective order.
From whom do the winds and waters of the great ocean arise?
It is said they arise from the dragon kings.
From what specific places do they each arise?
That is to say, as if water were emerging from the crown of its head, or as if wind were emerging from its tail.
For what reason does the ocean water, stirred by the wind, produce various waves that never cease?
It is said to be due to two factors. What are these two?
First, because there exist primary elements (mahābhūta) of the same kind; second, because it is so by the very nature of things (dharmatā).
What is the meaning of this?

Within that great element of water there is also the great element of wind, and within that great element of wind there is also the great element of water; because they exist mutually, they combine and cooperate to produce various waves, which continue in a constant and uninterrupted succession.
If the water element did not contain that wind element, the wind would be unable to cause the water to move.
If the wind element did not contain that water element, the water would be unable to turn with the wind.
Why is this? Because the four great elements arise together and function together, being inseparable from one another.

Yet, as for the fact that when one great element is clearly manifest, the others are not perceived with such clarity, this is because their increasing and decreasing characteristics are not identical.
Furthermore, from time immemorial, by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is likewise with fundamental awakening (*mūlabodhi*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
The Great Dragon King is a metaphor for the dharma of the one mind.
The wind is a metaphor for the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
That which has not yet emerged from the tail illustrates the inferior characteristics of this dharma.
The water is a metaphor for the true mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
That which emerges from the crown of the head displays the supreme and wondrous form of this Dharma.
The presence of the wind element within that water element is a metaphor for fundamental ignorance within the heart of the intrinsically pure *tathāgatagarbha* (original awakening).

The fact that the water element also exists within that wind element is a metaphor for the presence of the fundamental Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha) within the storehouse of fundamental ignorance (mūlāvidyā).

This is the primary intent of this treatise: the aspect of difference (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*) is presented first, followed by the aspect of sameness (*sabhāga-lakṣaṇa*); one should contemplate them according to their respective explanations.
In the *Sūtra on the Inexhaustible Treasury of All Buddhas*, it is stated:
"Within the great ocean of afflictions dwells the Perfect Tathāgata, who proclaims the principle of the eternal abiding of the true mark."
Within the true nature of original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya), there exist sentient beings of ignorance who give rise to waves of immeasurable and boundless afflictions.
Such a great matter is the realm of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and is therefore not something that can be known by ordinary worldlings or those of the two vehicles.
Having already explained the gate of the purity of the primordially existent nature-wisdom, next is explained the gate of unimpeded mastery over karmic activity.

That is to say, within this gate, taking the primordially existent nature-wisdom as the basis, one gives rise to the activity of responsive transformation, manifesting various kinds of sublime and wondrous physical forms for all practitioners to serve as objects for the eye faculty;
and producing various kinds of sublime and wondrous sounds to serve as objects for the ear faculty.
They give rise to various kinds of supreme and wondrous fragrances as objects for the nose faculty;
they manifest various kinds of supreme and wondrous flavors of the Dharma as objects for the tongue faculty;
and they bring forth various kinds of supreme and wondrous tactile sensations of samādhi as objects for the body faculty.
Various profound treasuries of Dharma appear, serving as objects for the mental faculty (*manas*).

In their respective order, these are: the Tathāgata Radiance-Sun-Moon-Jewel-Virtue; the Tathāgata Pure-Brahma-Sound-Voice; the Tathāgata Perfected-Flowing-Fragrance-Accumulation; the Tathāgata Equal-Unmixed-One-Taste; the Tathāgata Clearly-Manifested-Marks-of-Awakened-Touch; and the Tathāgata Wisdom-Penetrating-All-Pervading. They fully accomplish the teaching and benefiting of beings—unhindered and sovereign according to the time, place, and capacity of their faculties—without moving a single thought yet pervading the three periods of time, and without dividing a single body yet filling the ten directions while performing the deeds of a Buddha.

Regarding the "characteristics of the inconceivable activity" as described in the original text: because it relies on the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*), it is able to produce all superior and wondrous objects. That is to say, the characteristics of immeasurable merit are eternally uninterrupted; they manifest in various ways, spontaneously corresponding to the faculties of sentient beings, so that they may obtain benefit.

The detailed exposition on the gate of the intrinsically aware nature (anuloma-prakṛti-āśraya-pariśuddha-jñāna) defiled by adventitious stains has been explained. Next, the detailed exposition on the gate of the intrinsically pure nature (prakṛti-viśuddha-jñāna) will be explained.
The root text says:
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the essence of awareness, there are four kinds of great meanings; it is equal to space and like a pure mirror.

What are the four? First is the mirror of emptiness as it truly is: it is far removed from all characteristics of mental objects, and no phenomena can appear within it, because it does not possess the quality of cognitive illumination.

The second is the mirror of causal perfuming, which is truly non-empty; all worldly objects appear within it, neither emerging nor entering, neither being lost nor destroyed, as it is the eternally abiding single mind, because all phenomena are identical with true reality.
Furthermore, it cannot be defiled by any defiled phenomena, for the essence of wisdom is immovable and fully endowed with the untainted (anāsrava) influence that permeates sentient beings.

Third is the mirror of the transcendence of dharmas (*dharmaviniḥsṛti-ādarśa*), which means that non-empty dharmas emerge from the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), being free from the characteristics of conjunction and being purely clear and luminous.

Fourth is the mirror of the perfuming of conditions; because it issues forth from the Dharma and brings about liberation, it universally illumines the minds of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate roots of goodness by manifesting itself in accordance with their thoughts.
The Commentary states:
This is an extensive explanation of the section on the intrinsically pure fundamental awakening (*prakṛtiviśuddha-mūlābodhi*).
Within each of these four great meanings, there are two aspects that are inseparable from those great meanings.
What are these two? First, the meaning of equality with space; second, the meaning of being like a mirror.
As stated in the original text: "Furthermore, the essential characteristics of awakening have four kinds of great meanings, because they are equal to empty space and resemble a pure mirror."
What is called the "mirror of emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā-ādarśa*)?
It possesses two meanings; what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Within the intrinsically pure original awakening, it is free from deliberative cognition as such;

it is free from the reality of delusive objects. It demonstrates the emptiness of the meaning of detachment, like a *maṇi* jewel on a lotus pedestal, because by mentioning one, the other is demonstrated.
The Treatise states:

Within the essential nature of the intrinsically pure original enlightenment (*prakṛtiviśuddha-mūlajñāna*), one is far removed from all conceptualizations, discursive thoughts, and the consciousnesses of manifold proliferation (*prapañca*). Because it accomplishes the principle of a single flavor and equality, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
It is called "real" because it is far removed from all false objects and their various phenomenal aspects, thereby achieving the definitive characteristic of ultimate truth;
it is called "empty" because it is intended to manifest the meaning of such removal.

"Mirror" is a metaphorical designation; here, "mirror" specifically refers to the *maṇiśilā* (crystal) mirror, and not to various other types of mirrors such as those polished with oil or other substances used as metaphors.

Why is this? If one takes this maṣīpāda pearl mirror and places it in a single location, and before the mirror one heaps up various stones, or various foods and drinks, or various ornaments, or even other similar pearl mirrors, no other images will appear within that pearl mirror; for only the similar pearls will appear with distinct clarity.

The mirror of emptiness as it truly is is likewise so: within this mirror, there is only the establishment and accumulation of pure qualities of the same kind, for all various heterogeneous dharmas of faults and afflictions are entirely absent.
As the original text asks: "What are the four?
First is the mirror of emptiness as it truly is, which is far removed from all marks of the mind's objects because no phenomena can appear therein.
Why is it that for each [of the three natures] there are two meanings, yet only the analogy to a mirror is shown, while the meaning of emptiness is not explicitly revealed?
Because by citing one meaning, another meaning is simultaneously indicated.
