First is the universal causal condition of the origin, and second is the universal causal condition of the derivative.

Regarding the "universal condition of the origin," this refers to fundamental ignorance and the mind of original enlightenment; they possess the sense of being causal conditions in relation to the six coarse characteristics.

Regarding the term "pervasive at the end," it refers to the fact that when the activity of the mental factors (karmas) is compared to the three characteristics, they possess the sense of being conditions for one another.
Furthermore, there are two additional layers of causal conditions.
What are the two? First, the causal conditions from above to below; second, the causal conditions from below to above.
Regarding "from above to below," ignorance is the beginning and retribution is the end; each subsequent stage provides its power without exceeding its numerical order, acting as a causal condition.

Regarding the "lower and upper," the fruit-retribution is the beginning and ignorance is the end; the "upper-upper" and its application of power do not exceed these categories because they function as causes and conditions.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing do not abide for even a single moment, for they would otherwise lack cause and condition.
Furthermore, the phenomena of causes and conditions are empty and without a master, for their actual intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, that which is unapprehendable is such because even its non-apprehension cannot be apprehended.
One should carefully examine and discern these matters according to their respective order.

Having already explained the "Gate of Comprehending the Meaning to Reveal the Doctrine and Generate Understanding," next is explained the "Gate of Resolving Doubts through Exegesis Following the Text.
Within this, there are two gates.
What are these two? First is the section on the general indication; second is the section on the detailed explanation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing consist in sentient beings revolving in dependence upon mind, thought, and consciousness—this refers to the first section.
What meaning does this passage clarify?
It is intended to demonstrate the distinction between the basis (*āśraya*) and that which depends upon it (*āśrita*). What is the basis?
This refers to the mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). What is it that can serve as its support?
It is none other than sentient beings.
When one speaks of "sentient beings," what phenomena are meant?
They refer to the mind (*manas*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Why are the mind and mental consciousness called "sentient beings"?
The mind (*manas*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arise from the convergence of all defilements; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
Yet, they possess no separate self-nature (*svabhāva*), having the mind alone as their substance. For this reason, it is said that they evolve in dependence upon the mind.
The section on the general presentation has already been explained; next, the section on the detailed exposition is presented.

Within this, there are two chapters: first, the transformation of the manas is explained, and subsequently, the transformation of the mental consciousness is explained; the structure of the text is evident.
What is the meaning of this? This constitutes a general inquiry regarding the two turnings.
From this point forward, an explanation will be provided in detail.
Upon which sūtra is this teaching on the transformation of the mind (cittapariṇāma) established?
This refers to the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*. What is taught therein?
In that *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
Although the various consciousnesses are immeasurable in number, they are merely transformations of the manas;
there is no other dharma. Why is this so?
It is because this manas-consciousness is fully endowed with eleven meanings and is capable of performing all functions.
In that sūtra, the eleven names for these meanings were not explained individually in brief; therefore, the commentator fully enumerates the eleven distinct names to clearly demonstrate them.
What are the eleven kinds of names? First is fundamental ignorance; second is the aspect of karma;

third is the aspect of transformation; fourth is the aspect of manifestation; fifth is the aspect of cognition; sixth is the aspect of continuity; seventh is the consciousness of karma; eighth is the evolving consciousness; ninth is the manifesting consciousness; tenth is the consciousness of cognition; eleventh is the consciousness of continuity. These are called the eleven.

As stated in the original [text]: "Based on the ālayavijñāna, it is said that ignorance arises through non-awakening; because it is able to see, able to manifest, and able to grasp objects, giving rise to a continuous succession of thoughts, it is called 'manas'."
This manas has five further names; to speak of them in detail, the fifth is called the "continuing consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*), because it is associated with mindfulness and is uninterrupted.

In the *Mūla-bhūmi-sūtra*, it is stated that the Great Manas-consciousness possesses twelve transformations, because its fundamental support, original enlightenment (*mūla-ajñāna*), is counted as one.
What is the difference between the two terms "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "mark" (*nimitta*), such that their number is further increased and they are established as distinct?
They are vastly different.
In what way do they differ?
This means that all the various defiled phenomena associated with the retinue each possess two meanings.
What are these two? First, the meaning of spiritual clarity; second, the meaning of dullness and obscurity.
The meaning of "divine understanding" (*shenjie*) is based on the aspect of flowing forth from original enlightenment (*benjue*);
the meaning of "dark dullness" (*andun*) is based on the aspect of flowing forth from ignorance (*wuming*).

The name "consciousness" (*shi*) is established based on the former gate, while the name "phenomenon" (*xiang*) is established based on the latter gate; the distinction between these two gates should be understood in this way.
Why is this so? That which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) accords with original enlightenment (mūla-awakening), because its meaning is that of comprehension and understanding.
That which is called "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) accords with ignorance (avidyā), because its meaning is that of turning away from the fundamental.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Nitya-buddhadhātu-sūtra*:
"By what means is it known that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature?
The answer is:
Because all sentient beings possess mind and consciousness, one should know that they possess buddha-nature.
Why is this? "Buddha" means "the Awakened One," for he is able to skillfully illuminate and penetrate all phenomena.
Because this awareness exists within the bodies of sentient beings, all sentient beings are thus able to obtain the faculty of discerning consciousness.
For what reason is it called "manas" (the mind)?
This is because there are two meanings. What are these two?
First, the meaning of "faculty" (indriya); second, the meaning of "body" (kāya).
Regarding the meaning of "root" (*mūla*): it signifies the sense of being able to produce [something].
Regarding the meaning of "body" (*kāya*): it signifies the sense of being a basis of reliance.
For what reason do fundamental ignorance and the intrinsically pure awakened mind (*anāsrava-bodhi*) each possess both causes and conditions in accordance with their defiled states?
Because they are mutually related.
What is the meaning of this?

It means that when fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are considered in relation to the three consciousnesses, fundamental enlightenment serves as the cause and ignorance serves as the condition.
Taking those two together in relation to the three characteristics, ignorance is the cause and original enlightenment is the condition.
Why is this so? Because that which is proximate acts as the cause, while that which is remote acts as the condition.

Why were the characteristics of discriminating wisdom and the characteristics of continuity previously described as subdivisions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), yet now subsumed under the manas-consciousness in this text?
It is because one wishes to establish that the manas and the mental consciousness are of a single essence and not two distinct entities.
If that is so, why are the coarse aspects omitted and not taken into account?
In reality, they are all mental, but since the principle is already fully exhausted [by this], they are merely omitted for brevity; therefore, the Sūtra says that there is nothing it does not do.

However, the reason for establishing the transformation of the mental consciousness separately is to establish the dharma-gate of the supported and the support; by citing this to resolve the three characteristics, one should extensively penetrate the nature of the manas.

Furthermore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the ālayavijñāna is not definitively the ālaya, the manas is not definitively the manas, and the manovijñāna is not definitively the manovijñāna.

Because they lack fixed nature, the ālayavijñāna and manas, manas and ālayavijñāna, the manovijñāna and ālayavijñāna, and ālayavijñāna and manovijñāna are all, respectively, the ālayavijñāna, are all manas, and are all manovijñāna; yet they are also, likewise, all none of these.

Because they are thus without fixed nature, they are all impermanent; because they are impermanent, they are not real; because they are not real, they are all illusory transformations; because they are illusory transformations, their self-nature is empty and non-existent; because their self-nature is empty, they are definitively quiescent; and because they are quiescent, even quiescence itself is quiescent.
In the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, it is stated as follows: Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said, “The inconceivable and inconceivable aggregate:

the seven and five do not arise; the eight and six are quiescent; the nine marks are empty and non-existent. There is existence within emptiness, yet no existence; there is emptiness within non-existence, yet no existence.”
...and so on, as stated above, the Buddha said that to see [them] is to be deluded. Why is this?
All phenomena are without arising and without marks; they have no inherent names from the beginning and are entirely empty and quiescent.
The characteristics of all phenomena are likewise thus, and the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise thus; since even the body does not exist, how could there be seeing?
Having already explained the "Gate of Resolving Doubts through Exegesis Following the Text," next is explained the "Gate of the Distinctions in the Functions of Successive Karmic Activities."
The root text states:

Because it causes the good and evil karma of immeasurable past lives to be preserved without loss, and because it enables the fruition of present and future suffering and pleasure to be realized without discrepancy, it causes one to suddenly recall events already past in the present, while inadvertently harboring false anxieties regarding future matters.
The treatise says:
This evolving consciousness possesses three meanings.
What are these three?

First is the meaning of gathering [the past] so as not to lose it; second is the meaning of the accomplishment of the fruition of karma; third is the meaning of the pervasive objectification of deluded thought. What is the first meaning?

This continuous consciousness is able to give rise to the afflictions that moisten karma, and it sustains all various kinds of wholesome and unwholesome karma produced by past ignorance, thereby enabling them to function as the power that brings about fruition. As the original text says: "It sustains the wholesome and unwholesome karma of immeasurable past lives and so forth, ensuring they are not lost."
What is the meaning of "intermediate"?

This continuous consciousness (*saṃtāna-vijñāna*) can further give rise to the defilements that moisten rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*), thereby enabling the karmas already completed to result in a determined retribution that is established and assigned accordingly. Furthermore, as in the original [text], it can accomplish the fruits of suffering and pleasure in the present and future without any discrepancy.
What is the subsequent meaning?

This evolving consciousness of the continuum expands its objects of perception, and its discrimination becomes even stronger. It gives rise to feelings of pleasure or displeasure toward objects already known; it increases feelings of attachment or aversion toward present objects; and because it fails to comprehend unknown objects, it falsely discriminates them. Consequently, as before, it causes one to suddenly recall past events that have already occurred and to unconsciously engage in false anxieties regarding future matters.
In this way, this consciousness continues through birth and death without interruption; therefore, it is called the "continuing consciousness" (*prabandha-vijñāna*).
Having explained the section on the distinctions in the functional activity of continuity, next I shall explain the section on how all phenomena revolve solely within the mind.
The text says:
"For this reason, the three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind; apart from the mind, there are no objects of the six sense-fields.
What is the meaning of this?"
Since all dharmas arise from the mind and are produced by deluded thoughts, all discrimination is simply the discrimination of one's own mind.

The mind does not see the mind, for no characteristic can be apprehended; one should know that all worldly realms exist and are sustained solely in dependence upon the ignorant, deluded mind of sentient beings.
Therefore, all phenomena are like reflections in a mirror, having no substantial essence that can be apprehended.
They are merely the false imaginings of the mind; for when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise, and when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
The Commentary says:
For what purpose is this passage intended?
It is to demonstrate that all phenomena are merely the revolving of the mind, and that there are no phenomena apart from it.
Why is this so? Because the existence or non-existence of all differentiated phenomena follows the existence or non-existence of the mind.
Since all phenomena are but mind, does this mind exist?
Since mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are likewise unapprehendable, if that is so, how is the thesis that "there is only mind" established?
This too is mind; by what is it directly known?
The sūtra text is clear.
How is it stated? It is said thus in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
Because I teach that the measure of mind is a mind devoid of mind,
and furthermore, because of the phrase "the unattainability of the mind," the meaning of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is established.
By means of the phrase "the mind-measure that is without mind," the meaning of the differentiation of illusions is established.
Furthermore, by means of the meaning of the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), all phenomena are established.
Through the meaning of the differentiation of illusion, the principle of emptiness is revealed.

Furthermore, because they are observed as characteristics, there are no two fixed entities; because there are no two entities, there is not even one entity; and because there is not even one entity, non-existence itself is not established.
One should examine these in their proper sequence.

Having explained the gateway to the transformational characteristics of the expansive manas, next is explained the gateway to the transformational characteristics of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates objects).
The original text says:
Furthermore, that which is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the continuous consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).

Based on the deepening attachment of ordinary beings, who falsely reckon in terms of "self" and "what belongs to the self," various deluded attachments follow after objects as they grasp at conditions, discriminating the six sense-fields; this is termed the mental consciousness, and it is also called the discriminative consciousness (*vibhaṅga-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, it is also called the "discriminative consciousness of phenomena" (*vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna*), because this consciousness increases based on the afflictions of views and craving (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā-kleśa*).
The treatise states:
Within this very passage, there are four sections.

What are the four? First, the gate of discerning the commonality of the provisional person; second, the gate of the arising of the characteristics of transformation of the coarse and heavy [defilements]; third, the gate of establishing the distinctions of names; and fourth, the gate of revealing the establishment of the basis.
Regarding the section on "Distinguishing the Provisional Person," three types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are cited to distinguish them from the noble ones (*ārya*) on the stages (*bhūmi*).
What are these three ordinary beings?
First, the rootless, blind, and deaf ordinary being; second, the hair-tip and difficult-to-corner ordinary being; third, the adamantine and unchanging ordinary being—these are called the three.

Regarding the passage from the original text: "The gateway of the arising of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) based on ordinary beings," this refers to those sentient beings belonging to the category of the wrongly fixed (*mithyā-niyata-rāśi*). Because they constantly give rise to consciousnesses of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-vikalpa*), grasping at all various objects, these states become increasingly deep, boundless, and without beginning or end; they perpetually increase without interruption. Thus, as the original text states: "Because grasping becomes ever more profound."

If we consider sentient beings belonging to the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi), although they perceive the characteristic of cessation as definitely unwholesome and do not give rise to mental attention toward it, because the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna) has not yet appeared before them, they take various objects and bodily parts as their basis and recklessly cling to "I" and "mine," refusing to relinquish them; thus, they are as they were originally, reckoning "I" and "mine."

Regarding sentient beings at the stage of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*), although they have already accomplished the *prajñā* of the emptiness of persons and have awakened from the dream of differentiated characteristics, because the wisdom of the true emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) has not yet manifested before them, they give rise to various attachments and firmly cling to the reality of dharmas. Because their deliberations follow after specific objects and they cannot penetrate the principle of equality, they harbor various false attachments, clinging to and discriminating among the six sense objects according to those objects—just as described in the original text.
Regarding the establishment of the gateway of names, there are three kinds. What are these three?
First, the subtle names based upon the substratum; second, the coarse and manifest names based upon the substratum; and third, the names that accord with objects. These are called the three.
What is its initial name?

This consciousness is established by relying on that subtle manas as its foundational basis; therefore, it is called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*), because its original designation is "mental consciousness."
What is its name?

This consciousness relies upon those five faculties, such as the eye, as its basis and discriminates the five sense objects; therefore, it is also called the "discriminating consciousness," for as the original text states, it is also named the discriminating consciousness.
What is the subsequent name?

This consciousness now evolves as a discrimination that takes phenomena (*vastu*) as its object; it has not yet taken suchness (*tathatā*) as its own object. Therefore, it is called the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*), for the original text further states that it is also named the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena."

Regarding the gate of revealing the basis: the two afflictions of seeing and cultivation permeate the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). By the power of this permeation, the coarse division of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is established; because it increases, continues, and constantly revolves to maintain its persistence, as stated in the root text: "This consciousness depends on the afflictions of views and craving for the purpose of growth."
The determination of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing from the beginning has been completed.
From this point forward, the inconceivable characteristics of the excellence of these causes and conditions will be revealed.
The text states:

"That consciousness which arises through the perfuming of ignorance cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can it be realized by the wisdom of the Two Vehicles. It is said that based on Bodhisattvas who, from their initial correct faith, give rise to the mind and engage in contemplation, they may gain partial knowledge upon realizing the Dharma-body; yet even at the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva, they cannot know it exhaustively—it is only the Buddha who fully comprehends it."
Why is this? This mind has been pure by its very nature from the beginningless past; yet, because of ignorance, it becomes defiled by that ignorance, and thus there is a defiled mind.
Although there is a defiled mind, it is eternally constant and unchanging; therefore, this meaning can be known only by the Buddha.

That which is called the nature of the mind is termed "unchanging" because it is eternally without thought; yet, because one does not realize the single dharma-realm, the mind becomes dissociated [from its true nature], and the sudden arising of thought is termed "ignorance."
There are six kinds of defiled minds. What are the six?
The first is the defilement associated with attachment, which is abandoned through the liberation of the two vehicles and by relying on the stage of faith.

The second is the defilement associated with non-interruption; by relying on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-pratipatti-bhūmi*) and training in skillful means, one gradually becomes able to relinquish it and attain the stage of the pure mind (*vimala-citta-bhūmi*), thereby achieving ultimate detachment.

Third is the defilement associated with the discrimination of knowledge (*vikalpa-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is gradually abandoned from the stage of possessing the precepts (*śīla-bhūmi*) until it is ultimately abandoned at the stage of the skillful means of signlessness (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*).
Fourth is the defilement dissociated from manifested form (*rūpa-asamprayukta-kleśa*), which can be abandoned by relying on the stage of mastery over form (*rūpa-vaśavarti-bhūmi*).
Fifth, the defilement dissociated from the mind that can be seen is abandoned by relying on the stage of mastery over the mind.
Sixth, the fundamental defilement dissociated from karma is abandoned by attaining the culmination of the bodhisattva stages and entering the stage of the Tathāgata.

Those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm observe and train in its severance from the stage of faith-correspondence; they attain partial detachment upon entering the pure mind-ground, until finally attaining ultimate detachment at the stage of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the meaning of "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*): it refers to the fact that although the mind, mental factors, and phenomena are distinct, they are known to have identical characteristics of cognition and objective conditions based on the differentiation between defilement and purity.

Regarding the meaning of "non-correspondence" (*asaṃprayoga*): it refers to the very fact that the mind is non-awakened, which is eternally without distinction, and thus does not differ from the characteristics of cognition and objective conditions.
Furthermore, the meaning of "defiled mind" is termed the "obstruction of afflictions," because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā*.
The meaning of "ignorance" is termed the "obstruction of wisdom," because it can obstruct the spontaneous wisdom of worldly activity.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because, by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to see and manifest, falsely grasping at objects in violation of the nature of equality.

Since all dharmas are eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristic of arising, ignorance fails to awaken and thus falsely opposes the dharmas; consequently, one is unable to attain the various kinds of knowledge that accord with all objects within the world.
The treatise says:
Within this very text, there are thus five gates. What are these five?

First, the gate of citing persons to manifest their excellence; second, the gate of manifesting defiled conditions to resolve doubts; third, the gate of citing hindrances and showing their remedies through correspondence; fourth, the gate of manifesting the distinctions between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate; fifth, the gate of establishing two types of obstructions to distinguish their respective functions—these are called the five.
Within the first gate, there are three types of persons.
What are these three?

First, those for whom both the partial and the complete [attainments] are utterly severed: namely, ordinary beings fixed in error and all followers of the Two Vehicles. Because their ignorance is profound and their wisdom inferior, they are like those whose consciousness arises from the perfuming of fundamental ignorance; such is not something that ordinary beings can know, nor is it something that the wisdom of the Two Vehicles can awaken to.

The second is the person who possesses the potential but has not yet reached fulfillment; this refers to those at the fifty stages, because their *prajñā* of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) is not yet perfected. As the original text states: "Relying on the Bodhisattva, from the initial arousal of the mind through right faith and observation, even if one realizes the Dharma-body, one attains only a partial knowledge; thus, up to the ultimate stage of the Bodhisattva, one cannot know it exhaustively."

Third, there are those who possess fulfillment but lack partiality; because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is universally manifest in the state of Buddhahood, as the root text says, "only the Buddha exhaustively realizes it.
These are called the three.
Having already explained the section on elevating persons to demonstrate their excellence, next is explained the section on demonstrating defiled conditions to resolve doubts.
This contains two points. What are these two?
The first is the gate of permanence and impermanence; the second is the gate of impermanence and permanence. Regarding the gate of permanence and impermanence:

the self-characteristic of the originally awakened mind has been definitively and eternally abiding since beginningless time. Its essential nature is unchanging, for there is no time when it is not impermanent, nor any place where it does not undergo transformation. As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: "Why is this? Because this mind, from its very origin, is pure by nature, yet through ignorance it is defiled by ignorance, and thus there exists a defiled mind."

Regarding the gate of the permanence of the impermanent: this fundamental awakened mind has been both eternally permanent and impermanent since beginningless time; it is eternally subject to transformation because there is no time when it does not abide permanently, nor any place where it does not remain unchanging. Thus, as stated in the original text, although there is a defiled mind, [the fundamental mind] is eternally and constantly unchanging.
"Therefore, this meaning can be known only by the Buddha" concludes the section on excellence.
From here onward, two further lines explain the preceding two lines; the textual structure is clear.
Having already explained the gate of displaying the conditions for defilement to resolve doubts, next is explained the gate of citing obstacles, showing remedies, and assigning them accordingly.
Within this very gate, there are two intended meanings. What are these two?
First is the gate of the stages of the concordant antidote; second is the gate of the stages of the fundamental antidote. Regarding the gate of the concordant antidote:

the six types of concordant characteristics follow their respective order, beginning with the generation of the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and ending with sublime awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because one should abandon [the afflictions] accordingly.
As stated in the original text, there are six kinds of defiled minds. What are these six?

First is the basis for the defilement associated with attachment, which is abandoned through the liberation of the two vehicles and the stage of faith-correspondence; this is explained in detail up to the sixth, the basis for the fundamental defilement dissociated from karma, which is entered upon the exhaustion of the Bodhisattva stages and abandoned upon reaching the Tathāgata stage.

Regarding the gate of fundamental antidotes: beginning with the great power of ignorance and extreme joy and ending with wondrous enlightenment, one is liberated accordingly. As stated in the original text, for those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm, they observe and train toward severance from the stage of correspondence with faith; upon entering the stage of the pure mind, they attain liberation according to their capacity, until finally, at the stage of the Tathāgata, they are able to achieve ultimate liberation.
Within the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), how are the fundamental characteristics and their secondary characteristics, as well as their respective antidotes, to be distinguished?

It should be understood that what is severed by subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is called ignorance (*avidyā*), while that which is severed by the wisdom of the fundamental body (*mūla-jñāna*) is called a secondary characteristic (*anulakṣaṇa*). Thus should it be known.
As it was explained regarding the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā*), so it is for all the subsequent stages as well.

Having already explained the section on identifying obstacles and demonstrating their remedies through correspondence, next is explained the section on distinguishing between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
What is meant by the meaning of "association" (*saṃprayoga*)?
As for the meaning of association, it refers to the distinctness of the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) within a mental state (*citta-kalāpa*).
What is a mental state?
This refers to the mind of original enlightenment following defilement.
How does it give rise to thoughts of dharmas?
It means that, based directly upon ignorance, false dharmas grow and arise.
For what reason is it called "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*)?
It is because they exert mutual power upon one another.
Why, then, are these two dharmas said to be distinct?
Because they are fundamentally distinct; as the original text states, the meaning of "concomitance" (saṃprayoga) refers to the fact that the mind and mental factors are different.

The basis for mental factors is defilement, while the basis for the category of the mind is purity. Since these two phenomena are each distinct from one another—like water and fire—how can it be said that they constitute the meaning of concomitance?
Because the characteristic of knowing and the characteristic of the object are in harmonious accord.
How is it that they are said to be in harmonious accord?
It is because within the mental state (*cittakalāpa*), mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛti*) proceeds through their mutual non-separation and their coming together in union.
What is meant by "the concordance of the characteristics of the object"?

It is because the objects of these two categories are identical, as stated in the original text: "Because one knows that the characteristics of the object and the characteristics of the conditions are identical, based on the distinction between defilement and purity."
In the Mahāvajra-samādhi-sūtra it is said:
"The three types of sameness are established as identical because they are different; if they were identical, they would not be different."
If that is so, why does the sūtra of our own school state:
"The three types of coarse defilements proceed by way of two meanings"?
What are these two ways they proceed?
The first is contrary turning (virodha-parāvṛtti) and the second is conforming turning (anuloma-parāvṛtti), as explained at length.
Such statements are made by proceeding upward in reverse order and downward in direct order; they possess no other underlying intention.
The meaning of non-conjunction contradicts the characteristic of conjunction; this should be carefully examined.

Having already explained the section on distinguishing between the appropriate and inappropriate through the gate of manifestation, next is explained the section on establishing the distinct functions of the two types of obstruction through the gate of differentiation.

Those afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are characterized by a nature of great distraction, whereas the wisdom of *tathatā* is characterized by direct quiescence; because they are thus mutually contradictory, the former is established as an obstruction. As the original text states: "Furthermore, the meaning of the defiled mind is called the afflictive hindrance, because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā*."

That nature of wisdom which is obstructed and vast as a boundless ocean is the nature of the wisdom that performs karma and possesses intelligence; because these two are thus contradictory, it is established as an obstruction. As in the original meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is called "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), for it can obstruct the natural wisdom of worldly activity.
What is the meaning of this? Below, its causes and conditions are revealed; one should examine and discern them carefully.
Furthermore, what is the distinction between the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and the two obstructions (*nivaraṇa*)?

The establishment of the "two hindrances" is based on that which is invariably severed, while the establishment of the "two obstructions" is based on that which may or may not be severed. One should know it thus; one should contemplate it thus.
The section on the determination of the excellence of causes and conditions from the beginning is hereby concluded.
*Śāstra on the Explanation of Mahāyāna*, Fascicle Four.
*Śāstra on the Explanation of Mahāyāna*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamata of the Yao Qin dynasty by imperial decree.
From this point onward, the specific characteristics of arising and ceasing are revealed.
The text says:
Furthermore, as for the analysis of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, there are two kinds. What are these two?
First, because it is coarse and associated with the mind; second, because it is subtle and dissociated from the mind.

Furthermore, that which is coarse within the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); that which is subtle within the coarse and coarse within the subtle is the realm of Bodhisattvas; and that which is subtle within the subtle is the realm of Buddhas.
These two kinds of arising and ceasing exist based on the perfuming of ignorance; that is to say, they depend upon causes and they depend upon conditions.
Dependence upon causes refers to the meaning of non-awakening;
dependence upon conditions refers to the meaning of the deluded construction of objective realms.
If the cause ceases, then the condition ceases; because the cause ceases, the dissociated mind ceases, and because the condition ceases, the associated mind ceases.
Question: If the mind ceases, how does it continue in succession?
If it is a continuity, how can you say it is ultimately extinguished?
The answer is:
that which is called "extinguished" refers only to the extinction of the mind's manifestations, not the extinction of the essence of the mind.
Just as wind possesses the characteristic of movement by depending upon water, if the waves and the water were to perish, then the wind would be severed and have no basis for support.

Because the water does not perish, the characteristics of the wind continue in succession; it is only because the wind perishes that the characteristic of movement perishes accordingly, not because the water perishes.

Ignorance is likewise: it moves in dependence upon the substance of the mind. If the substance of the mind were to perish, sentient beings would be cut off and have nothing to rely upon; because the substance does not perish, the mind is able to continue in succession. It is only when delusion ceases that the characteristics of the mind cease accordingly, but it is not the case that the wisdom of the mind perishes.
The Commentary states:
Within this text, there are naturally five sections. What are these five?

First, the gate of demonstrating characteristics through the simultaneous establishment of both the heading and the explanation; second, the gate of correlating characteristics with the provisional person; third, the gate of revealing the coarse and subtle bases; fourth, the gate of the sequential order of fundamental awakening and its counteractives; fifth, the gate of initiating questions and answers to resolve doubts.

Regarding the statement that the "Gate of Demonstrating Characteristics" is established through both the indicator and the explanation: this is because coarse and heavy arising-and-ceasing is associated with the mind, whereas subtle arising-and-ceasing is dissociated from the mind.
What is meant by "coarse and heavy arising and ceasing," and with which consciousness is it associated?
It is so called because it is terminal; it is associated with the *vikaḷpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects).
What is meant by "subtle arising and ceasing"?
With which consciousnesses is it not associated?
It is so called because it is "terminal," as it is not associated with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) during the three stages.
Upon which sūtra did the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa rely to compose this commentary?
It was the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra. How is it explained in that sūtra?
That is to say, in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* of the Single Main Branch, it is stated as follows:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing do the various consciousnesses have?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which cannot be known through discursive reasoning."
The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravāha-utpāda*) and arising as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-utpāda*).
They have two kinds of abiding, namely, abiding as a continuous flow and abiding as a characteristic.
They have two kinds of cessation, namely, cessation as a continuous flow and cessation as a characteristic.
Furthermore, in another recension of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it is said:
"Mahāmati, there are two kinds of cessation of the various consciousnesses."
What are these two? First, the cessation of characteristics; second, the cessation of continuity.
There are two kinds of birth.
What are these two? First, arising through characteristics; second, arising through continuity.
There are two kinds of abiding.
What are these two? First, abiding by way of characteristics; second, abiding by way of continuity.
Furthermore, it is stated thus in the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding all phenomena of mind and consciousness, how many characteristics of impermanence are there?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If the subtle consciousness bound by the existence of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) possesses superior-grade [afflictions], it is not free from arising and ceasing.
If the subtle consciousness bound by the existence of the intermediate transition (*antarābhava*) possesses medium-grade [afflictions], it is not free from arising and ceasing."
If one turns away from the subtle consciousness bound by distant constraints, there remains a lower grade that is not free from arising and ceasing.
If one universally discriminates the coarse consciousness, there remains a separation from the face and mirror that is not free from arising and ceasing.
"What is the meaning elucidated by these three versions of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*?

It is intended to reveal the distinct characteristics of the two kinds of arising and ceasing—the coarse and the subtle; therefore, within the sūtra, only the names are set forth without explicitly showing their meanings."

For this reason, Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, in accordance with what is partially consistent and what is inconsistent, reveals two kinds of arising and ceasing—the coarse and the subtle—as stated in the original text: "Furthermore, when distinguishing the characteristics of arising and ceasing, there are two kinds."
What are the two? First, because the coarse [factors] are associated with the mind; second, because the subtle [factors] are dissociated from the mind.

Having thus explained the section on the simultaneous establishment of the headings and their explanations by way of indicating their characteristics, next is explained the section on the provisional person through the mutual correspondence of general characteristics.
Within this context, there are three types of nominal persons.
What are the three? First, non-retrogressive ordinary beings; second, those with partial purification; and third, those with complete purification—these are called the three.
With what kind of association does the first person take as their own objective realm?

It is because they take the defilement of associated grasping (*saṃprayukta-kleśa*) as their own objective realm; as the original text states, it is "the coarsest among the coarse, the objective realm of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)."
By what defilements do intermediate beings take as their own objective realm?

It is because they take the latter two [aspects of] the corresponding [consciousness] and the first two [aspects of] the non-corresponding [consciousness], as well as one portion of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), as their own objective realm; thus, as the text states, these are the realms of Bodhisattvas, being the subtle within the coarse and the coarse within the subtle.
Why do later generations take the non-associated defilements as their own objective domain?

It is because they take one part of the "moving aspect" (iṅgitanimitta) that arises in conjunction [with the mind], along with the entirety of the "karmic aspect" (karmanimitta) that functions independently, as their own objective domain; for, as the text states, that which is "subtle within the subtle" is the objective domain of the Buddhas.
Having already explained the gateway of the provisional person as categorized by their respective characteristics, next is explained the gateway that reveals the bases of the coarse and the subtle.
Within this, there are two kinds of bases. What are these two?
First is the general [explanation], and second is the specific.
As for the general: both types of arising and ceasing take ignorance as their basis. As for the specific:
the two types of arising and ceasing each take their respective causes and conditions as their bases, according to their sequence.

As stated in the original text, these two types of arising and ceasing exist based on the perfuming of ignorance; that is to say, they depend upon causes and conditions. Dependence upon causes refers to the meaning of non-awakening, while dependence upon conditions refers to the meaning of the false construction of objective realms.
Upon which sūtra is this treatise based?
It is the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra. How is it explained in that scripture?
It is stated thus in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* (Shunliu version):
"Mahāmati! The inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*)."
The grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination constitute the cause of the *vijñapti-mati-vijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena).
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:

"Moreover, as for the causes of non-separation from defilement, there are the perfuming of the conceivable and the perfuming of the inconceivable, as well as the transformation of the conceivable and the transformation of the inconceivable."

Furthermore, regarding the separation from the causes of defilement, it is said: "The various fierce winds of false conceptualization manifest in the mirror-like consciousness," and so forth, as explained at length.
What dharma is called "inconceivable perfuming"?
That which is referred to is precisely fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
For what reason is it called "inconceivable perfuming"?
It is because it is profoundly deep.
What is meant by "profound"?
It refers to the fact that all sentient beings, from the level of the *vajra* down, do not comprehend this state; therefore, it is called "inconceivable perfuming.
As with perfuming, so too is transformation.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states as follows:
"The conceivable and the inconceivable" refers to those who have returned to the state of the Vajra.
Having explained the gate of revealing the basis for the coarse and the subtle, next is explained the gate of the sequential order of the remedies of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

This refers to the wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), which proceeds by gradually applying antidotes in successive order, beginning with fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) and ending with the characteristic of cessation.
However, the "severance" herein does not consist in abandoning ignorance as its mode of severing; rather, it is not a severance achieved through the act of cutting away.
If that is so, how is the meaning of "severance" established?

It means that because the afflictions are severed and the mind ceases to arise, this is called the sequence of the path of treatment for original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). As stated in the root text: "If the cause is extinguished, then the condition is extinguished; because the cause is extinguished, the dissociated mind is extinguished; and because the condition is extinguished, the associated mind is extinguished."
Having already explained the gate of the sequential order of the counteractive measures of original enlightenment, next is explained the gate of initiating questions and answers to resolve doubts.
Within this very gate, there are two intended meanings. What are these two?
The first is the gate of closing through dual difficulty; the second is the gate of opening and penetrating to resolve doubts—the textual characteristics of which are evident.
Fundamental awakening and clear wisdom sever fundamental ignorance, such that the three kinds of subtle defilements are forever extinguished and do not arise.
Once the three subtle [states] are absent, the six coarse minds can no longer arise; these nine types of mind—three and six—are forever extinguished and do not emerge.
Consequently, the wisdom of original enlightenment cannot exist of itself.

Why is this so? Because the thirty-six kinds of mind are not merely ignorance; they are also co-existent with original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*), for the union of the true and the delusive is what is termed the "thirty-six minds.

Now, if one were to say that these thirty-six minds are extinguished, then original enlightenment would likewise be extinguished and cease to exist. How, then, could it be said that the mind of original enlightenment continues on until reaching the state of false certainty (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*)?
Therefore, it is asked: "If the mind is extinguished, how can it be continuous? This is the first crux.

If you say that original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) is a dharma of merit and not a dharma of cessation, being eternally continuous and without interruption, how can one then say that the thirty-six kinds of mind are forever extinguished and do not arise?
Therefore, the statement, "If it is a continuity, how can one speak of its ultimate cessation? constitutes the second objection.
From this point onward, an explanation is provided to resolve doubts; as the textual structure is clear, no further commentary is required.
The analysis of the characteristics of arising and ceasing from the beginning has been completed.
From this point forward, the meaning of the uninterrupted process of mutual perfuming and mutual production between the defiled and the pure is demonstrated.
The text states:
Furthermore, because there are four kinds of dharmas that function through the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*), defiled and pure dharmas arise without interruption.
What are these four?

First, pure phenomena are called *tathatā* (suchness); second, all causes of defilement are called *avidyā* (ignorance); third, the deluded mind is called the *karmic consciousness*; fourth, the deluded objects are the so-called six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Regarding the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*): it is like a worldly garment which, though actually devoid of fragrance, comes to possess a fragrant scent because it has been perfumed by someone with incense.
This is also the case here: although the pure dharma of *tathatā* is actually devoid of defilement, it manifests the appearance of defilement because it is perfumed by ignorance;
and although the defiled dharma of ignorance is actually devoid of pure activity, it possesses the function of purity because it is perfumed by *tathatā*.
How does the perfuming that gives rise to defiled phenomena continue without interruption?

It is said that because there is ignorance based upon the *tathatā* (suchness), this ignorance—which is the cause of defiled phenomena—perfumes the *tathatā*. Because of this perfuming, there arises the deluded mind; and because there is the deluded mind, it in turn perfumes ignorance.
Because they do not understand the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they fail to realize that thoughts arise and manifest as delusive objects.

Due to these delusive objects acting as conditions for defiled dharmas, they subsequently perfuse the deluded mind, causing it to cling to them and create various karmas, thereby undergoing all manner of suffering of body and mind.
This meaning of the perfuming of false objects is twofold. What are the two?
First, the perfuming that increases the proliferation of thought; second, the perfuming that increases grasping.
The meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is twofold. What are the two?
First is the fundamental perfuming of the karmic consciousness, which enables arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas to undergo the suffering of birth and death.

Second, it is the perfuming that increases the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects), because it enables one to undergo the suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings.
There are two meanings of the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā*). What are these two?
First is the fundamental perfuming, because it can accomplish the meaning of the karmic consciousness;
second is the perfuming of views and attachments that arise therefrom, because it can accomplish the meaning of the discerning consciousness of phenomena.
How does the perfuming that gives rise to pure dharmas proceed without interruption?

It is because true thusness exists that it can perfume ignorance; and by the power of the causes and conditions of this perfuming, it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek nirvana.
Because this deluded mind possesses the causes and conditions of aversion and seeking, it immediately perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness) and gains self-confidence in its own nature.
It realizes that the mind is falsely moving and that no external objects exist beforehand, and thus practices the dharma of detachment.

Because one knows, as it truly is, that there are no preceding objects, one gives rise to compliant practice through various skillful means, neither grasping nor recollecting. Eventually, through the power of long-term cultivation, ignorance is extinguished. Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise; because the mind does not arise, objects are accordingly extinguished. Since both causes and conditions are extinguished together, all mental characteristics are exhausted; this is called attaining nirvana and accomplishing spontaneous karma.
The meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is twofold. What are the two?

First is the perfuming of the *vikalpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), which occurs because ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and others, weary of the suffering of birth and death, gradually advance toward the Unsurpassed Way according to their respective capacities.
Second is the perfuming of the mind (*manas*), which refers to the fact that all bodhisattvas, having generated courageous resolve, swiftly proceed toward nirvāṇa.
There are two meanings to the perfuming of *tathatā*. What are these two?
The first is the perfuming of the intrinsic nature; the second is the perfuming of function.
Regarding the perfuming of the intrinsic nature: from beginningless time, it has been endowed with untainted dharmas.
As for that which functions through perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is fully endowed with the nature of acting as the objective sphere for inconceivable karma.
Based on these two meanings, there is constant perfuming.
Because of the power of this perfuming, it enables sentient beings to become weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek nirvana.
Confident that one’s own person possesses *tathatā*, one resolves to practice.
A question is asked:

If this is the case—that all sentient beings equally possess *tathatā* and are all permeated by it—how can there be such immeasurable distinctions as having faith or lacking faith, or being earlier or later?
All should simultaneously realize for themselves that they possess the *tathatā* (Suchness) dharma and diligently cultivate skillful means to enter Nirvāṇa equally.
The answer is:

Although *tathatā* is fundamentally one, there are immeasurable and boundless instances of ignorance (*avidyā*), because from the very beginning their intrinsic natures have differed in degree, being either thick or thin.

The distinctions among the higher afflictions that exceed the sands of the Ganges arise from ignorance; the distinctions among the afflictions of self-view, craving, and attachment also arise from ignorance. Since all such afflictions arise based on ignorance with infinite preceding and succeeding variations, only a Tathāgata can know them.
Furthermore, all Buddha-dharmas have causes and conditions; they are accomplished only when causes and conditions are fully assembled.

For example, the fire-nature within wood is the direct cause of fire; yet if a person lacks knowledge and does not employ skillful means, it is impossible for that fire to spontaneously burn the wood.

Sentient beings are likewise; although they possess the power of the perfuming of the true cause, if they do not encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends, and others to serve as conditions, it is impossible for them to spontaneously sever their afflictions and enter Nirvana.

Even if there is the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharmas have not yet acquired the power of perfuming, one will likewise be unable to ultimately weary of the suffering of birth and death or joyfully seek nirvana.

If the causes and conditions are fully present—namely, possessing the power of one's own habitual perfuming, and being protected by the compassionate vows of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—one is able to give rise to a mind that detests suffering, believe in the existence of nirvana, and cultivate roots of goodness.

Because the cultivation of roots of goodness is brought to fulfillment, one encounters Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who provide instruction, benefit, and joy; it is through this that one is able to advance toward the path to Nirvana.
That which functions as perfuming is precisely the power of external conditions for sentient beings.
Thus, external conditions have immeasurable meanings, which are briefly explained as being of two kinds. What are these two?
First, differentiated conditions; second, equal conditions.

Regarding the specific condition (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*): this person relies upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, from the initial generation of the mind and the beginning of the quest for the Way until the attainment of Buddhahood. Throughout this interval, whether they are seen or remembered—whether as kinsmen, parents, or relatives; as servants; as friends; or as enemies; or through the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), and so forth—all such immeasurable conditions of action, by the power of the perfuming of great compassion, are able to cause sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness, because they obtain benefit through seeing or hearing them.
These conditions are of two kinds. What are the two?
The first is the proximate condition, because one attains liberation swiftly.
The second is the distant condition, because one attains liberation after a long period of time.
These two conditions—the proximate and the distant—are further divided into two types each. What are these two?
The first is the condition for increasing practice; the second is the condition for receiving the Way. Regarding the condition of equality:

all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas vow to deliver all sentient beings; through natural permeation, they never abandon them. By virtue of the power of the wisdom of identical essence, they manifest karmic activities according to how beings see and hear them.
It is said that sentient beings rely upon samādhi to attain the equal vision of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, this distinction between the cultivation of essence and function is twofold.
What are the two? First is non-correspondence:

this refers to ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds. Because they practice by means of the熏習 (vāsanā) of the mind and mental consciousness, relying on the power of faith, they have not yet attained a non-conceptual mind that corresponds with the essence, nor have they attained the practice of sovereign karma that corresponds with its function.

Second is "already conjoined," which refers to Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body who have attained non-discriminative mind and are conjoined with the wisdom-activity of all Buddhas; they practice spontaneously by relying solely on the power of the Dharma, as they permeate True Suchness (tathatā) and thereby extinguish ignorance.
Furthermore, the perfuming of defiled dharmas has continued uninterrupted since beginningless time, yet it ceases immediately upon attaining Buddhahood;
the perfuming of pure dharmas, however, is never interrupted, persisting until the end of the future.
What is the meaning of this?

Because the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharmakāya manifests; it then gives rise to the perfuming of its functioning, and thus there is no interruption.
The Commentary states:
Within this very text, there are five sections. What are these five?

First, the gateway of the general outline; second, the gateway of establishing names and providing a brief indication; third, the gateway of the comprehensive explanation of perfuming (*vāsanā*); fourth, the gateway of detailed analysis and exposition; fifth, the gateway of distinguishing between the exhaustive and the inexhaustible.
Within the first gate there are six meanings. What are these six?

First is the meaning of mutual dependence and mutual establishment, which is intended to demonstrate that all phenomena, whether defiled or pure, are established through mutual dependence, and that there is no phenomenon that is established solely by itself.

Second is the intention that fundamental non-existence is emptiness and not a state of having existence (*bhāva*), meaning that one wishes to demonstrate that the various names for all defiled and pure phenomena are provisionally established within fundamental non-existence, as none of them possess their own inherent names.

Third is the intention to manifest emptiness through mutual dependence and mutual formation, meaning that one wishes to demonstrate that because defiled and pure phenomena are observed through their characteristics, they have possessed no self-substance from the very beginning and are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Fourth is the intention of natural voidness and non-obstruction, meaning that one wishes to demonstrate that because all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, they are naturally empty; and because they are neither obstructive nor non-obstructive, they always function as the principle of non-obstruction.

Fifth is the intention that is neither made nor created, which is natural; this means one wishes to demonstrate that whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, all phenomena mutually permeate and mutually produce one another without interruption, because the principle of *dharmatā* (the nature of things) is such.
Sixth is the intention of not guarding its own nature and being non-abiding; this means one wishes to demonstrate the meaning of the *dhāraṇī* of dependent origination regarding all phenomena.

This general indication of such immeasurable meanings is therefore called the "Gate of the General Indication of the Essential Framework. As the text states: "Furthermore, because there are four kinds of dharmas that perfuse one another, and because defiled and pure dharmas arise in an uninterrupted succession."
The gateway of the general outline has already been explained; next is the gateway of establishing names and providing a brief indication.
Within this gateway, there are two sections. What are these two?
First is the gate of the pure true dharma-characteristics; second is the gate of the defiled false dharma-characteristics.
That which is called "true" refers to the treasury-wisdom of original enlightenment, which is intrinsically pure by nature.
That which is called "delusion" refers to the fundamental ignorance that is devoid of intrinsic substance and characteristics.
Within the gateway of defiled delusion, there are three types.
What are these three?
First is ignorance, second is karmic consciousness, and third is the objective realm.
These four dharmas—one true and three delusive—constitute the fundamental enumeration of names for the activity of perfuming.

In this present passage, one instance is cited; however, there are others that include both [the prior and subsequent] as well as those within the intermediate state, which should be examined with care. Why is this so?
Because all defiled dharmas possess the nature of being perfumed (*vāsanā*). As the original text asks: "What are the four?"

First, pure phenomena are called True Suchness; second, all causes of defilement are called ignorance; third, the deluded mind is called the karmic consciousness; and fourth, the deluded objects are the so-called six sense-fields.
The section on establishing names and providing a brief indication has already been explained; next is the section on the general explanation of perfuming (vāsanā).
Within this section, there are two sub-sections. What are these two?
First is the gate of skill in inference and analogy; second is the gate of establishing through the conjunction of the dharma and the analogy.

Regarding the gate of skill in inference and analogy: for example, a garment from its very origin has neither fragrance nor foul odor, but remains entirely scentless. Yet, when people enter the *paṇḍagāyasaṭhita-uḍa* forest, it acquires a foul odor due to the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of *maitreya*;
and when they enter the *brahmadaṇḍi-tāla* forest, it acquires a fragrant scent due to the perfuming of *dharmakīrti*. Thus it is.
Just as in the world, clothing has no fragrance in itself, yet through the perfuming of incense by a person, it comes to possess a fragrant scent;

so too, when the analogy and the teaching are combined to establish this gate, the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise: its self-nature is pure, and its untainted qualities (*anāsrava-guṇa*) have been consistently luminous since beginningless time, being neither dark nor defiled. Yet, because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), it possesses darkness;
the ocean-store of the treasury of ignorance has been consistently dark since beginningless time.
There is neither the light of wisdom nor the category of purity; yet, because it is perfumed by primordial enlightenment (*mūlābodhi*), there is the function of purification.

Thus, defilement and purity are merely provisional designations; defilement is not truly defiled and purity is not truly pure, for both are illusory transformations lacking any real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

As stated in the original text, this is also the case here: the pure dharma of true suchness (tathatā) is in reality devoid of defilement, yet because it is perfumed by ignorance (avidyā), the appearance of defilement arises;
the defiled dharma of ignorance is in reality devoid of pure activity, yet because it is perfumed by true suchness, the function of purity arises.
Having already explained the section on the general interpretation of perfuming (vāsanā), next is the section on detailed analysis and exposition.
Within this section, there are four subsections. What are these four?

First, the gate of the powerful mutual permeation of dark qualities; second, the gate of the powerful mutual permeation of white qualities; third, the gate of initiating questions and answers to resolve doubts; fourth, the gate of citing conditions and explaining extensively to open up understanding.
Within the first gate, there are two gates. What are these two?
First, the gate that poses general questions and provides general answers to reveal the essential doctrine; second, the gate that returns to the general to provide specific and detailed explanations.
Within the second gate, these two gates are fully present; one should examine them carefully.
Within the fourth gate, there are likewise two gates. What are these two?

First is the gate of the general indication of the rules for determination; second is the gate of the individual demonstration of causes and conditions for the arising of understanding. Their characteristics may be seen as explained in their respective order.

Regarding the question, "How is it that the defiled dharmas arise through perfuming and continue without interruption?"—this is the general inquiry, meaning it is a comprehensive question concerning the principle that all black factors (defilements) mutually perfume and give rise to one another in an uninterrupted succession.
From this point onward is the section providing the comprehensive response.

Within this very section of the response, from the "Pure and Sublime Treasury" (*viśuddhasubhagarbha*) up to the "Coarse and Heavy" (*dausthulya*), the sequence is explained by gradually progressing from the fundamental toward the derivative, becoming increasingly refined. One should carefully examine the order of these explained characteristics.
Fundamental ignorance cannot exist of itself; it must rely upon True Suchness (*tathatā*) in order to abide. Why is this?
The nature of True Suchness is like the realm of empty space; it ultimately and truly presides over both obstruction and non-obstruction, acting as a refuge because it is unimpeded.
As stated in the original text: "Because of reliance upon the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), there exists ignorance (avidyā).

Once this ignorance has acquired its own basis, its power becomes preeminent and its functional capacity sovereign; it is able to permeate True Suchness, causing it to produce delusive phenomena, increasing the aspect of non-comprehension and adding the function of dullness. This is like an affectionate father giving birth to sons and daughters.
As the original text states: "Because there is the cause of defiled phenomena such as ignorance, it perfumes True Suchness; because of this perfuming, there arises the deluded mind.

Thus, once this subtle karmic consciousness—the deluded mind—has arisen from its own substance due to ignorance, it in turn perfumes ignorance, causing it to increase, just as a son, having been born, nurtures his father who gave him life."

Because the power of such habitual perfuming increases further, one is unable to penetrate the equality of the perfect single mind that accords with reality; consequently, the deluded thoughts of the evolving consciousness arise, producing the false objects of manifest appearances. Thus, the ocean of birth and death becomes deeper, and the shore of nirvana becomes ever more distant.

As the original [text] states: because there is a deluded mind, it immediately perfumes ignorance; because one does not understand the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), awakening is absent and thoughts arise, manifesting delusive objects.

Thus, the wind of these objects returns to perfume the ocean of the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), giving rise to the waves of the seven consciousnesses. This consciousness delights in and clings to the dust of objects, while those objects face the eyes of the consciousness; thus, one universally creates various evil karmas, fully undergoes all retributive suffering, revolves within the cycle of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), and the thief-waves of the four poisons surge forth.

As it says in the original text: "Because there are objective realms and defiled dharmas as conditions, they immediately permeate the deluded mind, causing it to become attached through recollection and to create various kinds of karma, thereby undergoing all manner of suffering of body and mind."

Having already explained the section on the general question and general answer that reveals the core doctrine, next is explained the section on returning to the general to provide detailed, specific expositions.
Within this section, there are three layers. What are these three?
The first is the objective realm, the second is the deluded mind, and the third is ignorance; these are called the three.

Since each of these three types has two aspects, they constitute the number six. Following their respective order, the first is treated as the last and the last as the first, thus revealing them in gradual succession.
What is the first layer?
Because these false objects possess the power of real perfuming, they increase the notion of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*);
because they possess the power of perfuming as such, they prolong the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*).

Because the two types of grasping—toward persons and toward phenomena—arise in their entirety, all categories of higher-level afflictions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are fully activated; therefore, this is called "object-conditioned perfuming" (*viṣaya-vāsanā*).
As stated in the original text, there are two kinds of meanings regarding the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of these delusive objects. What are the two?
First, the perfuming that increases the proliferation of thought; second, the perfuming that increases the proliferation of grasping.
What is meant by "heavy" in the middle?

Because the deluded mind of karmic consciousness possesses the power of superior permeation, even those who have already attained liberation—the sages of the Three Vehicles—are still made to undergo the subtle suffering of the transformation-body (*pariṇāmi-śarīra*).

Because it also possesses the power of inferior permeation, all ordinary beings who have not yet attained liberation are made to undergo the coarse suffering of the segmented body (*bhājana-loka*). For this reason, it is called the permeation of the deluded mind.
As stated in the original [text], there are two kinds of meanings regarding the perfuming of the deluded mind. What are these two?
First is the fundamental perfuming of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), which causes Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas to undergo the suffering of birth and death.

Second, it is because the habituation of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects) increases, whereby one is able to undergo the suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings.
Why is it called "heavy" later on?
Because it is the fundamental essence of the *avidyā-āvāsabhūmi* (ground of the dwelling of ignorance), it can permeate both the initial and the final stages, causing them to reach fulfillment.
Because it penetrates and pervades [all things], it is able to cause the perfuming consciousness (*vāsanā-vijñāna*) to achieve fulfillment.
Why are only the beginning and the end mentioned, while the middle is not explicitly revealed?
There are two reasons for this.
What are these two? First, the intention of accomplishing existence; second, the intention of accomplishing emptiness.
What is meant by the intention of accomplishing existence?
By citing the existence of the extremes, one shows that they exist within the middle.
What is meant by "the intention of accomplishing emptiness"?
By citing the absence of the middle, one reveals the emptiness of the extremes.
What is the meaning of "later"?
It is because it is so stated in the sūtras. Which sūtra is it?
This refers to the *Vāsanā-sūtra*. How is it explained in that sūtra?
In the *Vāsanā-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:

The evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the manas—these three consciousnesses—are not accomplished through ignorance (*avidyā*). Why is this?
Fundamental ignorance is accomplished only at the extremes, not in the middle.
The subsequent meaning of this passage directly explains that sutra; therefore, it is clearly known that this principle is established.
As in the original [treatise], there are two kinds of meanings regarding the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*). What are these two?
First is the fundamental perfuming, because it can accomplish the meaning of the karmic consciousness;
second is the perfuming of views and attachments that arise from it, because it can accomplish the meaning of the discerning consciousness of phenomena.
Having already explained the gate of the power of mutual perfuming among black factors, next is explained the gate of the power of mutual perfuming among white factors.

Regarding the question, "How does perfuming give rise to pure dharmas so that they are not severed?"—this is a general inquiry, as it universally asks about the meaning of how all white factors mutually perfume, give rise to one another, and continue without interruption.
From this point onward is the section providing the general response.
Within this very section of the response, there are two types of perfuming (*vāsanā*). What are these two?
The first is the beginningless, spontaneous perfuming; the second is the perfuming established from the point when [existence] begins.
As for the beginningless perfuming, it exists because from time immemorial there have been the two positions of cause and effect.
The initial presence of perfuming occurs because of the power of cultivation and because there are two stages: cause and fruit.
What are the characteristics of this original cause and fruit?
They consist of the stages of the three worthies and ten sages from time immemorial, as well as the fruits of the three bodies and four virtues.
What are the characteristics of the beginningless cause and effect?

It is because at the time of current practice, there is for the first time the ten stages (*bhūmi*) that have been beginningless, thereby manifesting the cause and effect that has primordially existed.
Regarding the sequence of these fundamental causes and effects:

because there have been, since beginningless time, ten kinds of fundamental awakened true wisdom (*mūla-avabodha-satya-jñāna*) and ten kinds of the *tathatā* dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are able to permeate the ten kinds of derivative ignorance (*śākhā-pratyaṅga-avidyā*).
Because there is one kind of dharma-realm mind (*dharmadhātu-citta*), it is able to permeate fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*); this is termed the "fundamental stage" (*mūla-bhūmi*).
As stated in the original text: "Because there is the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), it is able to permeate ignorance.
Regarding the sequence of the initial cause and effect:

although one has not yet attained the stage of the ten faiths, by the power of this fundamental permeation, one naturally feels revulsion for the suffering of birth and death within one's own mind and seeks the bliss of nirvāṇa.

By the power of this, one immediately perfumes the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), gaining self-confidence in the Buddha-nature and entering the stage of the Ten Faiths; knowing that the mind is illusory, one enters the stage of the Ten Understandings; knowing that objective realms are empty, one enters the stage of the Ten Practices; and cultivating the dharmas directed toward transcendence, one enters the stage of the Ten Transferences.

Because they know that the objective realm is empty through the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-prajñā*), they initiate practices that accord with the nature of the *dharmadhātu* through immeasurable skillful means; they neither grasp at nirvāṇa nor dwell upon saṃsāra, entering from the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama*).

Due to the long-term perfuming of past habituation, the path of liberation is generated; ignorance is suddenly severed, and because the root is exhausted, the branches and twigs all vanish. Since both the root and the branches of the dark categories are non-existent, one attains the nirvana of the Dharma-body and accomplishes the karmic functions of the response and transformation bodies; this is called the Initial Ground (Prathama-bhūmi).
