Regarding the analogy of the jewel, it refers to the treasure of the great maṇi gem.
Where would such a jewel be found?
Such a jewel would be found in yellow stone.
What is the color of such a jewel?
It is deep yellow. What is its physical form like?
This means it is like a square seat, for it has neither length nor shortness.
As for the dimensions of its size and appearance,
they are one zhang.
Such jewel-treasures are fully present within all yellow stones; there is no yellow stone that lacks the maṇi.
What is the sequence of their respective abiding characteristics?
That is to say, the first is the jewel, the second is gold, and the third is stone.

Regarding this mani-jewel that measures one *vyāma*, while those various yellow stones may be extremely small or extremely large and differ from one another, how could it be said that they all pervade everything?

This maṇi jewel possesses a sublime power; although it is but one fathom in size, it pervades all that is large, medium, and small without exception, meeting no obstruction, and may thus be said to pervade all places.
Because this treasure exists within that stone, its color is yellow;
one should examine it closely. This is called the "analogy of the treasure.
As the original text answers:
It is like a great maṇi jewel. Regarding the metaphor of natural purity:
such a jewel is extremely brilliant in its essential nature because it is free from the accumulation of dust; therefore, this is called the metaphor of natural purity.
Because its fundamental nature is luminous and pure, the metaphor of defilement is as follows:
just as this jewel can be obstructed by ores, stones, and the like, such that its brilliant appearance cannot manifest, this is called the metaphor of defilement.
Because it inherently possesses the impurities of ore and filth, it is called the "analogy of the multitude of people.

This refers to those who are utterly impoverished and utterly indolent, as well as those who do not seek jewels and those who are diligent and delight in seeking jewels; thus, it is named the analogy of the multitude of people.
As the original text states: "If a person, though mindful of the nature of a jewel, does not employ various skillful means to grind and refine it, it will ultimately never become pure.
Having already explained the section on the skillful application of metaphors, we shall next explain the section on the establishment of the correspondence through synthesis.
In the analogy of the jewels, what dharma does the "great maṇi pearl" represent?
It represents the originally enlightened Buddha-nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*). Why is this so?
The originally enlightened Buddha-nature is hidden within the continuum of the bodies of sentient beings, resembling that jewel.
As for the term "yellow stone," what dharma does it metaphorically represent?
It represents the continua of all sentient beings.
Why is this so? Because the Buddha-nature is concealed within the bodies of all sentient beings, much like that stone.
As for the description of its color as yellow, what dharma does it metaphorically represent?
This is used as a metaphor for the meaning of the Buddha-nature’s immutability. Why is this so?
Because the Tathatā-Buddha-nature is firm and unchanging, it resembles that gold.
As for the statement that "it is like a square seat having neither length nor shortness," to what dharma does this serve as a metaphor?
It serves as a metaphor for the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness), because it is equal and devoid of increase or decrease. Why is this so?
This Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is of a single flavor and equal, without any differentiation, as it resembles that seat.
As for the statement "one zhang," what dharma does it metaphorically represent?
It represents the Dharma of True Suchness being fully complete and perfect, without any deficiency or omission.
Why is this so? Because the *dharmakāya* of *tathatā* is fully endowed with all myriad virtues and lacks nothing, it resembles that *cintāmaṇi*.
When it is said that this jewel is found entirely complete within yellow stone, and that there is no yellow stone that does not contain a *maṇi*, what phenomenon is this intended to illustrate?

This is illustrated by the fact that the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) pervades the various bodies of all sentient beings; for there is no sentient being who lacks the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) of True Suchness. Why is this so?
This nature of *tathatā* is free from the fault of being non-pervasive, for it resembles that jewel.
As for the statement regarding "the first jewel, the second gold, and the third stone substance," to what phenomena do these serve as metaphors?
This is because there is a sequential order corresponding to the metaphors, as the phenomena gradually manifest in increasing coarseness. Why is this so?

When the ocean of the four marks evolves and is established from the wisdom of original enlightenment, they gradually manifest in increasing coarseness according to their respective sequence, resembling those three [metaphors].

It is said that this maṇi jewel possesses a sublime power such that, though it is only one *vyāma* in size, it pervades all things—large, medium, and small—without exception; to what dharma should this be compared?

This illustrates that the original enlightenment of true thusness possesses inconceivable activity, which pervades the bodies of all beings—whether small, such as mosquitoes, or large, such as dragons—without any hindrance or difficulty. Why is this so?
This *tathatā* (suchness) dharma is equal in nature and pervades both the ordinary and the holy, resembling that jewel.
When it is said that this treasure exists within that stone such that the stone’s color appears yellow, what dharma does this metaphor represent?
This is because all sentient beings possess the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) and the characteristics of mind. Why is this so?
Because all sentient beings possess an awakened mind and a consciousness that discriminates, they are like that stone.
Having already explained the section on the analogy of the jewel and its correspondence, next is explained the section on the analogy of purity and its correspondence.
As for the statement, "This jewel is of a nature that is exceedingly bright and pure, far removed from the accumulation of dust," to what dharma does this correspond?
The analogy of intrinsic purity refers to the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) being pure and luminous because it is free from defilement.

Having explained the section on the correspondence between the analogies of purity and their meanings, next is the section on the correspondence between the analogies of defilement and their meanings.
To say that such a jewel can be obstructed by gold, stone, and the like, such that its bright characteristics cannot manifest—what dharma does this metaphor represent?
It represents the intrinsically pure mind being shrouded and concealed by ignorance, so that its untainted virtuous qualities cannot manifest.
Having already explained the gateway of the concordant synthesis through the analogy of defilement, next is explained the gateway of the concordant synthesis through the analogy of persons.
As for the two kinds of persons mentioned, what phenomena do they correspond to?
This is an analogy for those who seek the jewel of the Buddha-dharma, whether they be extremely diligent or extremely indolent;
it is as stated in the original text: "because such sentient beings exist.

Having already explained the door of establishing the correspondence through combined exposition, next is explained the door of generating understanding through the manifestation of the teaching of the Dharma.

Within this section, the Dharma teaching, its application, and the simile are presented in their proper sequence to generate understanding in the practitioner; these should be carefully contemplated and explained, as the meaning of the text is clear and does not require further separate exposition.

Just as the essential nature of the dharma-body of original *tathatā* is empty and pure, yet it is defiled by immeasurable afflictions, so too, even if a person contemplates *tathatā*, they will not attain purity without practicing various methods through skillful means. This is because these defilements are immeasurable, boundless, and pervasive throughout all phenomena; therefore, one must cultivate all wholesome practices as their antidote.
Having already explained the section on providing the correct answer to resolve those objections, next is explained the section on the benefits gained by practitioners who cultivate goodness.

This means that if there are sentient beings who sever all evils and cultivate all virtues, they will naturally and spontaneously attain the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā), thereby illuminating and penetrating the darkness of ignorance, and being free from all doubt and fear.
As stated in the original text: "If a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they naturally accord with and conform to the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
Having explained the section on the benefits gained by those who practice wholesome conduct, I shall next explain the section on the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of practice.
Within this section, there are four gates. What are the four?

First, the gate of the fundamental basis of all practice; second, the gate of subduing evil karma so that it does not arise; third, the gate of generating and increasing roots of goodness; and fourth, the gate of boundless and impartial vows. These are called the four.
As it was briefly stated in the original [text] that there are four kinds of skillful means,
within the first gate there are two gates. What are these two?
The first is the gate of the accomplishment of prajñā through non-abiding; the second is the gate of the accomplishment of great compassion through non-abiding. These are called the two.

Regarding the gate of the accomplishment of prajñā through non-abiding: it refers to the contemplation that all phenomena, from the very beginning, are neither born nor extinguished, are ultimately quiescent, and are entirely non-existent, because one does not abide in saṃsāra.
As the original text asks: "What are the four?
First is the fundamental expedient of practice, which means observing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unborn, thereby departing from deluded views and not abiding in birth and death."

Regarding the statement that "great compassion achieves the gate of non-abiding," it means observing that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; thus, cause and effect are not empty, and karmic retribution likewise exists. It refers to taking as one's ultimate object the ocean-like realm of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, thereby embracing them while not abiding in *nirvāṇa*.

As in the original [teaching], one contemplates that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and that the fruits of karma are never lost; thus, giving rise to great compassion, one cultivates various merits to gather and transform sentient beings, for one does not abide in nirvana.
Regarding the phrase "because it accords with the non-abiding nature of reality," this demonstrates both the conditions and the conclusion of the two types of non-abiding path-practice.
Although the dharma-gates of cultivation are immeasurable, the non-abiding path is their most fundamental root; therefore, it is called the "fundamental expedient of practice."
Having already explained the gateway that is the fundamental basis for all spiritual practice, next is explained the gateway of subduing evil karma so that it does not arise.
What is the purpose of this gateway?

It is intended to demonstrate that the practitioner should give rise to pure mental states such as shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), thereby preventing all immeasurable unwholesome actions, gradually diminishing them until they are extinguished and no longer allowed to increase.
As in the original text, the second is the "skillful means for cessation," meaning that through shame, remorse, and repentance, one can cease all unwholesome dharmas so that they do not increase.
The phrase "because it accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and is free from all faults" summarizes its conditions.
Having already explained the gateway of subduing evil karma so that it does not arise, next is explained the gateway of generating and increasing roots of goodness.
What meaning does this gateway clarify?

It is intended to demonstrate that practitioners should respectfully make offerings to, prostrate before, praise, rejoice in, and entreat all Three Jewels, thereby increasing their faith, eliminating karmic obstructions, and aspiring for unexcelled, great Bodhi.

As stated in the original text, the third is the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness, which consists of diligently making offerings to and prostrating before the Triple Gem; praising, rejoicing in, and requesting the Buddhas; and because of one’s sincere and profound devotion to the Triple Gem, faith increases, whereby one is able to aspire to the unsurpassed Way.
Furthermore, because they are protected by the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they are able to eliminate karmic obstructions and ensure that their roots of goodness do not regress.
"Because they accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and are free from the obstruction of delusion" summarizes these conditions.
Having already explained the gateway of generating and increasing roots of goodness, next is explained the gateway of the boundless equality of vows.
What meaning does this gateway clarify?

It is intended to demonstrate that the practitioner should give rise to an ocean of vast vows as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions; cultivate an ocean of causal practices as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions; gather an ocean of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions; and accomplish an ocean of the fulfillment of results as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions—all of these being entirely without exception.

As the original text states, the fourth is the skillful means of the equality of the great vows; that is to say, to make a vow to transform and deliver all sentient beings without exception throughout the exhaustion of the future, causing them all to ultimately attain the nirvana without remainder.
"Because it accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without interruption" summarizes its conditions.
From this point forward, the text reveals the characteristics of this superior accordance.
For what reason are all four concluding sections uniformly designated as "accordance with the nature of phenomena"?

This is to reveal that the nature of phenomena is like space: its essence is vast, perfect, and without limit; its characteristics and functions are unimpeded and sovereign, being without beginning or end.
Those practitioners who cultivate all four gates are likewise compliant and conformable to suchness, because their *āśaya* is vast, perfect, and without limit.
Just as the dharmatā of this [mind] is vast and pervasive throughout all sentient beings, it is equal and non-dual, free from thoughts of self and other, because it is ultimately quiescent.
Having explained the gateway of skillful means in cultivation, I shall next explain the gateway that reveals the merit of generating the bodhicitta.
What meaning does this passage clarify?
It is intended to demonstrate that a bodhisattva who has entered the stage of the initial resolve gives rise to a vast and perfect mind that accords with the nature of the dharma-realm.

Through the wisdom of concordant contemplation, one perceives the Dharma-nature body; because one perceives the Dharma-body, the power of aspiration becomes sovereign. By virtue of this power of aspiration, one gives rise to great compassion toward sentient beings throughout the immeasurable and boundless dharma-realm. Because this great compassion is exceedingly profound, eight kinds of manifestations for peaceful and blissful transformation appear—acting in accordance with the time, place, suitability, and necessity, providing benefit and peace in a manner that is perfectly harmonious and such-like.

As it is said: because the Bodhisattva has given rise to this mind, he attains a partial vision of the Dharmakāya; by virtue of seeing the Dharmakāya, he is able to manifest eight kinds of manifestations for the benefit of sentient beings according to his power of vows—namely, descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving home, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering Nirvāṇa.

The section on the gate of manifesting the merit of generating the resolve has already been explained; next is the section on the gate of distinguishing the superior from the inferior to reveal their differences.
Within this gate, there are two sub-sections. What are these two?

The first is the gate that distinguishes [the practitioner] from those on the stages (*bhūmi*), and the second is the gate that distinguishes them from those still bound by all fetters; these are called the two.

Regarding the gate that distinguishes from those on the stages: it means that a Bodhisattva in the Stage of Resolving the Mind is only termed a body of illusory transformation and reflection, and cannot be termed a Bodhisattva of the True Suchness Dharma-body (*tathatā-dharmakāya*).

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have not yet emerged from the residual karma of beginningless time; wherever they are born, they remain inseparable from subtle suffering. This is contrary to the case of bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi).

As stated in the original text, this bodhisattva is not yet designated as having attained the Dharma-body because, throughout immeasurable past eons, their out-flowing (sāsrava) karma has not been definitively severed; thus, wherever they are born, they remain subject to subtle suffering.

Regarding the statement that distinguishes this from the gate of those still bound by fetters: it refers to Bodhisattvas in the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), who possess no characteristics of karmic causes that function in conjunction with fetters, and thus have no retributive fruits of birth associated with fetters.
Why is this so? Because they turn [the wheel of Dharma] through the fulfillment of great vows and skillful means.
As stated in the original text, they are not bound by karma, because they possess the sovereign power of great vows.

Having already explained the section on distinguishing the superior and inferior to clarify their differences, next is explained the section on resolving doubts through the general application of sūtra texts.
Within this section, there are five distinct types of sūtra citations.
What are the five? First, in the Mañjuśrīpramuditā-dhāraṇī-sūtra, it is said as follows:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The World-Honored One has constantly proclaimed among the great assembly:
‘The fifty minds are the root of the causal practices for the ocean of fruits adorned by the mind; all practitioners must traverse this path to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.’”
"Among these fifty sons in their hearts, how many belong to the category of regression,
and how many belong to the category of certainty?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now analyze and explain it for you.”

"Good son! The ten stages of reality (bhūmi) are called the stage of abiding in the Vajra-prajñā; the preceding forty minds are called the stage of the crystal-bead-like following-turning dedication."
"You should know it thus; you should contemplate it thus.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

It is intended to demonstrate that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Great Being constitute the realm of having attained true realization, which is termed the "stage of non-retrogression" (*avaivartika-bhāga*).
The forty types of mind prior to this have not yet attained realized wisdom and are therefore termed "regressive" (*hāna-bhāgīya*).
Second, the *Sūtra on the Natural Infusion of Original Enlightenment and Great Compassion* states as follows:
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
Regarding what you previously asked concerning the so-called "signs of regression," this matter is most excellent and inconceivable among the inconceivable;
it is something that foolish ordinary beings and bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved their minds cannot know.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha made a sincere exhortation, and the Buddha addressed Mahāprabha, saying:

"Good son, what is called the 'characteristic of retreating at the joints' refers to the mind of faith. Among these four stages—the stage of generating the mind, the pure ground, the vajra-mind, and the [final] stage—all are termed 'parts subject to retreat. The intervals between each of these are termed 'parts free from retreat. For this reason, it is said to be the characteristic of retreating at the joints."
Now, what meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It is intended to demonstrate that the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is vast, perfect, and boundless.
Thirdly, it is stated thus in the *Mahāpratilambhadhāraṇīsūtra*:
There are ten kinds of mental stability that are definitively non-retrogressive and possess the principle of no loss.
For what purpose does this scriptural passage now clarify?

It is intended to demonstrate that bodhisattvas of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) initiate vast roots of goodness within the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and thus they definitively abide in the adamantine stage (vajrapada).
Fourth, the *Pañcavidyā Sūtra* states as follows:

"The ten kinds of concentrated mind neither regress nor advance, neither come nor go, neither exit nor enter; they are perfected with all virtues without any deficiency. Therefore, it is called the 'naturally abiding mind.'"
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?

It is intended to demonstrate that within the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), the merit of fruition is already perfected; there is nothing further to advance toward and no longer anything from which to regress, as it naturally abides eternally without deficiency.
Fifth, in the *Bodhisattva-kaṇṭhābharaṇa-mūla-karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"O sons of good family!
If one practices the ten faiths for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to ten kalpas, one will attain entry into the ten abodes."

At that time, from the first stage through the sixth stage, if this person cultivates the sixth *prajñāpāramitā* such that correct contemplation manifests before them, and further encounters the protection of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they emerge into the seventh stage and abide permanently in non-retrogression. Prior to this seventh stage, it is termed the "stage of retrogression."
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It is intended to demonstrate how to exhort and spur on those sentient beings who are inferior and indolent, so as to cause their courageous minds to increase.
In this treatise, we shall for now provide a reconciliation based on the *Mūlakarma* (Fundamental Karma); this should be carefully examined.

For instance, when the sūtras state that there are those who fall back and descend into the evil realms, this is not an actual falling back; rather, it is spoken thus to inspire those beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and are prone to indolence, so as to cause them to become courageous and diligent.

Having already explained the section on resolving doubts through the general scriptural texts, we now present the section on praising the merit of generating the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
What is the purpose of this section?
It is intended to demonstrate that bodhisattvas who have generated the resolve are free from the two fears, as their minds are resolute and unshakable.
What are called the two kinds of fear?
First is the fear of being born below, because one is extremely terrified by birth in the inferior realms;
second is the fear of being born above, because upon hearing of sublime objects, one’s mind becomes timid and weak, leading to extreme terror.
Being free from these two fears is therefore called the merit of generating the bodhicitta.
As the original text states: "Furthermore, once this Bodhisattva has generated the mind, they remain far removed from cowardice and never fear falling into the stages of the Two Vehicles."

This is because even upon hearing that one must undergo diligent practice and difficult austerities for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to attain *nirvāṇa*, one does not become discouraged.
Furthermore, by knowing through faith that all phenomena have been *nirvāṇa* from the very beginning, this serves as the summary of the causal conditions for these two kinds of merit.
The section on the "Determination of the Arising of the Mind through the Accomplishment of Faith" from the beginning has already been concluded.
From this point onward, as the textual expressions across the various gateways are clear, there is no need for further explanation.
The Commentary on the Mahāyāna Śāstra, Scroll Seven.
The Commentary on the Mahāyāna Śāstra, Scroll Eight.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamata of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Having already explained the Section on Exposition, the Section on the Practice of Faith is now presented.
Within this section, there are seven gates.

What are the seven? First, the gateway of the correspondence between that which is remedied and the remedy; second, the gateway of the classification of the categories of faith; third, the gateway of skillful means in cultivation; fourth, the gateway of the extensive explanation of the counteracting of demonic activities; fifth, the gateway of praising the merits of samādhi; sixth, the gateway of the benefits and losses resulting from the possession or lack of the two wheels; and seventh, the gateway of exhorting the inferior toward the superior so as not to regress. These are called the seven.
Regarding the gateway of the correspondence between that which remedies and that which is remedied, what are its characteristics?
The original text states:
"In this regard, based on sentient beings who have not yet entered the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), the section on the cultivation of faith is taught."
The Commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "herein, those sentient beings who have not yet entered the group of those destined for rightness," this refers to that which is to be remedied, namely, the sphere of those to be converted.
The "Section on the Practice of Faith" refers to that which is capable of treatment—namely, the teaching that performs the transformation.
What is the extent of the realm to be transformed?
This refers to encompassing sentient beings within two groups.
What are these two? First, the group of those fixed in error; second, the group of those who are not fixed. These are called the two.
Why is this? Because both of these beings have not yet entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
As for what is meant by "being in accord," what are its characteristics?
This means that within each of the two types of sentient beings, the teaching is accorded to their respective capacities.
What are these characteristics of accord?
For those sentient beings who are fixed in the category of the wicked (mithyā-niyata-rāśi), the gateway of faith is taught.
Because he wishes to benefit those sentient beings of the indeterminate group, he teaches the gates of practice. Why is this so?
It is because such is the nature of the Dharma regarding the sequence of entry.
This means that for those who have not yet developed faith, it causes faith to arise first; for those who already possess faith, it leads them directly to practice.
Furthermore, it universally benefits all.
Having explained the gateway of the correspondence between the remedies and the objects to be remedied, next is explained the gateway of the classification and analysis of the categories of faith.
The text says:
What is the nature of faith?
How is one to practice?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of faith.
What are the four? First is faith in the root, which means delighting in mindfulness of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).

Second, they believe that the Buddha possesses immeasurable merit; they constantly mindfully seek to draw near to him, making offerings and showing reverence, thereby initiating roots of goodness and aspiring for all-knowledge.
Third, one has faith that the Dharma brings great benefit, because one constantly contemplates and practices the various pāramitās.

Fourth, one has faith that the Saṃgha is able to correctly practice for the benefit of both self and others, because one always delights in drawing near to the assembly of bodhisattvas to seek and learn their authentic practice.
The Commentary states:
Within this passage, there are three sections.
What are these three?

First, the gate of directly inquiring into the categories of faith; second, the gate of directly inquiring into the categories of practice; third, the gate of providing a brief answer to reveal the nature of faith—these are called the three.
To speak of the "direct inquiry into the categories of the stage of faith" means to inquire generally about the measure of faith;
as in the text: "What kind of faith?
To speak of the "direct inquiry into the categories of the stage of practice" means to inquire generally about the measure of practice.
As the original text asks, "How should one practice?
there are three gates within this third gate.
What are these three?
First is the gate of general response, second is the gate of general inquiry, and third is the gate of detailed response.
As for the gate of general response, it refers to providing a general answer to what has been stated.
As the original text briefly states that there are four kinds of faith, the term "general inquiry" refers to inquiring about the entirety of what has been taught.
As the original text asks: "What are the four?"
Within the third gate, there are four types of gates. What are the four?

First, the gate of faith in the source that brings the mind to equanimity; second, the gate of faith in the Buddha and rejoicing in his meritorious qualities; third, the gate of faith in the Dharma and diligent cultivation through practice; fourth, the gate of faith in the Saṃgha that causes the mind to be free from contention. These are called the four.

Regarding the gate of "Faith as the Foundation for Making the Mind Equal": it means that taking the delight in faith as the fundamental root of the True Suchness (tathatā) principle, all various minds—which have arisen through diverse differentiations by the power of ignorance—are brought together into one and made equal.
As stated in the original text, "the first is the root of faith," which means one takes delight in recollecting the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma.

Regarding the statement, "one has faith in the Buddha and delights in the gate of his meritorious qualities," this refers to taking delight in faith in the Unsurpassed Greatly Awakened One, the World-Honored Tathāgata, and joyfully seeking all his immeasurable and boundless merits.

As stated in the original text, secondly, it is because one believes that the Buddha possesses immeasurable merit, constantly recollects him, draws near to him, makes offerings to him, and honors him, thereby initiating roots of goodness and aspiring for all-knowledge.

Regarding the gate of practice through faith, Dharma, and diligence: it refers to delighting in faith in the Buddhas of the three periods of time as one’s own kind father, one’s own kind mother, and one’s own kind teacher; [a faith] that cannot be corrupted or destroyed, that is neither born nor extinguished, and which is the immovable principle of space and vajra. It possesses inconceivable within the inconceivable supreme benefits, for it constantly and perpetually, at all times and in all places, practices all the factors conducive to enlightenment.
As stated in the original text, the third [point] is that faith in the Dharma brings great benefit because one constantly recollects and practices the various *pāramitās*.

Regarding the statement "faith in the Saṃgha is the gateway to a mind free from strife," this refers to delighting in faith in the entire, immeasurable assembly of Bodhisattvas who take the two supreme practices as their internal virtue. Whether far or near, at whatever time one hears, sees, or reflects upon them, one approaches the Saṃgha and, with a sincere heart, listens to and receives various profound Dharmas, various profound sūtras, various profound treatises, various profound principles, and various sublime matters without interruption.

As stated in the original text, the fourth is faith in the Saṅgha, because they are able to correctly practice for their own benefit and the benefit of others, and because they always delight in drawing near to the assembly of bodhisattvas to seek learning and practice according to reality.
Having explained the section on the classification of the categories of faith, next is explained the section on the skillful means of practice.
The root text says:
"There are five gates of practice that can bring this faith to fulfillment."
What are the five? First is the gate of giving; second is the gate of precepts; third is the gate of patience; fourth is the gate of diligence; and fifth is the gate of tranquility and insight.
How does one practice the gate of generosity?
When seeing anyone who comes seeking, one gives away all one's wealth according to one's ability, abandoning one's own stinginess and greed so as to bring joy to others.
If one sees beings beset by calamity, terror, or peril, one should bestow fearlessness according to one's own capacity.

If there are sentient beings who come seeking the Dharma, one should explain it to them through skillful means according to what one understands; one must not crave fame, profit, or honor, but should instead keep in mind only the benefit of oneself and others, dedicating such merit toward enlightenment.
How does one practice the gate of precepts? It is said:

not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not engaging in double-tongued speech, not using harsh words, not speaking falsehoods, and not engaging in frivolous chatter; and remaining far removed from greed and envy, deception, flattery, malice, and wrong views.

If one has left the household life for the sake of subduing afflictions, one should likewise distance oneself from clamor and dwell constantly in tranquility; one should practice such disciplines as fewness of desires, contentment, and the dhūta austerities, and even regarding minor transgressions, one should give rise to fear, shame, and remorse, and reform.

One must not treat lightly the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata; rather, one should guard against censure and reproach so as not to cause sentient beings to give rise to false transgressions and offenses.
How, then, does one practice the gate of patience?

This means that one should endure the afflictions caused by others without harboring a desire for retaliation; furthermore, one should likewise endure the phenomena of gain and loss, defamation and fame, praise and blame, and suffering and pleasure.
What is the gateway to the practice of diligence?

It means that regarding all wholesome deeds, the mind does not slacken or retreat; one establishes a firm resolve, remaining far removed from cowardice and weakness. One should reflect that since the distant past, one has pointlessly endured all manner of great physical and mental suffering without any benefit. Therefore, one should diligently cultivate all meritorious virtues to benefit oneself and others, swiftly escaping all forms of suffering.

Furthermore, if a person, although practicing with faith, is afflicted by various demonic spirits and ghosts due to the heavy burden of grave sins and evil karmic obstructions accumulated from previous lives; or is entangled by the myriad affairs of the mundane world; or is tormented by the suffering of illness—because there are such numerous obstacles as these, one should be courageous and diligent, performing prostrations to the Buddhas during the six periods of the day and night, repenting with a sincere heart, requesting [the Buddhas to teach], rejoicing [in merit], and dedicating [merit] toward Bodhi without ever ceasing. This is because, by doing so, one will be freed from all obstacles and one's roots of goodness will increase.
How does one practice the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
That which is called "stopping" (*śamatha*) refers to the cessation of all objective appearances, as it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of *śamatha*.

What is called "contemplation" refers to discerning the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, because it accords with the meaning of *vipaśyanā* contemplation. How does it accord?
It is because one gradually cultivates these two meanings without letting them diverge, so that they both manifest simultaneously.

If one practices *śamatha*, one should dwell in a quiet place, sitting upright with the mind correctly settled. One does not rely on the breath, nor on forms and colors, nor on space, nor on earth, water, fire, or wind; nor even upon what is seen, heard, sensed, or known. All mental conceptions are eliminated as they arise, and even the thought of "eliminating" is discarded, because all phenomena are fundamentally without marks (*animitta*); in every moment they do not arise, and in every moment they do not cease.
Furthermore, one must not follow the mind as it wanders toward external objects, nor subsequently attempt to eliminate the mind with the mind;
if the mind becomes distracted and scattered, one should immediately draw it back and abide in right mindfulness.
One who possesses right mindfulness should know that there is only mind and no external objects.
Furthermore, this very mind has no self-characteristic and cannot be apprehended from moment to moment.

Whether rising from one's seat, going or coming, advancing or stopping, or in whatever action one performs, at all times one should constantly maintain mindfulness of skillful means and observe accordingly. Through long-term practice until it becomes pure and mature, the mind will attain stability.

Because the mind abides [in this state], it gradually becomes sharp and intense; by following this, one enters the samādhi of *tathatā*. One deeply subdues the afflictions, the faculty of faith increases, and one swiftly achieves the stage of non-retrogression. However, those who harbor doubt and lack faith, who slander [the teaching], who possess heavy karmic obstructions, or who are characterized by arrogance and indolence—such persons are unable to enter.
Furthermore, by relying on this samādhi, one knows that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic.
That is to say, the dharma-body of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings are equal and non-dual; this is called the Samādhi of One Practice.
One should know that suchness is the root of samādhi; if a person practices it, they will gradually be able to give rise to immeasurable samādhis.
The Commentary states:
Within this passage, there are five gates.

What are the five? First, the section that provides a general indication in response to the preceding questions; second, the section that thoroughly addresses what was stated in the general inquiry; third, the section that briefly answers by establishing the number of gates; fourth, the section that briefly asks and extensively answers through detailed exposition; and fifth, the section that praises the excellence of the samādhi. These are called the five.
Regarding the statement "the general heading that answers the preceding questions," this refers to providing a comprehensive response to those prior inquiries.
As it says in the root text: "There are five gates of practice through which one can accomplish this faith."
Regarding the "gate of explaining the general inquiry through thorough penetration," this refers to thoroughly explaining the subject matter of that general inquiry;
as the root text asks: "What are the five?
Regarding the "gate of establishing the number of categories through a concise response," this refers to establishing the number of the major categories.

As stated in the original text, there are five gates: first, the gate of giving; second, the gate of precepts; third, the gate of patience; fourth, the gate of diligence; and fifth, the gate of śamatha-vipaśyanā.
For what reason is the sequence as such?
This is because the sequential method for practicing the six perfections is thus;
furthermore, within the section on the "Brief Question and Extensive Answer" (liao-wen kuan-da san-shuo men), there are five gates, and therefore these five gates should be carefully examined.
Within each of these five gates, there are two gates respectively.
What are these two? First is the gate of concise questioning; second is the gate of detailed answering. These are called the two.
One should carefully examine and discern the sequence and number [of the gates] without confusion.
Regarding the first practice, the gate of giving (*dāna*), the statement "How does one practice the gate of giving? constitutes the brief introductory question, which is to say, the opening inquiry.
Therefore, the subsequent gates should be understood in this same manner.
Within the gate of the detailed response, there are three kinds of giving.
What are these three?
First is the gift of material wealth; second is the gift according to suitability; third is the gift of the Dharma teachings.

Regarding the gift of material wealth: it means that if any sentient being comes to me and begs for what I possess, I do not hesitate, but bestow it upon them at all times and in all places, without any sense of regret or attachment.
What things are called "wealth"? How many kinds of wealth are there?
It is because there are two kinds of wealth.
What are the two? First, internal things; second, external things—these are called the two.
Within internal things, there are also two kinds.
What are these two? First is the formless, and second is the formed.
That which is called "formless" refers to the mind-consciousness.
That which is called "possessing form" refers to the various sense faculties.
If there were sentient beings who came to me and begged for my mind and consciousness, I would not begrudge them, but would give them at any time to bring them joy.
If there are sentient beings who come to me and request any of my various excellent physical faculties for their own use, I do not begrudge them; I give them away at all times to bring them joy.
These are called the two kinds of internal wealth.
Within external objects, there are likewise two kinds. What are these two?
The first consists of those with consciousness, and the second consists of those without consciousness.
That which is said to have consciousness refers to categories such as wives, children, and slaves.
That which is said to be without consciousness refers to categories such as palaces, houses, clothing, and ornaments.
If there are sentient beings who come to me and beg for such things, I do not begrudge them, but give them at all times to bring them joy.
These are called the two kinds of external wealth.

As stated in the original text: "If one sees anyone who comes seeking something, one should give away all one's wealth according to one's ability, thereby abandoning one's own stinginess and greed and causing the other to rejoice."
The giving of material wealth has already been explained; next, the giving according to what is appropriate will be explained.

What is meant by "giving according to what is appropriate"? It refers to cases where some sentient beings have impaired or lost their five faculties and cannot be complete; or where some sentient beings suffer immeasurable illness and pain and find no peace; or where some sentient beings are dull-witted and lack clarity. At such times, the practitioner, following the standard of a noble person, acts according to what is appropriate, what is fitting, what is suitable, and what is required for them. Being able to skillfully select and skillfully discern [the needs], they remove those beings' suffering and affliction so as to bring them joy; therefore, it is called "giving according to what is appropriate."
As stated in the original text: "If one sees others beset by calamity, fear, or peril, one bestows fearlessness according to one's own capacity.
Having explained giving in accordance with what is appropriate, the giving of the Dharma will now be explained.
What is called the gift of the Dharma?

It refers to when sentient beings—whether at the proper or improper time, whether kin or not kin, whether noble or ignoble, whether foolish or wise, whether male or female, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, whether human or non-human—come before me seeking the Dharma. At such times, I do not begrudge it; rather, I give rise to an immeasurable, boundless, vast, and perfect mind of great compassion. I decisively sever their doubts, eliminate their afflictions, and gradually increase their wisdom. By thus gathering in these people so they do not fall into the evil realms and lead them to unsurpassed, great Bodhi, it is therefore called the gift of the Dharma.

As stated in the original text: "If there are sentient beings who come seeking the Dharma, one should explain it to them through skillful means according to what one can understand; one should not crave fame, profit, or honor, but should instead contemplate only self-benefit and the benefit of others, dedicating [the merit] toward Bodhi."
The practice of the gate of giving has already been explained; next, the practice of the gate of ethical discipline will be explained.
Within this gate, there are four sections. What are these four?

First is the gate of establishing the characteristics of the precepts to mark the fundamental principle; second is the gate of accomplishing the superior states of the categories of precepts; third is the gate of fulfilling the practice of precepts without disparagement; fourth is the gate of guarding [the precepts] so as not to allow slander. These are called the four.

Regarding the statement "establishing the characteristics of the precepts to mark the gateway of the fundamental principle," this refers to establishing ten kinds of purity in order to prevent the transgression of the precepts.
As the text asks: "How does one practice the gateway of the precepts?"

That is to say: refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from double-tongued speech, refraining from harsh speech, refraining from false speech, and refraining from frivolous speech; and because of remaining far removed from greed and envy, deception, flattery and crookedness, malice, and wrong views.

Regarding the "gate of the superior station for accomplishing the aggregate of ethical discipline," this means that if one wishes to be fully endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline, one should always remain far removed from distracted and cluttered environments, and should always draw near to peaceful and superior stations, dwelling therein without ever abandoning them.

As stated in the original text: "If one has left the household life, for the sake of subduing afflictions (*kleśa*), one should likewise remain far removed from clamor and always dwell in tranquility.

Regarding the gate of not disparaging the complete observance of precepts: this refers to practicing various sublime conducts and giving rise to deep faith, such that one must never treat with contempt or belittle the precept concerning the prohibition against [approaching] a teacher's wife (*mātṛgrāma*) as established by the Tathāgata.

As previously practiced, one cultivates such conduct as fewness of desires, contentment, and the dhūta ascetic practices; even regarding minor transgressions, one gives rise to fear, shame, and remorse, and does not treat lightly the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata.

Regarding the gate of guarding against slander: it refers to protecting and upholding the precepts that are the eyes of the Buddhas so as never to lose them; being fully endowed with self-benefit; ensuring that various negligent and disparaging sentient beings do not give rise to deluded thoughts, transgressions, or faults; and being fully endowed with the benefit of others through the perfect adornment of the ocean of Great Enlightenment.
As stated in the original text, one should guard against censure and reproach so as not to cause sentient beings to give rise to groundless faults or transgressions.
Having explained the gate of practicing ethical discipline (*śīla*), next is explained the gate of practicing patience (*kṣānti*).
Within this section, there are two gates. What are the two?
First, the gate that demonstrates the brief patience of subduing the self; second, the gate that demonstrates the extensive patience of non-self. These are called the two.

Regarding the statement "to display the brief patience that subdues those who follow my school": this means that if there are sentient beings who create conditions for a malicious intention (*āśaya*) that causes distress to one's mind, the practitioner at that time is able to endure it with a mind that remains unmoved by such affliction.
As the original text asks: "How does one practice the gate of patience?
It means that one should endure the afflictions caused by others, without harboring a desire for retaliation.

Regarding the statement "to reveal the gate of vast patience and non-self," it refers to those sentient beings who, with various material goods such as food, drink, clothing, and so forth, bestow upon me benefit and joy.
There may be sentient beings who, appearing with various terrifying forms such as swords and staves, come before me to destroy my physical body and its environment, depriving me of my sovereignty;
or there may be sentient beings who, with various foul words such as coarse speech and slander, revile and disparage me from afar or nearby;
or there may be sentient beings who praise my person with various virtues such as right abiding.
Regarding such various matters as these, his mind is impartial, firm, and immovable like Mount Sumeru; for it is as stated in the original text:
"One should likewise endure the dharmas of gain and loss, defamation and praise, renown and insignificance, suffering and pleasure."
The practice of the gate of patience has already been explained; next, the practice of the gate of diligence will be explained.
Within this gate, there are two sub-gates. What are these two?
First is the general presentation of the gate of diligent practice; second is the specific explanation of the gate of diligent practice.

Regarding the general presentation of the gate of diligent practice: it refers to the fact that one’s mind becomes increasingly superior toward all manner of sublime matters, exerting oneself with diligence that never ceases.
As the original text asks: "How does one practice the gateway of diligence?
It means that regarding all wholesome deeds, the mind does not slacken or retreat; one establishes a firm resolve and remains free from cowardice."
Within the detailed explanation of the gateway of the practice of diligence, there are two gateways. What are these two?
First, the gateway of the practice of diligence free from obstructions; second, the gateway of the practice of diligence with obstructions.
Regarding the gate of diligent practice that is free from hindrances, it means that the practitioner reflects as follows:

"From beginningless time in the past, I have only experienced a false and unreal body and mind, and have been entirely unable to experience a vajra-like, indestructible body and mind; this is due to no other cause or condition than my failure to apply myself diligently to sublime practices."

If I am indolent and do not practice as before, then even as I move toward the future, I shall again experience a false body and mind that is entirely devoid of benefit, with no prospect of liberation.

If I myself cannot even achieve liberation and have lost all benefit for my own sake, how much less can I rescue the various other sentient beings suffering in existence and fulfill the benefit of others?

Having formed this thought, he immediately gave rise to a mind of great diligence, practicing the ocean of causal conduct and adorning the fruit of perfected virtues, so as to establish the two benefits without deficiency or partiality.

As stated in the original text: One should reflect that from the distant past until now, one has pointlessly endured all manner of great suffering of body and mind without any benefit; therefore, one should diligently cultivate all merits so as to swiftly bring oneself and others away from all suffering for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others.

Regarding the gate of diligence for those whose practice is obstructed: it refers to those sentient beings who, because of residual karmic obstructions from beginningless past, are harassed and distracted by Māras, non-Buddhists, and malevolent spirits, and thus cannot practice;
or those sentient beings who, being entangled by the various affairs of the present life, cannot practice;
or those sentient beings who, being oppressed and tormented by all manner of illnesses and sufferings, cannot practice.

Although such sentient beings hear the rules and venerable words with their ears, and behold with their eyes the signs of scriptural teachings and explanations, they are unable to diligently practice them or give rise to a mind of weary detachment and seeking.

However, if one’s mind is courageous and diligent, giving rise to various sublime and wondrous skillful means and maintaining a sense of capability, the ocean of karmic obstructions will gradually subside and the mountain of merit will ever-increasingly rise in height; thus, one will not be tossed by the eight winds nor bound by the nine fetters.

As stated in the original text: Furthermore, even if a person practices with faith, because they have accumulated many grave sins and evil karmic obstructions from previous lives, they may be harassed and disturbed by Māras, heterodox spirits, and various ghosts; or they may be entangled by various worldly affairs; or they may be afflicted by the suffering of illness—there are many such obstacles as these.

Therefore, one should be courageous and diligent, performing prostrations to all Buddhas during the six periods of the day and night; with a sincere heart, one should repent, entreat, rejoice, and dedicate [merit] toward Bodhi without ever ceasing, so that one may escape all obstacles and cause one's roots of goodness to increase.
Having already explained the gate of practicing diligence, next I shall explain the gate of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Within this gate, there are four sections. What are these four?

First, the gate of the general heading and general explanation of the wheel of cessation; second, the gate of the general heading and general explanation of the wheel of contemplation; third, the brief explanation and definitive analysis of the gate of conformity; and fourth, the extensive explanation and definitive analysis of the wheel of cessation—these are called the four.

Regarding the statement that provides a general heading and a general explanation for the gate of the wheel of cessation (*śamatha*): it means to still the mind that discriminates and knows, and to obstruct thoughts of distraction, abiding in the single nature of quiescence, not emerging from the marks of all objective spheres, because it accords with the meaning of the *samādhi-lakṣaṇa-dhāraṇī-vipaśyanā*.
As the original text asks: "How does one practice the gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā?
That which is called 'stopping' (śamatha) refers to the cessation of all objective appearances, because it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of śamatha."

Regarding the statement "the gate of the general heading and general explanation of the wheel of contemplation," this refers to clarifying the principles for discerning causes and conditions, and carefully analyzing the characteristics of impermanence; it is so called because one is able to skillfully penetrate and skillfully fully know the meaning of the contemplation of *sthitārala* (the fixed and revolving) in accordance with the heading.

Regarding "contemplation" as stated in the original text, it refers to discerning the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, because it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the phrase "brief explanation of the gate of accordant determination," it means that when meditative concentration (*samādhi*) accords with that contemplation at any given time, then that contemplation accords with that concentration during that time; this is because they are fully complete and do not deviate from one another.
As the original text asks, "How does one accord with [the practice]?
It is because one gradually cultivates these two meanings without letting them fall away from one another, so that they both manifest simultaneously.
Within the extensive explanation and determination of the section on the wheel of *śamatha*, there are four gates.

What are the four? First, the gateway of the causes and conditions for accomplishing the wheel of *śamatha*; second, the gateway of directly demonstrating the practice of the wheel of *śamatha*; third, the gateway of the benefits gained from practicing the wheel of *śamatha*; and fourth, the gateway of distinguishing between those who enter and those who do not. These are called the four.
Within the first section, the gate of causes and conditions for accomplishing the wheel of śamatha, there are fifteen types. What are these fifteen?

First, the causal condition of dwelling in a quiet place; second, the causal condition of being solitary and without companions; third, the causal condition of residing in an auspicious location; fourth, the causal condition of possessing sufficient clothing; fifth, the causal condition of possessing sufficient food and drink; sixth, the causal condition of establishing boundaries for protection and purity; seventh, the causal condition of constructing a dwelling; eighth, the causal condition of not letting speech issue forth; ninth, the causal condition of fashioning an image for sitting; tenth, the causal condition of sitting upon that seat; eleventh, the causal condition of the proper timing for coming and going; twelfth, the causal condition of having wise friends and virtuous associates; thirteenth, the causal condition of discerning the correct from the erroneous through seals; fourteenth, the causal condition of planting the forest trees of goodness; fifteenth, the causal condition of internalizing the wheel of syllables. These are called the fifteen kinds of great causal conditions.

Regarding the causes and conditions for dwelling in a quiet place: it means that, in order to cultivate the gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*, one dwells in secluded places such as mountain forests, far removed from the distractions of inhabited villages.
Why is this so? Because within a place of distraction, it is difficult to accomplish the gateway of that wheel of *śamatha*.

As for the phrase "a unique and exclusive causal condition," it means that if one is practicing that gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*, it is not reasonable for two people to dwell together within a single realm.
Why is this? Because they would mutually disturb one another.

Regarding the statement that the quarters where one dwells must have favorable conditions: this means that if one is practicing the gate of the wheel of *śamatha*, one may dwell in either the eastern or western regions, but one must not dwell in the northern or southern regions.
Why is this? Because there is the wheel of discernment (*vitarka*).

Regarding the causes and conditions for being fully provided with robes: it means that if one wishes to cultivate the door of the wheel of tranquility (*śamatha*), one must necessarily use three types of robes.
What are the three? First, yellow; second, red; third, white.
This is because these three robes are used simultaneously.
Why is this? Because the *vikhara* insects cannot enter it.

Regarding the phrase "the conditions for being fully supplied with food and drink," this means that if one wishes to cultivate the gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*, one must necessarily use dried *laṅkāma-īdaya*; other grains and the like cannot be used.
Why is this so? Because that *gamayeya* possesses the nature of a seer (*ṛṣi*).

Furthermore, since there would otherwise be no purpose for [the use of] *vānīra* and so forth, when utilizing the seasons, one would use only its own internal [measure], as there would be no fixed rule.

Regarding the causes and conditions for establishing a boundary and purifying the site: it means that if one wishes to practice the gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*, one should recite the Great Deity Mantra one hundred and ten times within a radius of one *krośa* from one's own chamber.
What are its characteristics?
They are as follows; namely, one recites the mantra:

*Taṃ yathā*: Nara-te vakhani amogha-khaṭe baba-ā-baba-yi-ta ja-khana u-ha-i-ta-te am-am-am-am-te tta-vattata-ye mana-sicite khada-ni-ba kharani-ku-ha-a-ha-ku-ta-si am-ṭa-ta-te mahā-gayate mahā-agayate gandhani arā-rā-rā-rā-rā-rā-rā-rā-rā-ate svāhā. Once this mantra has been recited, one immediately performs the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) for protection and purification.
Why is this? Because various kinds of poisons cannot enter it.
Regarding the causes and conditions for constructing a dwelling, if one intends to build a dwelling for the cultivation of meditative concentration, one must fulfill ten requirements.
What are the ten? First is the matter of the gateways: they face only toward the east and not toward any other direction.
Second is the matter of elevation and depression: the eastern side gradually rises while the western side gradually descends.
Third is the matter of its dimensions and corners, because it measures one *zhang* on each side.
Fourth is the matter of its layers, because it consists of ten layers.
Fifth is the matter of the materials used for its construction, because only five types of materials are employed and no others.
What are the five? First, gold; second, silver; third, copper; fourth, iron; and fifth, pine wood—these are called the five.
Sixth is the matter of the door panels being flush, because their dimensions are equal and without distinction.
Seventh is the matter of the door being double-layered, because it consists of ten layers.
Eighth is the matter of the door pivots, because they produce no sound.
Ninth is the matter of the walls and enclosures; they are one zhang high and ten layers thick.
Tenth is the matter of entering and exiting; for within each of those gates, mantras are recited.
What are its characteristics?
They are as follows: when one wishes to emerge [from obstruction], one should recite this mantra:

*Namāyate mahā-kubine āravate dhadhāgatu pañcāciśi cacasranate vajrima-vima vajrima-ana anaśicini śici svāhā.* If this divine mantra is recited one thousand times, then at that very moment, all shall be opened and made passable.
If one wishes to enter, one should recite the mantra as follows:

Namo namjina | Namo vaśita | Namo nmaditi | Namo nmadriṇa | Namo gandhane svāhā. Once this divine mantra has been recited fifteen hundred times, the gates will all open and close in accordance with the proper time.

Regarding the statement that "speech does not issue forth from conditions," this means that when practicing the gateway of the wheel of cessation (*śamatha*), one does not utter speech at any time or in any place.
Why is this so? Because consciousness emerges in accordance with verbal expression.
Regarding the causes and conditions for creating a seated image: if one intends to create a seated image for the practice of meditative concentration, one must possess five requirements.
What are the five? First is the matter of the material substance, because it is made of pine wood;
second is the matter of the height measurement, which must be exactly half the height of one's own body, neither more nor less.
Third is the matter of the square corners, because each side within one direction measures four *chi*;
fourth is the matter of the orientation, because it faces only the eastern direction and no other;
fifth is the matter of the seating implements, because only yellow *dhāraṇī* [cloth] and a yellow sitting mat are used.
These are called the five.

Regarding the causes and conditions for sitting upon that seat: it means that if one wishes to cultivate the gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*, one should sit upon that seat while being endowed with ten matters.
What are the ten? First, the matter of the feet: the two big toes at the ends of the knees must be joined together so that there is no discrepancy.
Second, the matter of the knees: the two knees must be held level and gathered so that there is no discrepancy.
Third is the matter of the waist being upright: because the waist is straight and free from curvature or crookedness.
Fourth is the matter of the hands being aligned: the two hands face each other, with the right hand below and the left hand above, or the left hand below and the right hand above.
After one day has passed, they change and transform one after another without being lost or forgotten;
this is also because his hands are placed upon the bases.
Fifth is the matter of the neck: the substance of his neck is upright and motionless, for it is established in meditative concentration.
Sixth is the matter of the face: the features of his face are neither upturned nor downturned, so as to maintain a level appearance.
Seventh is the matter of the mouth: the features of his mouth are neither too wide nor too narrow, for its opening is centered.
Eighth is the matter of the nose’s characteristics: it emits the inhalation and exhalation of breath without discrepancy, because it does not emit [the breath] unevenly.
Ninth is the matter of the eyes’ characteristics: the dimensions of the eye-faculties are neither too high nor too low, being spread out in equilibrium.

Tenth is the cessation of the activity of the eyes: one places them in their respective locations within the wheel of the syllables of the Great Void (*mahā-ākāśa*), because they are never separated from it.
These are called the ten.

Regarding the timing and conditions for entering and exiting [the practice], it means that if one practices the gate of that wheel of cessation (*śamatha-cakra*), one uses only the two periods of dawn (*bhaṭṭā*) and noon (*madhyāhna*), as there is no entering or exiting during the remaining times.

Regarding the phrase "the causes and conditions for knowing virtuous friends": this refers to having those of profound wisdom as one's companions when practicing the gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*.

Regarding the phrase "knowing through the seal the causes and conditions of the false and the true": this refers to when practicing the gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*, one must employ the vajra-seal according to the measure of the reflected image; by doing so, one immediately comes to discern what is false and what is true.
What are its characteristics?
They are as follows, reciting the mantra:

*Taṇḍita hoṇa-udate parakīṭani cakhini-taye am-aśite na svāhā*. Once this divine mantra has been recited four thousand six hundred and fifty times, two syllable-wheels (*akṣara-cakra*) will then appear within that image: a wheel of the syllable "Ya" for those who are heterodox, and a wheel of the syllable "Sa" for those who are upright and honest; by this they are distinguished.

Regarding the "causes and conditions for planting the forest of virtuous trees," this refers to the planting of two kinds of great auspicious grass before and within one's own dwelling for the sake of those who practice the gateway of the wheel of *śamatha*.
What are the two? First, pine wood; second, pomegranate wood—these are called the two.

Regarding the "causes and conditions for wearing the wheel of syllables," this means that if one is a person practicing the gateway of the wheel of cessation (*śamatha*), they must certainly wear the wheel of the syllable *Bhrūṃ*.
Where is it worn? It is said to be at the "square-inch" location [the heart].
For what reason must this wheel be entrusted to this place?

This is because this wheel of syllables is the great benefactor of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, of all infinite and boundless Bodhisattvas, of great benevolent teachers and elders, of great benevolent parents, of great benevolent Heaven and Earth, and of the great benevolent ocean.
For these reasons, this wheel should be entrusted to those who practice *śamatha*.

Although such reasons are immeasurable, this Mahāyāna treatise clarifies only the primary reason and does not explain the others; this is simply because citing the first encompasses the subsequent ones.
As in the original [text]: "If one practices *śamatha*, one dwells in a quiet place.

Thus, the section on the causes and conditions for accomplishing the wheel of *śamatha* has been explained; next, the section on the direct demonstration of the practice of the wheel of *śamatha* will be explained.
Within this section, there are seven gates. What are the seven?
First is the gate of the resolute mind, for the mind is fixed upon the principle of true emptiness, which is neither born nor extinguished.
First, because one sits upright with right intention as in the original [instruction].
Second, regarding the gate of non-attachment to the body: one is able to skillfully penetrate that this body is empty and non-existent, for its fundamental self-nature cannot be apprehended.

As it is said in the original: "Because one does not rely on the inhalation and exhalation of breath, does not rely on form and color, does not rely on space, and does not rely on earth, water, fire, or wind;

thirdly, because one does not cling to the gateway of mind-consciousness, being able to skillfully penetrate and realize that the nature of the deliberating and knowing mind is empty and non-existent, having nothing at all."

As in the original text, up to the point where one does not rely on seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, all conceptualizations and recollections are eliminated, because even the notion of elimination itself is discarded.
From this point onward, one brings about the emptiness of body and mind, which is devoid of causes and conditions.

As it is said in the original text: because all dharmas are fundamentally without marks, arising not in every thought-moment and ceasing not in every thought-moment, and because one cannot follow the mind to dwell upon external objects.
Fourth is the gate of non-attachment and non-attaching, because the mind that is capable of dispelling [distractions] is itself also eliminated.
As the original text states: "Thereafter, one uses the mind to eliminate the mind.
Fifth is the gate of the convergence of gathering and dispersal, because it gathers the scattered and moving mind and places it within oneness.
As it says: "If the original mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately collect it and abide in right mindfulness.
Sixth is the gate that reveals right mindfulness, which reveals that all phenomena are but a single mind.

One who possesses right mindfulness from the outset should know that there is only mind and no external objects; furthermore, this very mind lacks any intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it cannot be apprehended in any single moment of thought.
Seventh is the gate of constant practice without separation; for such a concentrated mind is never abandoned or severed, remaining in continuous succession at all times and in all places.

As stated in the original text: "If one rises from one's seat, whether going, coming, advancing, or stopping, at all times one constantly maintains mindfulness of skillful means and observes accordingly.
Thus, the gate of directly demonstrating the practice of the wheel of *śamatha* has been explained; next, the gate of the benefits gained from practicing the wheel of *śamatha* will be explained.

This means that if there is anyone who can cultivate this samādhi, gradually progressing further and further, they will exhaust the ocean of afflictions, topple the mountain of karmic obstructions, enter the samādhi of true thusness, realize all dharmas, and reach the stage of non-retrogression.

As it is said: "Because one has long practiced until it is thoroughly matured, the mind attains stability; through this stability of mind, it gradually becomes sharp and intense, allowing one to enter the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā) in accordance with it. Thus, afflictions are deeply suppressed, faith increases, and one swiftly achieves the stage of non-retrogression."

The section on the benefits gained from practicing the wheel of *śamatha* has already been explained; next, the section on distinguishing between those who enter and those who do not will be explained.
Within this section, there are two points. What are these two?
First is the inclination toward entry, and second is the lack of inclination toward entry.
Regarding the inclination toward entry: it refers to those sentient beings who enter into the profound Dharma with minds free from doubt;
or those sentient beings who, upon hearing the most profound Dharma, their minds become resolute and do not give rise to disbelief.
There may be sentient beings who, upon hearing the profound Dharma, immediately revere it and do not give rise to slander;
there may be sentient beings who lack heavy karmic obstructions; there may be sentient beings who lack a mind of pride; and there may be sentient beings who lack a mind of indolence.
Thus, these six types of persons enter the Buddha-lineage with certainty and without doubt; this is what is meant by "entering the intent.

As for those who do not enter the intent, it refers to those sentient beings who, being contrary to these six [conditions], permanently sever the seeds of the Triple Gem with certainty and without doubt; this is what is meant by "not entering the intent."

As stated in the original text: "It is because those such as these—namely, those who harbor doubt, lack faith, slander [the teaching], possess the karmic obstructions of grave offenses, are arrogant, or are indolent—are unable to enter."
Having already explained the gate of brief questions and detailed answers presented in a scattered manner, next is explained the gate of praising the excellence of samādhi.
Within this gate, there are two sub-gates. What are these two?
First is the gate of the boundless excellence of the essence, and second is the gate of the inexhaustible excellence of the retinue; these are called the two.

Regarding the gate of the boundless excellence of the essence: by practicing this samādhi, one penetrates all the infinite dharmas of the Buddhas, for they are of the same substance, a single characteristic, and without distinction.

As stated in the original text: "Furthermore, by relying on this samādhi, one realizes that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic; namely, that the dharma-body of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings are equal and non-dual. This is precisely what is called the 'samādhi of one practice.'"

Regarding the gate of the inexhaustible excellence of the retinue: it refers to the samādhi of suchness, which serves as the true foundation for all immeasurable and boundless vajra-samādhis, being able to give rise to and increase them.
As stated in the original text: "One should know that suchness (*tathatā*) is the root of samādhi, for if a person practices it, they will gradually be able to give rise to immeasurable samādhis.
*Śikṣānanda’s Commentary on the Mahāyāna*, Scroll Eight;
