Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that *śamatha* (calm abiding) can only be established in dependence upon *vipaśyanā* (insight), and is not calm abiding by its own nature; and that *vipaśyanā* can only be established in dependence upon *śamatha*, and is not insight by its own nature; for there is neither *śamatha* nor *vipaśyanā* [independently].

Furthermore, this is intended to demonstrate that calm abiding (*śamatha*) is itself insight (*vipaśyanā*), and insight is itself calm abiding, because calm abiding and insight are of one essence and without distinction.
This should be carefully examined and discerned according to their respective order.

Because he has originally given rise to such a vow, at all times and in all places, he practices and studies all forms of wholesome virtue according to his capacity, never abandoning them, with a mind free from indolence, except when sitting and single-mindedly attending to *śamatha*.

If there is anything else whatsoever, one should observe all that which ought to be done and that which ought not to be done; whether walking, standing, lying down, or rising, one should always practice both śamatha and vipaśyanā together.

That is to say, although one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen, one simultaneously contemplates that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the karmic actions of good and evil and their retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed.
Although one contemplates the retribution of good and evil karma through causes and conditions, one simultaneously realizes that their intrinsic nature is ungraspable.
Having explained the gate of the two wheels turning together without separation, next is explained the gate of revealing what the two wheels counteract.
If there is a practitioner who cultivates the wheel of *śamatha*, what faults does it serve as an antidote for?

It serves as an antidote to the fault of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who cling to existence, and the fault of those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who delight in emptiness; it is because it completely severs and abandons both.

As stated in the original text: "If one practices *śamatha*, it serves as an antidote to the ordinary person’s attachment to the world and enables the abandonment of the timid views of the two vehicles.
Now, if a practitioner cultivates the wheel of *vipaśyanā*, what faults does it serve as an antidote to?

This means that it serves as an antidote to the fault of inferiority found in those of the two vehicles, who distance themselves from great compassion and fail to rescue beings from their manifold sufferings;

and to the fault of delighting in evil found in ordinary beings, who are constantly indolent, unable to exert diligence, and fail to cultivate wholesome qualities—since both [the Great Vehicle and the Lesser Vehicle] lead to liberation.

As stated in the original text: "If one practices contemplation, it serves as an antidote to the fault of the two vehicles' failure to give rise to great compassion and their narrow-mindedness, and it keeps one far removed from the ordinary person's failure to cultivate roots of goodness."
Having already explained the gate of revealing the defects that are remedied by the two wheels, next is explained the gate of summarizing the simultaneous operation of the two wheels.
This summary is provided because of the great faults incurred when one practices while deficient in either wheel as described above.

For this reason, as stated in the original text, these gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā mutually assist and perfect one another and are not to be separated; for if śamatha and vipaśyanā are not complete, there is no way to enter the path to bodhi.

Having already explained the gate of benefit and loss regarding the presence or absence of the two wheels, next is explained the gate of exhorting the inferior toward the superior so as not to regress.

The original text says: "Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds may become timid and weak. Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they fear that they cannot always encounter the Buddhas to personally receive and make offerings to them; they dread that the faculty of faith will be difficult to perfect and thus intend to retreat. One should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to protect and sustain the faculty of faith: namely, by means of the causal condition of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one shall, according to one's vow, be born in the Buddha-lands of other directions, where one constantly sees the Buddhas and is forever separated from the evil realms."
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates their cultivated roots of goodness with the vow to be born in that world, they will immediately attain rebirth there; because they constantly behold the Buddha, they shall never fall back."

If one contemplates that Buddha’s *tathatā*-dharma-body and constantly and diligently practices it, one will ultimately attain birth [therein], because one abides in right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The Commentary states:
Within this passage, there are seven sections.

What are the seven? First, the gate of demonstrating the approach to the provisional person; second, the gate of taking refuge in the teachings to be studied; third, the gate of the decline of faith due to aversion toward one's dwelling place; fourth, the gate of the Tathāgata’s superior skillful means; fifth, the gate of attaining a supreme and wondrous state through the power of reliance; sixth, the gate of attaining a stable state in a good realm from which there is no regression; seventh, the gate of citing sūtras to corroborate what has been taught. These are called the seven.

Regarding the statement "displaying the gate of approaching the provisional person," this refers to displaying those inferior sentient beings who have attained the four types of mind prior to the stage of the ten faiths but do not further advance.
As stated in the original text:

"Furthermore, regarding sentient beings," it says that those of the lower grade among the ten stages of faith take refuge in the gates of the teachings to be studied because they are beginners learning the profound and boundless Mahāyāna.

This refers to that which all Buddhas take as their teacher: it is unmoving throughout the three periods of time and unchanging through the four marks [of existence], for it is the naturally and eternally abiding great path prior to and upon the stages.
As it says in the original text regarding those who first study this Dharma:

"Those who feel aversion toward their dwelling place and regress from the gate of faith" refers to sentient beings at the lower grade of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Although they have personally heard and received this profound Dharma-gate, because their mental faculties are extremely inferior, they fear the two great matters and are unable to advance; thus, they are prone to regression.
What are these two? First, the land; second, the superior conditions.

Regarding the land, it refers to this Sahā world, where the environment is coarse and evil and sentient beings are turbid and chaotic; thus, to give rise to a pure mind and diligently engage in practice is extremely difficult and urgent.
Why is this so? Because within that mind, adverse objects are constantly and eternally present at all times and in all places, for they are never abandoned from the very face of the advancing mind.

Regarding "superior conditions": in this world, where both the environment and its inhabitants are turbid and chaotic, the appearance of all Buddhas in the world is extremely rare, and the timing for immeasurable Bodhisattvas to respond to and meet sentient beings is exceedingly remote.
The appearance of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the world corresponds to whether the mirror of the sentient being’s mind is pure or impure.
For this reason, when those practitioners do not encounter superior conditions and experience extreme fear, they give rise to the intention to retreat.

This is because those who originally sought right faith find their minds timid and weak; dwelling in this Sahā world, they fear that they will not always be able to encounter the Buddhas to personally receive and make offerings to them, and they dread that the mind of faith will be difficult to perfect, thus intending to retreat.

Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata’s gate of superior skillful means," it refers to the fact that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess inconceivable, profoundly deep, and most sublime great skillful means; by virtue of this, they are able to skillfully sustain and protect the faith of those people, causing them to progress toward ever-greater excellence.
What is called the supreme and wondrous skillful means?
It is the skillful means of single-mindedly recollecting the Tathāgata.
How does one single-mindedly recollect?

This means focusing one's attention on the various aspects of the environment and inhabitants of the Pure Lands in other directions, maintaining that mindfulness in a continuous stream so that it does not cease.

As the original text states: "One should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to protect and sustain faith; this is because of the causal condition of single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha."

Regarding the gate of attaining the supreme and wondrous state through the power of reliance: it is because, by means of the inconceivable power of skillful means of all Tathāgatas, one attains rebirth in the Land of Wondrous Bliss in accordance with one's own vows.
As it is said in the original [text], one attains birth in a pure land of another direction in accordance with one's vows.

Regarding the statement "attaining the gate of certain non-retrogression in a favorable place": having been born in that land, one beholds with the eyes the Tathāgata endowed with the marks and signs; hears with the ears the holy ones proclaiming profound and wondrous sounds; and is forever free from ill repute. Remaining unmoved from meditative concentration, the ocean of the mind becomes clear and pure, and the body becomes bright and radiant, because one relies upon the wondrous, correct, and pure state.
As it says in the original: "Because one constantly beholds the Buddha and is forever separated from the evil realms.

Regarding the statement that he cites sutras to prove his own exposition, this refers to the inclusion of the phrasing from the original sutra to which the characteristics of the teaching correspond, thereby praising the explanatory text of his own discourse.
Since the scriptural passage cited clearly explains the characteristics [of the practice], it need not be further expounded. As stated in the sutra:

"If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates their cultivated roots of goodness with the vow to be born in that world, they will immediately attain rebirth there; because they constantly see the Buddha, they shall never fall back."
If one contemplates the Tathatā-Dharmakāya of that Buddha and constantly and diligently practices it, one will ultimately attain birth there, because one abides in right concentration.
Having explained the section on practicing faith, next is explained the section on the benefits of encouraging practice.
The text states:
"Thus have I fully expounded this Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas.

If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to right faith regarding the profound realm of the Tathāgata, and who, free from slander, enter the path of the Mahāyāna, they should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it; in the end, they will be able to reach the unsurpassed way."

If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to cowardice or weakness, you should know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and will surely receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas.

Even if someone were able to transform all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm so that they practice the ten wholesome paths, it would not equal a person who, for the duration of a single meal, correctly contemplates this Dharma; the latter’s merit surpasses the former beyond comparison.
Furthermore, if a person upholds this treatise and observes and practices it for even a single day and night, the resulting merit will be immeasurable, boundless, and beyond description.
Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to praise their merits for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, they could not exhaust them. Why is this?
This is because the qualities of the *dharmatā* are inexhaustible;
the merit of this person is likewise thus, having no limit.
Any sentient beings who slander and do not believe in this treatise shall undergo great suffering for immeasurable eons as the retribution for their transgressions.

Therefore, sentient beings should simply rely on faith and must not disparage it; for to do so would deeply harm themselves as well as others, severing the seeds of the Triple Gem. This is because all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying upon this Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas enter the Buddha-wisdom by practicing according to it.

One should know that past bodhisattvas have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma; present bodhisattvas are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma; and future bodhisattvas shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma. Therefore, sentient beings should diligently practice and study it.
The Commentary states:
Within this passage there are eight sections.
What are these eight?

First is the section that summarizes what was previously explained; second is the section that exhorts others to practice by highlighting the benefits; third is the section that reveals the merit of faith and the avoidance of doubt; fourth is the section that demonstrates superiority through analogies and contrasts; fifth is the section that extols the merit of receiving and upholding [the teaching]; sixth is the section that instills fear by highlighting the faults of slandering; seventh is the section that extensively explains the excellence [of the teaching] while avoiding slander; eighth is the section that summarizes the practice and exhorts others—these are called the eight.
Regarding the statement "raising the previously explained summary gate," this means that a single general term is used to summarize the eight kinds of Mahāyāna.
For what reason are the remaining dharmas not summarized in this manner?
This is because it raises the root to encompass its branches;
that is, as the root is, so too is this Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas, which I have already explained in summary.

Regarding the statement on "raising the benefits to exhort others toward the gate of cultivation": it means that by accumulating the ocean of causal practices, one adorns the fruit of the Dharmakāya; thus, one should uphold this treatise and contemplate its principles, maintaining them constantly and continuously without interruption.

As stated in the original text: "If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to right faith regarding the profound realm of the Tathāgata, and who, free from slander, enter the path of the Mahāyāna, they should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it; for by doing so, they will ultimately reach the unsurpassed way."

Regarding the statement "the gate of manifesting the merit of faith that dispels doubt": it means that when sentient beings hear this Mahāyāna Dharma-gate of profound, supreme, and vast excellence, their minds neither harbor doubt or fear, nor do they feel cowardice; they neither despise nor slander it. They give rise to a mind of certainty, a firm mind, a mind of reverence, and a mind of loving faith. One should know that such persons are truly the children of the Buddha; they do not sever the lineage of the Dharma, the lineage of the Saṃgha, or the lineage of the Buddha. Constantly and perpetually continuing, they increase further and further until the end of the future. Furthermore, they are personally granted predictions of enlightenment by all Buddhas and are protected and remembered by all immeasurable Bodhisattvas.

As stated in the original: "If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to cowardice or weakness, one should know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas, for they will surely receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas."

Regarding the statement that "analogy serves as a superior gateway for demonstration," this means that even if someone were able to skillfully guide and transform all sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm, leading them all without exception to practice the ten wholesome paths of action, it might still be that another being, for the duration of a single meal, contemplates and reflects upon this profound Dharma.

If one were to compare the merits of these two individuals, the merit obtained by the first person would be exceedingly minute, like the measure of a single fragment of a mustard seed broken into a hundred parts.
The merit obtained by this second person is exceedingly vast and great, for it is like the number of atoms in the dust of the worlds of the ten directions.

As the original text states: "Even if someone were able to transform all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm so that they practice the ten wholesome paths, it would not equal a person who, for the duration of a single meal, correctly contemplates this Dharma; the latter's merit surpasses the former beyond comparison."

Regarding the "Gate of Praising the Merit of Receiving and Upholding": this means that if there is a person who receives and upholds this treatise and contemplates its principles for even a single day or a single night, the merit attained therein will be immeasurable and boundless, beyond words and beyond calculation.

Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and three periods of time, were each to use tongues as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions to praise all the merits of that person for as many unspeakable eons as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions, they would still be unable to exhaust them.

Why is this so? Because the merits of the Dharmakāya and True Suchness are equal to the realm of empty space and are without limit; how much less could ordinary persons or those of the two vehicles be able to praise them?

If a person who upholds [this teaching] for even a single day and night obtains inconceivable merit, how much more so if they uphold, recite, contemplate, and investigate it for two days, three days, four days, or even up to a hundred days? It is inconceivable beyond the inconceivable, for it is unspeakable within the unspeakable.

As stated in the original text: Furthermore, if a person upholds this treatise and observes and practices it for even a single day or a single night, the merit they acquire will be immeasurable, boundless, and beyond description; even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to praise that merit for immeasurable, boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they could not exhaust it.
Why is this? It is because the qualities of the dharma-nature are inexhaustible.
The qualities of this person are likewise so, for they have no limit.

Regarding the "gate of raising the fault of slander to instill fear," this refers to those sentient beings who, toward these teachings of the treatise, give rise to a lack of faith, engage in refutation and slander, and fail to practice accordingly; because the retribution for the sins such beings incur consists of the most grievous sufferings among all possible sufferings for unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas.
As stated in the original text: because sentient beings who disparage and lack faith in this treatise will undergo great suffering for immeasurable eons as the retribution for their sins;
therefore, sentient beings should merely look up to it with faith and not engage in slander. This is the summary of the preceding analysis and exhortation to practitioners.
From this point onward, the causes and conditions are established to demonstrate the grave faults [of such behavior].

That is to say, within this Dharma, those who lack faith and engage in slander lose their own roots of goodness and damage the merit of others; they sever the seeds of the Triple Gem, for which there will be no period of renewal.
As stated in the original text, this is because [denying it] deeply harms oneself and also harms others, thereby severing the seeds of the Three Jewels.

Regarding the "exalted and extensive explanation of the door of avoiding slander," it means that all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have all taken the Mahāyāna as their fundamental basis for attaining perfect enlightenment; and all immeasurable Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have all taken the Mahāyāna as their fundamental basis for possessing the ocean of causes.

Regarding such profound and deep Mahāyāna teachings, if there are sentient beings who give rise to a lack of faith, engage in contentious debate, or slander them, such beings are also said to have destroyed all Buddhas, to have destroyed all Bodhisattvas, and to have severed the Tathāgatagarbha—the primordial awakening of the Buddha.
As it is said: because all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying on this Dharma, and because all Bodhisattvas enter the Buddha-wisdom by means of its practice;

one should know that past Bodhisattvas have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma, present Bodhisattvas are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma, and future Bodhisattvas shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma.
"Therefore, sentient beings should diligently practice and study" is the concluding summary of the section on exhorting others to practice;
one should examine and discern this carefully.
Having already explained the section on the benefits of exhorting practice, next is explained the section on the universal distribution of dedication.
The root text says:

"The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now explain in its entirety according to my capacity; May this merit, in accordance with the nature of reality, Universally benefit the entire realm of sentient beings."
The treatise states:
Within this single verse, there are three types of gates.
What are these three gates called?

First is the gate of summarizing what was previously explained; second is the gate of expanding virtues to make them extensive; third is the gate of bestowing universal benefit upon sentient beings—these are called the three.
Within the first gate, there are two types. What are these two?

First, the gate that universally and collectively subsumes all the gates previously explained; second, the gate that reveals the characteristics of the syllables that constitute the teaching. These should be carefully examined in their respective order.

The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas refers to the comprehensive and general inclusion of the previously explained gates; that is to say, it universally encompasses the thirty-three fundamental categories of dharmas.
What is the meaning of this?
To speak of "all Buddhas" refers to the non-dual Mahāyāna Dharma. Why is this so?
This non-dual dharma manifests in that Buddha because his merit is superior.
As it is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"Because the Perfectly Round Ocean attains the supremacy of all Buddhas, no other Buddha can achieve a Perfectly Round Ocean that is inferior to it."
If this is so, why does the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (Flower Ornament Scripture) state as follows:

"The Buddha Vairocana takes the threefold world as his body and mind; since the threefold world encompasses all phenomena without exception, there is likewise nothing that is not encompassed by that Buddha’s body and mind."
Although Vairocana Buddha encompasses the three worlds, because there is both encompassing and non-encompassing, there is no fault.
What is called "profound" refers to the fundamental dharma of the two levels of the eightfold Mahāyāna.
For what reason is it called "profound"?
Because these two successive Mahāyāna dharmas are extremely profound from the perspective of the gateway through which one enters them.
For this reason, the designation "profound" is established; one should reflect upon and discern this with care.
Regarding the meaning of "vast and great" (*vaipulya*): this refers to the two successive methods of entry.
For what reason is it called the meaning of "vast and great"?

Because each of these two successive methods of entry can extensively broaden its own dharma, can magnify its own dharma, and can establish the names and meanings for its own dharma; for this reason, the designation "vast and great" is established.
Having already explained the general door that comprehensively subsumes what was previously taught, next is explained the door that reveals the characteristics of the syllables used by the speaker.

The statement, "I shall now explain in summary according to my capacity," refers precisely to this door that reveals the characteristics of the syllables used by the speaker; it means that by means of these general syllables, all various kinds of speech are universally sustained.
In the section on the Establishment of the Thesis (*siddhānta-vibhāga*), the term "Mahāyāna" is the general [designation], which is precisely this [treatise]. Why?
Because a single word universally sustains all explanations, as it is intended to manifest that this *Mahāyāna-śāstra* is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
Having already explained the door of summary that encompasses what was previously stated, next is explained the door of expanding and spreading merit so as to make it vast.

To say that "this merit is dedicated in accordance with the nature of reality" (dharmatā) is precisely the door of expanding and spreading merit so as to make it vast; this means that the merit one has personally performed is dedicated toward the three spheres.
What are these three? First is *tathatā* (suchness);
second is the dharma of the one mind; third is original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) as Buddha-nature. These are called the three.
For what reason are they dedicated toward these three locations?

That is to say, one dedicates [merit] to True Suchness (*tathatā*) because one wishes to equalize the merits one has performed; or one dedicates them to the single mind (*ekacitta*) because one wishes to expand the merits one has performed; or one dedicates them to original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*) because one wishes to clarify the merits one has performed.
One should know it thus; one should contemplate it thus.
What benefit is there in such dedication?
It is said: because it is manifold.
What is the meaning of this?
It is like taking a single atom and placing it within the great earth; the atom placed therein is equal to that great earth without any distinction. The dharma-gate of dedication is likewise.

Furthermore, it is like pouring a single stream of water into the great ocean; the stream of water poured in is equal to that great ocean without any distinction. The dharma-gate of dedication is likewise.
Furthermore, it is like when a single small vessel is broken, it immediately becomes equal to great empty space without distinction; the dharma-gate of dedication is also thus.
Having explained the gate of expanding merit to make it vast, next is explained the gate of universally benefiting sentient beings through giving.

To speak of "universally benefiting the entire realm of sentient beings" refers to the gate of universal benefit bestowed upon sentient beings; that is to say, by raising up vast and perfect merit, one brings benefit everywhere throughout the realm of sentient beings.
The Great Being, with a heart of joy, exhorted the ocean-like assembly of immeasurable Buddha-sons:
"I have already transcended the three stages of 'hair-tip' and 'triangle,' and have passed beyond the four roots of birth and death."
The first asaṃkhyeya kalpa has now reached its completion; you have entered the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
O sons of the Buddha, as is fitting for you, take the bright mirror of the original Śākya with both hands and hold it before the face of the seven consciousnesses as they scatter their thoughts.
Seeing the defilements of the six sensory realms, one washes away the faults of attachment to dharmas and the self.
O sons of the Buddha, if you act thus, the three bodies—the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, and the Emanation-body—will appear perfectly before you like the unfolding of the syllable *I*.
Furthermore, the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity—
Just as one enters a pond and fully brings forth [its waters],
so too did he descend into the great ocean and the palaces of the nāgas; there, according to his capacity, he gazed upon the oceans of various sūtras,
numbering one hundred lakṣas in total.
The immeasurable and boundless meanings of its various distinctions are fully explained, encompassed, and established within the formal presentation of this Mahāyāna treatise.
Whoever holds the volume of this treatise in their own hands is said to be holding a hundred lakṣas of sūtras.
If one recites from one's own mouth the text of the fundamental portion,

being called a "reciter of a hundred lakṣas of sūtras," the merit obtained by this person is such that all the Buddhas and the assembly of great bodhisattvas in worlds as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions would each extend tongues as numerous as those very atoms.
Even if one were to speak of it without ceasing for as many eons as there are atoms, one could not exhaust it;
how much less could one observe its underlying principles or contemplate the meanings expressed by its words?
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having conceived a lack of faith, slander this treatise,
the karmic offenses they incur will be as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions.
May all the Buddhas and the assembly of great Bodhisattvas each extend tongues as numerous as those atoms.
Even if one were to speak of this for as many eons as there are atoms, never ceasing, one could not exhaust it;
yet the transgressions of such a person are extinguished without remainder, for no Buddha can save them from that.
Therefore, the practitioner returns to the fundamental source; One should rely on this treatise and practice accordingly.
Truly, one must not give rise to a lack of faith, Nor slander the profound Mahāyāna teachings.
May this exhortation spread far and wide, Pervading all the myriad, ineffable lands.
The Commentary on the Mahāyāna by Śrīlāta, Scroll Ten.
